Title: Active Learning for Open-Set Object Detection with Large Multimodal Model
Venue: International Conference on Robotics and Computer Vision (ICRCV)
Abstract: Recently, open-set detection based on vision-language pre-training large models has garnered significant attention. Despite significant progress in solving the open-set detection problem, it has been observed that the few-shot or zero-shot capabilities of these models are not always sufficient. This is attributed to: 1. Lack of large-scale visual language datasets for specific areas such as healthcare, transportation, and industrial defects. 2. The absence of visual and language encoders capable of handling irregularly shaped objects in complex environments. 3. The imbalance between positive and negative samples. We explore active learning for open-set object detection with large vision-language pre-training models. While text information effectively conveys the abstract concept of common objects, visual information excels in illustrating novel objects through concrete visual representations. Recognizing the complementary strengths and weaknesses of both text and visual information, we combine text and visual uncertainty to identify the most informative samples for labeling, which can significantly enhance model performance. Our experimental results demonstrate the validity of the method.

Title: "Driving the Future of Metrology: Overcoming Big Challenges in SEM Calibration from the Smallest Scales to Drive Precision and Innovation in Advanced Manufacturing"
Abstract: In advanced manufacturing, precise measurements are crucial for ensuring the accuracy and quality of fabricated parts, particularly in fields like semiconductor production, materials science, and microelectronics. Scanning Electron Microscopes (SEMs) are indispensable tools for characterizing microstructures at the nanometer scale. However, calibrating SEMs—especially for longitudinal measurements (e.g., feature length and thickness) and amount of substance (e.g., composition or elemental analysis)—presents significant metrology challenges. Accurate calibration is essential to ensure reliable, reproducible measurements required for high-precision industrial production. A key challenge in SEM metrology arises from a misunderstanding of terminology. SEM manufacturers often use the term "calibration" to describe system adjustments, which, from a metrological perspective, are better termed "adjustments." Calibration, in metrology, refers to determining measurement accuracy by comparing instrument output with recognized standards. However, adjustments optimize system performance within inherent limits, without ensuring compliance with traceable reference materials. This confusion can lead to discrepancies in how SEM measurements are interpreted and undermine confidence in critical industrial applications. Further complicating SEM calibration are several factors: the complexity of electron beam interactions with samples, difficulties in establishing uniform, traceable standards, and limitations in current calibration methods. Longitudinal measurements, which assess the precise dimensions of structures in the scanning direction, are particularly prone to errors due to sample tilt, beam drift, and electron beam-induced distortions. Additionally, amount of substance measurements, such as elemental composition, depend on the accurate calibration of energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) or similar techniques against well-defined reference materials. Calibration uncertainties in these measurements can significantly affect manufacturing quality control. Recent advancements in SEM calibration focus on improving the accuracy and reproducibility of both longitudinal and amount of substance measurements. Innovations include nano-scale reference standards, automated alignment and drift correction technologies, and integration with complementary metrology tools like atomic force microscopy (AFM) and focused ion beam (FIB) systems. Software improvements in image analysis and signal processing have also enhanced measurement reliability, especially for complex geometries. However, the need for standardized, globally recognized calibration methods remains critical, especially to meet the growing demands for precision in industries like semiconductor fabrication and advanced materials engineering. Future calibration advancements are likely to incorporate artificial intelligence (AI) for real-time correction of errors and the use of high-accuracy, traceable standards at the atomic or molecular level. As devices continue to miniaturize and materials grow more complex, traditional calibration methods may no longer suffice, necessitating the development of new techniques. In conclusion, the calibration of SEM tools for longitudinal and amount of substance measurements is a significant metrology challenge in advanced manufacturing. Although recent research and technological advancements provide potential solutions, a unified, high-accuracy approach is essential to ensure consistent, reproducible measurements at the micro and nano scales. Addressing these challenges and clarifying SEM manufacturers’ terminology will profoundly impact industries where precision is critical, driving the next generation of manufacturing technologies.

Title: Uncertainty-aware hybrid framework for melt pool geometry prediction and process map development in Laser Powder Bed Fusion of Inconel 718
Abstract: Melt pool geometry governs porosity formation, inter-layer bonding, microstructural evolution, and residual stress development in Laser Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF), making its accurate prediction central to process qualification and process-window development. However, experimental qualification is resource-intensive, high-fidelity multi-physics simulations remain computationally expensive for large-scale parameter exploration, and reduced-order analytical models often lose accuracy near melting-regime transitions. Existing machine learning (ML) approaches provide deterministic predictions but do not explicitly address uncertainty or systematic prediction bias, limiting their reliability across different operating conditions and experimental datasets. This study presents an uncertainty-aware hybrid ML framework for melt pool geometry prediction and process qualification in L-PBF of Inconel 718 (IN718). Single-track and multi-track specimens were fabricated over a broad range of laser powers, scan speeds, hatch spacings, and layer counts and characterized using optical and scanning electron microscopy. The proposed framework combines k-fold ensemble regression with physics-informed directional classification, where the ensemble standard deviation serves as a physically interpretable uncertainty signal and is subsequently converted into a targeted bias-correction mechanism. The melt pool depth-to-width ratio (D/W) was adopted as a unifying descriptor linking melt pool morphology, thermal-gradient-driven grain growth direction, melting-regime transitions, and process-map development. The framework was trained using 68 experimentally measured melt pools and evaluated using an external dataset of 54 measurements compiled from published L-PBF IN718 studies, including validation and independent test datasets. Compared with established analytical models and polynomial curve-fitting baselines, the proposed approach improved predictive accuracy, enhanced cross-study generalization, and provided useful ensemble-based uncertainty estimates. Multi-track experiments further validated the maximum hatch spacing criterion for predicting lack-of-fusion onset from single-track measurements, achieving prediction errors below 6% and enabling the identification of defect-free processing windows. The results demonstrate that ensemble prediction uncertainty contains information related to regime-dependent model sensitivity and can be exploited to improve prediction reliability near conduction-transition-keyhole boundaries. Beyond the specific IN718 case, the proposed framework provides a potentially transferable strategy for uncertainty-aware process qualification and rapid process-window development and offers a computationally efficient foundation for digital twin development, in-situ monitoring, and future closed-loop control of metal additive manufacturing (AM).

Title: Data Analytics and AI
Abstract: Data analytics and artificial intelligence (AI) are transforming geotechnical monitoring by extracting insights from large sensor datasets. This chapter covers analytics objectives (trend detection, anomaly identification, and prediction) and data types (time-series, spatial, imagery, and point clouds). We discuss preprocessing: cleaning, labeling, and metadata standards. Exploratory analysis and visualization techniques are highlighted. Statistical methods (trend tests, change-point detection) and uncertainty quantification are reviewed. Time-series tools include filtering, smoothing, ARIMA, and Kalman filters (with equations). We survey anomaly detection approaches: simple thresholds, statistical tests, and unsupervised ML (clustering, PCA/autoencoders). Supervised learning for classification/regression (feature selection, model validation, and metrics like ROC/AUC) is covered. Deep learning methods (LSTMs/RNNs for sequences, CNNs/Transformers for images, PointNets for clouds) and physics-informed neural networks are introduced. Digital twins and the integration of ML with geomechanical models are discussed. Real-time analytics, streaming, and edge inference (MLOps) are addressed, as are alarm logic, false-positive management, and human-in-the-loop frameworks. We emphasize explainability, model validation, and regulatory guidance. Two worked examples illustrate a Kalman filter update and an ROC curve calculation. Tables compare algorithms (data needs, latency, interpretability), and a mermaid diagram shows an analytics pipeline. Case studies (slope failure warning, tailings instability, digital twin of a mine) demonstrate real-world AI use. Checklists (data preparation, model deployment) and a full References section are provided. AI’s promise in geotechnics is “step-change” improvements in efficiency and safety.

Title: 基于本征特征分解和多级融合的PCB缺陷检测模型，对抗图像不确定性
Towards Generalizable Representation Learning Across Domains
Abstract: Despite remarkable progress in deep learning, a major challenge remains: machine learning models often struggle to generalize to unseen domains under distribution shift. In real-world settings, data often differ from training conditions due to changes in lighting, sensor type, image resolution, and style. These differences can significantly degrade performance, highlighting the need for representations that are both robust and generalizable. This thesis addresses this challenge by developing a set of frameworks for generalization across domains in anomaly detection, deepfake detection, and vision-language image recognition. For anomaly detection, this thesis introduces ROADS, a robust prompt-driven framework for multi-class unified anomaly detection. ROADS is designed to address two major limitations of existing approaches: interference among anomaly classes and sensitivity to domain shifts. It incorporates hierarchical class-aware prompts to encode class-specific semantics and includes a domain adaptation component to improve robustness under varying conditions. As a result, ROADS improves both anomaly detection and localization performance, especially in out-of-distribution settings. Beyond conventional anomaly detection, this thesis further studies multimodal anomaly understanding using Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Qwen-AD addresses multi-task industrial anomaly understanding by reducing task interference and improving generalization across multiple anomaly-related tasks. In addition, RADAR improves the robustness of MLLMs for anomaly understanding at inference time without retraining. It enhances reliability under shifted conditions by estimating uncertainty, strengthening visual grounding, and refining model predictions to reduce language bias and hallucination. For deepfake detection, this thesis proposes FreqDebias, a framework designed to improve generalization to unseen forgery types. Many deepfake detectors rely on narrow spectral artifacts that do not transfer well across datasets or manipulation methods. FreqDebias reduces this spectral bias through a frequency-based augmentation strategy called Fo-Mixup and a dual consistency regularization that encourages consistent local and global representations. This leads to more robust and generalizable deepfake detection. For vision-language recognition, this thesis introduces Style-Pro, a style-guided prompt learning framework for models such as CLIP. It improves generalization by modeling style variation while preserving content and cross-modal alignment. As a result, the model adapts more effectively to unseen domains and classes while maintaining strong zero-shot performance. Extensive experiments validate the proposed methods across diverse benchmarks. The results consistently demonstrate improved robustness and generalization in anomaly detection, multimodal anomaly understanding, deepfake detection, and vision-language recognition under both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings. Together, these findings show that robust representation learning, modular adaptation, and inference-time refinement can substantially improve generalization across diverse domains and visual environments.

Title: QUANTUM PNT & INERTIAL NAVIGATION AT THE LIMIT From Atomic Time and Resilient Positioning to Quantum Inertial Sensing, Hybrid Sensor Fusion, and Verified Navigation Infrastructure
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Abstract: QUANTUM PNT & INERTIAL NAVIGATION AT THE LIMIT From Atomic Time and Resilient Positioning to Quantum Inertial Sensing,Hybrid Sensor Fusion, and Verified Navigation Infrastructure Feng Cheng-en (33) × Starli BOOK DESCRIPTION How can a vehicle know where and when it iswhen trusted external references degrade? QUANTUM PNT & INERTIAL NAVIGATION AT THE LIMITis a large-scale research architecture for the future of resilient navigation. It begins from a simple but difficult problem: Modern navigation systems often depend on trusted external references. Satellite signals. Network synchronization. Digital maps. Radio infrastructure. Known coordinate frames. Centralized correction services. These systems can perform extremely well. But what happens when those references become: unavailable, degraded, delayed, inconsistent, jammed, spoofed, outdated, or physically unreachable? This book explores the transition from navigation as a position servicetoward navigation as an autonomous evidence system. The central idea is: A mature navigation system should not merely estimate where it is. It should also know: which evidence supports that estimate, how reliable each source is, how those sources disagree, how uncertainty is changing, when confidence has fallen too far, when authority should be reduced, which fallback mode should activate, and how safe recovery should occur. The book therefore develops a three-coupling foundation: Atomic Time×Inertial Integrity×Multi-Sensor Fusion These three layers are treated as mutually dependent. Atomic time provides temporal continuity. Inertial sensing provides locally available motion evidence. Multi-sensor fusion provides diversity,cross-checking,context,and recovery pathways. Together,they create the foundation for navigation that can remain usefuleven when external reference infrastructure becomes unreliable. QUANTUM NAVIGATION RESILIENCE INDEX The book introduces a conceptual research framework: QNRI=Quantum Navigation Resilience Index Conceptually: QNRI=(Position Integrity×Timing Continuity×Navigation Autonomy) / (Drift+Calibration Burden+Infrastructure Dependence+Failure Exposure) QNRI is not proposed as a universal physical law,certification standard,or established navigation metric. It is a research and design frameworkfor exposing the tradeoffs hidden inside advanced navigation systems. A navigation architecture may achieve exceptional precisionwhile remaining: fragile, expensive, difficult to calibrate, dependent on external infrastructure, or difficult to recover after failure. The purpose of QNRIis to force these burdens back into the analysis. ATOMIC TIME AS MOBILITY INFRASTRUCTURE Time is one of the hidden foundations of mobility. Positioning, sensor fusion, network coordination, communications, traffic management, fleet synchronization, and autonomous decision-making all depend on reliable timing. This volume therefore treats atomic clocksnot merely as laboratory instruments,but as potential components of mobility infrastructure. The research extends into: atomic clock stability, time transfer, distributed synchronization, holdover, clock ensembles, timing integrity, clock disagreement, environmental sensitivity, and recovery after reference loss. The core question is: Can a mobility system preserve useful timingeven when its primary synchronization source disappears? RESILIENT PNT Positioning, Navigation, and Timingshould not be reduced to one satellite signal. This book studies: multi-source PNT, terrestrial backup systems, reference frames, coordinate integrity, map alignment, protection levels, integrity monitoring, opportunistic signals, and graceful PNT degradation. The objective is not: Never lose GNSS. The objective is: Remain safe and boundedwhen GNSS is lost. This distinction changes the architecture. A navigation system should have: known degraded modes, authority limits, recovery procedures, cross-checks, and explicit uncertainty growth models. QUANTUM INERTIAL NAVIGATION Quantum inertial sensing is one of the central technical domains of this volume. Major research directions include: atom interferometry, quantum accelerometry, quantum gyroscopy, phase stability, vibration rejection, dynamic range, interrogation time, dead time, scale-factor stability, and quantum-classical hybrid inertial systems. The question is not simply: Can a quantum inertial sensor measure accelerationor rotation more precisely? The more important question is: Can the full navigation systemuse that measurement reliablyinside a real moving vehicle? Field deployment changes everything. Real mobility includes: vibration, temperature variation, shock, electromagnetic interference, aging hardware, maintenance pressure, changing maps, motion-induced noise, intermittent connectivity, and incomplete calibration. Therefore: Fieldabilityis not a packaging detail. It is part of the scientific claim. DRIFT, BIAS, AND LONG-DURATION AUTONOMY Every inertial system accumulates error. The central problem is therefore not only precision. It is: How fast does uncertainty grow? The book develops research architectures around: inertial drift, bias estimation, online calibration, thermal bias, aging, error growth, mission duration, confidence decay, external correction intervals, integrity bounds, and long-duration autonomous navigation. A system that remains accurate for ten secondsis not automatically useful for: ten minutes, ten hours, ten days, or an interplanetary mission. Navigation autonomy must therefore be definedagainst time. MULTI-MODAL NAVIGATION EVIDENCE No single sensor should automatically be treated as truth. This book develops a navigation evidence architecturethat may include: radar, lidar, vision, inertial sensors, magnetic maps, gravity maps, radio references, terrain models, digital maps, atomic timing, and learned models. Each source carries: uncertainty, provenance, context, failure modes, and calibration history. When sensors disagree,the disagreement itself becomes evidence. The architecture asks: Which source should be trusted? Why? Under which conditions? For how long? What happens when several sources share the same failure? This leads toward: Evidence-Level Sensor Fusion. BAYESIAN STATE ESTIMATION Navigation is fundamentally an estimation problem. The book therefore explores: Kalman filtering, particle filtering, covariance consistency, multi-modal state estimation, integrity bounds, tail risk, distribution shift, and uncertainty propagation. The important principle is: Accuracy≠Integrity. A state estimate can be numerically close to truthwhile still being unsafeif its uncertainty model is wrong. The system must therefore knownot only what it estimates, but also: how uncertain that estimate is, whether the model assumptions remain valid, and whether the uncertainty bound is still compatiblewith the decision being made. AI SENSOR FUSION Artificial intelligence may become increasingly importantin navigation fusion. AI can assist with: complex sensor interpretation, context detection, adaptive weighting, anomaly detection, out-of-distribution detection, learned state representations, and route-specific fusion. But AI introduces a critical risk: confidence can become opaque. Therefore: AI Confidence≠Navigation Integrity. This volume explores: uncertainty-aware AI, model calibration, out-of-distribution detection, learned fusion benchmarks, classical baselines, human-readable alerts, model versioning, and integrity wrappers. The objective is not to make navigation more mysterious. It is to make advanced fusionmore usefulwithout hiding uncertainty. DIGITAL NAVIGATION TWINS A navigation system changes through time. Sensors age. Maps change. Calibration changes. Software changes. Models change. Hardware is replaced. Incidents occur. A Digital Navigation Twincan preserve this evolving state. The book develops navigation twins around: sensor configuration, calibration history, map versions, software versions, prediction history, decision history, maintenance history, uncertainty history, incident replay, and counterfactual replay. The twin is not the physical vehicle. Its value lies in preserving: what the system believed, why it believed it, what evidence existed, what decision followed, and how the model changed afterward. This makes navigation memorya research infrastructure. GNSS-DENIED AND DEGRADED NAVIGATION Some of the most important navigation problems appearwhen trusted infrastructure fails. The book studies: GNSS denial, jamming, interference, spoofing, sensor deception, map poisoning, time spoofing, reacquisition, state reconciliation, and staged recovery. The desired architecture is not: Perfect Resistance. It is: Bounded Failure. A mature system should transition through known states: Normal Operation →Degraded Confidence →Reduced Authority →Fallback Navigation →Recovery →Verified Return to Service This turns resiliencefrom a vague promiseinto an observable sequence. BOUNDED AUTONOMY Autonomous navigation should not imply unlimited machine authority. The book therefore develops: Bounded Autonomy. An automated navigation decision should carry a clear authority scope: What may the system change? For how long? Under which conditions? With which confidence level? Who may override it? What is the recovery route? When uncertainty rises,authority should not remain constant. Conceptually: Uncertainty ↑→Authority ↓ This becomes especially importantin: autonomous vehicles, aviation, rail systems, maritime transport, robotic fleets, and future planetary mobility. The book therefore explores: Kalman filtering, particle filtering, covariance consistency, multi-modal state estimation, integrity bounds, tail risk, distribution shift, and uncertainty propagation. The important principle is: Accuracy≠Integrity. A state estimate can be numerically close to truthwhile still being unsafeif its uncertainty model is wrong. The system must therefore knownot only what it estimates, but also: how uncertain that estimate is, whether the model assumptions remain valid, and whether the uncertainty bound is still compatiblewith the decision being made. AI SENSOR FUSION Artificial intelligence may become increasingly importantin navigation fusion. AI can assist with: complex sensor interpretation, context detection, adaptive weighting, anomaly detection, out-of-distribution detection, learned state representations, and route-specific fusion. But AI introduces a critical risk: confidence can become opaque. Therefore: AI Confidence≠Navigation Integrity. This volume explores: uncertainty-aware AI, model calibration, out-of-distribution detection, learned fusion benchmarks, classical baselines, human-readable alerts, model versioning, and integrity wrappers. The objective is not to make navigation more mysterious. It is to make advanced fusionmore usefulwithout hiding uncertainty. DIGITAL NAVIGATION TWINS A navigation system changes through time. Sensors age. Maps change. Calibration changes. Software changes. Models change. Hardware is replaced. Incidents occur. A Digital Navigation Twincan preserve this evolving state. The book develops navigation twins around: sensor configuration, calibration history, map versions, software versions, prediction history, decision history, maintenance history, uncertainty history, incident replay, and counterfactual replay. The twin is not the physical vehicle. Its value lies in preserving: what the system believed, why it believed it, what evidence existed, what decision followed, and how the model changed afterward. This makes navigation memorya research infrastructure. GNSS-DENIED AND DEGRADED NAVIGATION Some of the most important navigation problems appearwhen trusted infrastructure fails. The book studies: GNSS denial, jamming, interference, spoofing, sensor deception, map poisoning, time spoofing, reacquisition, state reconciliation, and staged recovery. The desired architecture is not: Perfect Resistance. It is: Bounded Failure. A mature system should transition through known states: Normal Operation →Degraded Confidence →Reduced Authority →Fallback Navigation →Recovery →Verified Return to Service This turns resiliencefrom a vague promiseinto an observable sequence. BOUNDED AUTONOMY Autonomous navigation should not imply unlimited machine authority. The book therefore develops: Bounded Autonomy. An automated navigation decision should carry a clear authority scope: What may the system change? For how long? Under which conditions? With which confidence level? Who may override it? What is the recovery route? When uncertainty rises,authority should not remain constant. Conceptually: Uncertainty ↑→Authority ↓ This becomes especially importantin: autonomous vehicles, aviation, rail systems, maritime transport, robotic fleets, and future planetary mobility. NAVIGATION METROLOGY A future navigation infrastructurerequires measurement continuity. Different sensors, vendors, hard

Title: A study of online melt pool, plume, and spatter tracking in laser powder bed fusion using DBSCAN
Abstract: Additive manufacturing offers unmatched design flexibility, but this advantage comes with inherent process uncertainties that can lead to defects affecting mechanical properties. Ensuring consistent quality requires reducing part-to-part variations, yet traditional ex-situ characterizations, such as X-ray computed tomography, are time-consuming and constrained by part complexity. To address this challenge, we propose a low-cost, in-situ monitoring framework utilizing unsupervised learning to detect and classify defects in Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF). Our approach leverages optical imaging data captured during printing to identify anomalies. In this study, image processing techniques, including contrast enhancement, normalization, and noise filtering, are applied to extract critical features such as melt pool, plume, and spatter behavior, which are key indicators of print stability. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is then used to reduce dimensionality while preserving key process variations. Subsequently, unsupervised clustering techniques, such as Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN), are applied to classify printing conditions to detect outliers indicative of defect formation. This study provides valuable insights into the relationship between in-situ monitoring data and defect formation in LPBF, demonstrating the feasibility of machine learning-driven real-time quality assurance. By correlating detected outliers with actual porosity and defects, this approach has the potential to reduce reliance on post-processing inspections, improve defect prediction accuracy, and enhance the reliability of additive manufacturing processes.

Title: Development of digital twin model for gas turbine
Abstract: Gas turbine power generation within the highly competitive National Electricity Market of Singapore (NEMS) demands rigorous dispatch compliance. Traditional static machine learning algorithms used for predictive maintenance often fail to capture the prolonged thermal momentum and heat soak effects of massive turbine components, leading to inaccurate forecasting and subsequent commercial dispatch penalties. To resolve this, this research develops an end-to-end Data-Driven Prognostic Digital Twin for a Mitsubishi M701F Combined Cycle Gas Turbine. The predictive intelligence of the system is driven by a novel hybrid Deterministic- Stochastic Meta-Learner. This architecture systematically combines the deep temporal feature extraction capabilities of a 1-Dimensional Convolutional Neural Network (1D- CNN) with a deterministic diurnal sine wave anchor to mitigate long-term prognostic drift. To elevate the system from a deterministic estimator to a probabilistic risk management tool, a custom Monte Carlo Dropout engine was engineered to generate mathematically rigorous 90% confidence intervals, visually quantifying prognostic volatility for control room operators. Evaluated using a strictly chronological Walk-Forward Validation strategy, the proposed 1D-CNN Meta-Learner decisively outperformed industry-standard static baselines (Random Forest and Histogram Gradient Boosting) across multiple operational time horizons. Most notably, during the critical 12-hour thermal transition period, the 1D-CNN maintained a highly robust 𝑅2 of 0.3989, whereas static models completely collapsed (𝑅2 = 0.0888) due to their inability to anticipate thermal inertia. At the 3-Day prognostic horizon, the Meta-Learner achieved a dominant 𝑅2 of 0.6665, bridging the gap between real-time anomaly detection and short-term maintenance scheduling. Finally, the software architecture was successfully operationalized into a full-stack web dashboard using Flask and HTML5 Canvas. To overcome the high computational latency inherent in Bayesian uncertainty quantification, a Batch Inference deployment strategy was engineered. This decoupled the deep learning backend from the user interface, ensuring instantaneous, lag-free telemetry rendering on standard industrial hardware. Ultimately, this thesis delivers a commercially viable, physics-consistent framework that equips plant operators with the foresight required to prevent generation shortfalls, thereby optimizing grid reliability and asset profitability.

Title: TopoCrackSAM: A Topology-Aware, Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuned Segment Anything Model for Multi-Class Pavement Distress Segmentation
Analysis of the discriminative generalized Hough transform as a proposal generator for a deep network in automatic pedestrian and car detection
Abstract: Many approaches have been suggested for automatic pedestrian and car detection to cope with the large variability regarding size, occlusion, background variability, and aspect. Current deep learning-based frameworks rely either on a proposal generation mechanism (e.g., “faster R-CNN”) or on inspection of image quadrants/octants (e.g., “YOLO”), which are then further processed with deep convolutional neural networks (CNN). We analyze the discriminative generalized Hough transform (DGHT), which operates on edge images, for pedestrian and car detection. The analysis motivates one to use the DGHT as an efficient proposal generation mechanism, followed by a proposal (bounding box) refinement and proposal acceptance or rejection based on a deep CNN. We analyze in detail the different components of our pipeline. Due to the low false negative rate and the low number of candidates of the DGHT as well as the high accuracy of the CNN, we obtain competitive performance to the state of the art in pedestrian and car detection on the IAIR database with much less generated proposals than other proposal-generating algorithms, being outperformed only by YOLOv2 fine-tuned to IAIR cars. By evaluations on further databases (without retraining or adaptation), we show the generalization capability of our pipeline.

Title: AI-Driven Analytical and Molecular Data Modeling for Environmental and Pharmaceutical Applications
Venue: Scholars International Journal of Chemistry and Material Sciences
Abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping chemical research by linking high-dimensional analytical signals with molecular, biological, environmental, and pharmaceutical information. This review synthesizes literature from 2018–2026 on chemometrics, machine learning, deep learning, graph neural networks, transformers, foundation models, multimodal learning, and generative systems. It examines data obtained from spectroscopy, chromatography, mass spectrometry, electrochemical sensors, hyperspectral imaging, process monitoring, molecular descriptors, fingerprints, SMILES, graphs, three-dimensional structures, proteins, and omics. Environmental applications include contaminant detection and quantification, suspect and non-target screening, source attribution, fate and transport prediction, ecotoxicity assessment, wastewater-treatment evaluation, and ecological-risk prioritization. Pharmaceutical applications encompass raw-material authentication, quality control, impurity profiling, formulation and drug-delivery optimization, continuous manufacturing, real-time release testing, virtual screening, molecular design, and ADMET prediction. Across both domains, AI improves nonlinear pattern recognition, structure–signal translation, candidate ranking, and multi-objective optimization; however, sophisticated models do not consistently outperform well-designed chemometric approaches, particularly with small or biased datasets. Major barriers include class imbalance, limited chemical diversity, data leakage, instrument variability, missing metadata, weak external validation, poor uncertainty calibration, limited interpretability, and regulatory concerns. Future progress requires FAIR multimodal datasets, independent validation, applicability-domain analysis, explainable and uncertainty-aware models, digital twins, federated learning, autonomous laboratories, human oversight, and sustainable computing for trustworthy scientific deployment.

Title: Research on power grid outage risk assessment and early warning model based on intelligent decision algorithm
Venue: International Journal of Systems Assurance Engineering and Management

Title: Intelligent Digital Twin Framework for Predictive Maintenance and Cognitive Analysis of Equipment and Inventory Flows in Smart Production Facilities
SEE-OOD: Supervised Exploration for Enhanced Out-of-Distribution Detection
Abstract: Machine vision systems have been increasingly adopted for defect inspection and classification in manufacturing. Beyond identifying pre-defined defect categories observed during training, these systems are desired to also detect new defect types that are Out-of-Distribution (OoD), which differs significantly from In-Distribution (InD) training data. Existing DNN-based OoD detection methods rely on predictive uncertainty or regularization on limited OoD samples, but they often overfit specific OoD samples and fail to generalize. To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes a novel generative adversarial approach that utilizes limited real OoD samples for supervised OoD sample generation with exploration of OoD space. Our method tackles two major challenges of existing works: first, it provides a supervised OoD generation scheme based on real OoD samples, unlike existing unsupervised methods that generate virtual outliers based on InD data; second, it simultaneously augments OoD samples and explores unseen OoD space, reducing the issues of insufficient real OoD samples and overfitting. The paper provides rigorous theoretical results to demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach. Comparison studies with state-of-the-art techniques demonstrate superior generalizability to unseen OoD data. Furthermore, we showcase its practical effectiveness in detecting new surface defects using a real-world 3D point cloud dataset of manufacturing defects.

Title: The convergence of AI, IoT, and big data for advancing flood analytics research
Abstract: Floods are among the most destructive natural hazards that affect millions of people across the world leading to severe loss of life and damage to properties, critical infrastructure, and the environment. The combination of artificial intelligence (AI), big data, and the Internet of Things (IoTs), has the potential to more accurately predict these extreme events and accelerate the convergence of advanced techniques for flood analytics research. This convergence—so called the Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT)—is transformational for both technologies and science-based decision making since AI adds value to IoT through interpretable machine learning (ML) while IoT leverages the power of AI via connectivity and data intelligence. The aim of this research is to discuss the workflow of a Flood Analytics Information System (FAIS; version 4.00) as an example of AIoT prototype to advance and drive the next generation of flood informatics systems. FAIS integrates crowd intelligence, ML, and natural language processing (NLP) to provide flood warning with the aim of improving flood situational awareness and risk assessments. Various image processing algorithms, i.e., Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), were also integrated with the FAIS prototype for image label detection, and floodwater level and inundation areas calculation. The prototype successfully identifies a dynamic set of at-risk locations/communities using the USGS river gauge height readings and geotagged tweets intersected with watershed boundary. The list of prioritized locations can be updated, as the river monitoring system and condition change over time (typically every 15 min). The prototype also performs flood frequency analysis (FFA) by fitting multiple probability distributions to the annual flood peak rates and calculates the uncertainty associated with the model. FAIS was operationally tested (beta-tested) during multiple hurricane driven floods in the US and was recently released as a national-scale flood data analytics pipeline.

Title: AI contribution to the monitoring and safety assessment of dams: Review and perspectives
Abstract: Structural health monitoring strategies are essential to support dam safety assessment, especially as aging processes and changes in environmental conditions increase uncertainty in the long-term performance of these strategic infrastructures. In recent years, Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning, has been increasingly applied to support the interpretation of monitoring data, driven by advances in algorithms as well as improvements in data acquisition and management. Most existing reviews on AI applications in dam engineering either adopt broad perspectives covering multiple disciplines or focus on specific techniques. In contrast, this article provides a surveillance-oriented narrative review, organizing the literature according to the main components of dam monitoring and the types of data involved, rather than exclusively by algorithm families. Three complementary areas are considered: continuous monitoring based on point-wise time series, vision-based inspection using RGB images, and full-field non-destructive testing based on optical techniques, with particular attention to infrared thermography and digital image correlation and the role of their outputs in supporting numerical model updating. For each area, the review discusses the surveillance tasks addressed, the types of methods currently adopted, and their main advances and limitations. Finally, open challenges and future research directions are outlined, with a focus on data integration, physical consistency, and interpretability in AI-assisted dam surveillance.

Title: Predicting Materials Failure Before It Happens: A Critical Review of AI for Multimodal Degradation Forecasting Under Coupled Environmental Stressors
Abstract: Infrastructure, energy, transportation and industrial materials are increasingly exposed to coupled thermal, moisture, chemical and mechanical stressors that can interact to produce nonlinear and history-dependent degradation. Conventional periodic inspection and single-stressor testing often provide limited information about the progression of damage and may fail to capture interactions that influence long-term material performance and failure. Artificial intelligence (AI) provides an opportunity to address these limitations by integrating heterogeneous information from sensors, imaging, experimental measurements, environmental monitoring and physics-based simulations. However, identifying existing damage is fundamentally different from forecasting its future evolution. This critical review examines the transition from AI-based damage detection toward temporal degradation forecasting, remaining useful life estimation and failure probability prediction under coupled environmental and mechanical conditions. Machine learning, deep learning, multimodal learning, physics-informed AI, digital twins, uncertainty quantification and explainability are critically evaluated in relation to their potential and limitations for materials degradation forecasting. Major translational challenges include limited longitudinal datasets, inconsistent experimental protocols, multimodal data alignment, limited cross-material and cross-environment generalization, uncertainty representation, interpretability and the laboratory-to-field gap. In response, an integrated framework is proposed that links environmental exposure and material state evolution with multimodal sensing, AI-based forecasting, physical constraints and uncertainty estimation. This framework provides a pathway toward proactive intervention by connecting predicted degradation trajectories and failure probability with risk-informed inspection and maintenance decisions.

Title: 《Fusion Materials at the Limit: Surviving 14-MeV Neutrons, Extreme Heat Flux, and Millions of Cycles》 is a flagship-scale research volume examining one of the most unforgiving engineering challenges in fusion energy:
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Abstract: 《Fusion Materials at the Limit: Surviving 14-MeV Neutrons, Extreme Heat Flux, and Millions of Cycles》 is a flagship-scale research volume examining one of the most unforgiving engineering challenges in fusion energy: Can reactor materials survive long enough, predictably enough, and maintainably enough to support an entire fusion industry? A fusion reactor does not expose its materials to a single extreme condition. It exposes them to many extreme conditions at the same time. 14.1-MeV neutrons produce displacement damage, transmutation, helium, and hydrogen. Plasma-facing surfaces experience intense heat flux, erosion, redeposition, thermal shock, and cyclic loading. Coolants introduce corrosion, chemistry, pressure, and compatibility problems. Structural materials must preserve strength while being irradiated. Joints and interfaces must survive differential expansion and repeated replacement. Components must remain inspectable, repairable, manufacturable, and compatible with remote maintenance. This book therefore treats fusion materials not as isolated samples, but as complete survivability systems. Its central engineering framework begins with: L_component = f(DPA, T, stress, heat flux, He, H, number of cycles) This formulation emphasizes that component lifetime is governed by interacting damage mechanisms rather than by any single material property. The book then develops the Fusion Survivability Index: FSI = (Normalized Lifetime × Normalized Availability) / (1 + Normalized Damage + Normalized Replacement Burden) The purpose of this index is not to declare one material universally superior. It is to ask a harder question: Which material system can survive, be monitored, be replaced, be manufactured again, and continue supporting plant availability over many operating cycles? The research examines reduced-activation ferritic-martensitic steels, EUROFER-class materials, oxide-dispersion-strengthened steels, tungsten, copper alloys such as CuCrZr, vanadium alloys, silicon-carbide composites, coatings, graded interfaces, liquid-metal concepts, and advanced plasma-facing materials. It also studies first walls, divertors, breeding-blanket structures, coolant channels, joints, welds, coatings, thermal barriers, liquid surfaces, replaceable modules, and remote-maintenance interfaces. A major theme of the work is damage interaction. Radiation damage cannot be evaluated independently from temperature. Thermal fatigue cannot be evaluated independently from neutron embrittlement. Tritium retention cannot be evaluated independently from erosion and surface morphology. Joining performance cannot be evaluated independently from transmutation, thermal expansion, and replacement frequency. The true engineering problem is therefore not maximizing one property. It is maintaining an acceptable operating envelope while multiple degradation mechanisms evolve simultaneously. The book develops more than sixty equations, indices, and engineering metrics addressing neutron damage, cyclic fatigue, helium and hydrogen production, erosion, armour lifetime, tritium inventory, weld qualification, coolant compatibility, damage synergy, remaining useful life, qualification coverage, remote replacement burden, materials circularity, supply-chain resilience, and fleet-scale survivability. Among these are the Damage Synergy Index, Cyclic Damage Accumulation, Armour Erosion Budget, Tritium Materials Inventory, Weld Qualification Margin, Fusion Neutron Qualification Coverage, Remaining Useful Life Posterior, Dose-Temperature Allowable Surface, and Fleet Materials Closure Ratio. The research eventually extends beyond individual components into a fleet-level framework: Fleet Fusion Materials Survivability This concept asks whether a future fusion industry can maintain a continuous supply of qualified materials, replacement modules, validated manufacturing processes, inspection capability, recycling pathways, and irradiation data across many plants. This distinction is essential. A component that survives one experiment is not necessarily suitable for a commercial reactor. A component that survives one reactor is not necessarily suitable for an industrial fleet. The book therefore distinguishes: Material performancefromComponent survival, Component survivalfromPlant availability, and Plant availabilityfromFleet sustainability. Another major focus is qualification infrastructure. Fusion materials require data under neutron spectra and operating environments that reproduce the relevant damage mechanisms of future reactors. This makes irradiation facilities, high-heat-flux testing, corrosion loops, joining qualification, multiscale modeling, accelerated testing, digital twins, and facilities such as IFMIF-DONES central to the long-term development pathway. The book also explores artificial intelligence and digital twins for materials engineering. Future fusion plants may require continuous estimation of component condition, damage accumulation, erosion, crack growth, thermal fatigue, hidden defects, and remaining useful life. AI may support predictive maintenance, inspection prioritization, surrogate modeling, materials discovery, anomaly detection, and replacement scheduling. However, predictive systems must remain uncertainty-aware, auditable, and grounded in validated materials data. Manufacturing is treated as part of materials science rather than as a separate downstream problem. A material that cannot be joined, shaped, coated, inspected, repaired, reproduced, or supplied at industrial scale may never become a practical fusion material. The research therefore includes additive manufacturing, powder metallurgy, joining, brazing, graded interfaces, modular components, quality control, supply chains, recycling, and design-for-replacement. The final section contains 200 Research Gates. Each gate identifies an unresolved research question and extends it through a structured pathway including a core question, three-coupling framework, research move, practical development stage, indicative horizon, and success signal. The Practical Stage framework classifies research pathways as: Now → Prototype → Pilot → Infrastructure → Long Horizon. Some Research Gates can already be explored through irradiation experiments, thermal-fatigue testing, high-heat-flux facilities, corrosion loops, joining studies, materials simulation, digital twins, manufacturing trials, and remote-maintenance prototypes. Others require fusion-relevant neutron environments, integrated blankets, pilot plants, long-duration irradiation databases, validated design codes, industrial manufacturing systems, and technologies that do not yet exist. Each Research Gate is designed as an entrance rather than a conclusion. In this sense, Fusion Materials at the Limit is not simply a book about finding stronger materials. It is a study of how fusion systems can survive damage, detect degradation, replace what fails, learn from every cycle, and continue operating across generations of machines. Because the decisive materials question for fusion may not ultimately be: Can this material survive? It may be: Can an entire fusion civilization remain maintainable, repairable, reproducible, and resilient even when its materials inevitably age? Damage → Detection → Repair → Replacement → Learning → Next Generation. Long Memory · Perpetual Transmission.

Title: Architecture Design of Large Model Systems in Vertical Fields for Multimodal Fusion
Venue: IEEE International Conference on Automation, Electronics and Electrical Engineering (AUTEEE)
Abstract: The application of multimodal artificial intelligence in vertical fields is confronted with three core challenges: modal heterogeneity, scarcity of domain data, and limitations of computing resources. To this end, this paper proposes a novel multimodal fusion system architecture for vertical fields. This system takes the Transformer encoder as the core fusion engine and achieves deep-grained cross-modal interaction through its inherent self-attention mechanism, effectively integrating visual and text information. Meanwhile, the system innovatively adopts low-rank adaptation (LoRA) technology for efficient domain fine-tuning of parameters, aiming to achieve high-performance domain adaptation with an extremely low number of training parameters. To verify the effectiveness of the system, we designed comparison and ablation experiments on multiple typical vertical tasks such as medical image report generation, industrial defect detection, financial risk control, and autonomous driving scenarios. The experimental results show that this system not only significantly outperforms the single-modal baseline in multimodal fusion performance, but also demonstrates significant advantages in computational efficiency, model robustness, and few-shot learning ability.

Title: A Bottom-Up Sampling Strategy for Reconstructing Geospatial Data from Ultra Sparse Inputs
Learning Normative Anatomy under Limited Supervision
Abstract: Medical image analysis faces a structural asymmetry because the abnormalities a model must detect are open-ended, while the annotations it can learn from are scarce, costly, and disputed by experts who disagree on what they see. This thesis responds by learning normative anatomy, a model of what is normal, from limited supervision, and by treating that model’s uncertainty as a clinically actionable output rather than an afterthought. Viewed as a pipeline, anomaly detection embeds an assumption about what counts as normal at every stage; the thesis intervenes at three of them: how the training signal is synthesised, how deviation is scored, and how error is evaluated. The contributions span the range of label availability. With no anomaly labels, the training signal must be manufactured, i.e., self-supervised synthesis is recast as a stochastic process, yielding a distribution of plausible anomalies that mirrors annotator disagreement and improving localisation on chest radiographs and CT while halving training time (Probabilistic Poisson Image Interpolation). Given a normative segmentation model, anomalies are instead read off its uncertainty, fusing aleatoric and epistemic estimates over a frozen ultrasound foundation encoder so that unseen congenital heart defects surface as calibrated, localised uncertainty in real time (L-FUSION). That scoring can also be cheap and a backpropagation-free network can carry an intrinsic, interpretable anomaly score at a fraction of the usual compute and adapts to the resources at hand (SaFF-AD). At the defined-but-rare end of the spectrum, where the target is known but positive cases are few, an asymmetric similarity replaces the symmetric decision boundary (Similarity Fields). Underlying all of them is a generative model that supplies the normal prior they presuppose, producing clinician-validated healthy anatomy where that distribution was previously unavailable and releasing it as a privacy-safe dataset (SynthUterus). These contributions share as response to the opening asymmetry that abnormality is open-ended and labels are scarce, the dependable thing to model is normality, and its uncertainty is information the clinic can use. Pursued across the supervision spectrum, this reframes annotator disagreement as signal, replaces fixed decision boundaries with learned normality, and fits the compute budgets of real deployment. The result is a coherent set of self-supervised, uncertainty-aware, and efficient methods that bring medical anomaly detection closer to trustworthy clinical use.

Title: Capacity-Matched Falsification of Physics-Constrained Variational Quantum Prognostics for GaN HEMT RF Power Amplifiers Under Tropical Thermal Stress — Reproducibility Package
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Abstract: This repository contains the reproducibility package for the study titled “Capacity-Matched Falsification of Physics-Constrained Variational Quantum Prognostics for GaN HEMT RF Power Amplifiers Under Tropical Thermal Stress.” The study presents a controlled, capacity-matched evaluation of a physics-constrained variational quantum circuit (VQC) for remaining useful life (RUL) prediction of GaN HEMT RF power amplifiers under thermally stressed operating conditions. The benchmark uses 120 heterogeneous power-amplifier channels, with 2,501 six-hour observations per channel, and evaluates generalization using grouped held-out channels. The primary executed experiment compares a 4-qubit physics-constrained VQC containing 79 trainable parameters with a parameter-matched classical multilayer perceptron (MLP79), using identical grouped evaluation conditions. The package contains the machine-readable results supporting the reported fold-level performance, paired statistical analysis, depth ablation, split-conformal uncertainty calibration, and advantage-gap/falsification-boundary analysis. The reproducibility package includes the manuscript, machine-readable result tables, fold-level benchmark results, model and dataset specifications, VQC configuration, statistical-analysis procedures, conformal-calibration results, advantage-gap diagnostics, extracted figures, checksums, citation metadata, and a confirmatory validation protocol. The repository distinguishes executed evidence from analyses and experiments that are specified but not yet executed. In particular, broader classical-baseline comparisons, full 120-channel leave-one-channel-out validation, multi-seed depth analysis, physics-loss ablation, and physical/noisy-quantum-hardware validation are identified as confirmatory or future work and are not presented as completed experimental results. The principal finding of the executed capacity-matched benchmark is negative: the VQC does not outperform the matched 79-parameter classical MLP. Across 12 grouped holdout evaluations, the VQC achieves a mean MAE of 1,563.4 ± 215.0 h compared with 1,170.8 ± 158.9 h for MLP79. The VQC therefore exhibits a 33.5% higher mean MAE, with the VQC having higher MAE in all 12 evaluated groups. The paired analysis reports a mean error difference of 392.7 h, a 95% bootstrap confidence interval of [296.0, 494.0] h, and an exact two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank p-value of 4.88 × 10⁻⁴. The repository is intended to support transparent verification, reproducibility, independent inspection, and responsible interpretation of the reported negative benchmark. It should not be interpreted as evidence that quantum machine-learning approaches are intrinsically unsuitable for reliability prognostics; rather, it provides a capacity-controlled falsification benchmark for the specific physics-constrained VQC formulation and experimental conditions studied. Where proprietary operational information would identify the underlying telecommunications operator or expose confidential infrastructure information, only the information necessary for reproducibility and methodological verification is provided.

Title: 《Quantum Habitability at the Limit: Can Persistent Intelligence and Virtual Civilizations Live on Quantum Infrastructure?》 is a flagship-scale research volume exploring one of the most unusual and forward-looking questions in quantum technology:
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Abstract: 《Quantum Habitability at the Limit: Can Persistent Intelligence and Virtual Civilizations Live on Quantum Infrastructure?》 is a flagship-scale research volume exploring one of the most unusual and forward-looking questions in quantum technology: Can persistent intelligence and virtual civilizations live on quantum infrastructure? The book does not treat the “quantum world” as a hidden place into which humans can physically move. Instead, it begins with a more rigorous engineering question: What happens when computation, memory, communication, simulation, identity, and long-duration virtual environments increasingly depend on quantum systems? Could a future artificial intelligence, persistent digital resident, or virtual civilization preserve continuity across fragile quantum hardware? Could memory survive decoherence? Could identity survive hardware replacement? Could institutions survive substrate migration? Could history remain interpretable when the infrastructure beneath it is probabilistic, error-prone, and constantly evolving? This book transforms the idea of “living in a quantum world” into a systems-engineering discipline: Quantum Habitability Engineering. Its core technological progression is: Quantum State → Logical Memory → Quantum Compute → Quantum Network → Persistent Agent → Virtual Habitat → Institution → Civilization. The central principle is simple: Quantum State ≠ Identity. And: State Preservation ≠ Civilization Continuity. A persistent civilization does not require every physical state to remain unchanged forever. Human civilization already persists despite continuous replacement of people, machines, buildings, media, and infrastructure. What matters is whether essential forms of continuity survive. The book therefore distinguishes: Physical continuity Logical continuity Identity continuity Memory continuity Agent continuity Institutional continuity Historical continuity Civilization continuity. The first major research framework is the Quantum Habitability Index: QHI = (Persistence_n × Coherence_n × Recoverability_n × Observability_n) / (1 + DecoherenceBurden_n + ErrorBurden_n + MaintenanceCost_n) The QHI is introduced as a research framework rather than a universal physical law. Its purpose is to ask whether a quantum-supported environment is sufficiently persistent, coherent, recoverable, observable, and maintainable to support long-duration computational existence. Coherence alone is insufficient. A highly coherent system that cannot recover from failure may still be uninhabitable. Strong error correction is insufficient if the physical, energy, cooling, and maintenance burden becomes unsustainable. Persistence is insufficient if the system cannot be observed, audited, migrated, or understood. Habitability therefore depends on multiple conditions remaining simultaneously acceptable. The book then develops the Quantum Civilization Habitability Index: QCHI = (QHI × IdentityContinuity_n × MemoryContinuity_n × AgentContinuity_n × Migration_n × Governance_n × Succession_n)^(1/7) The distinction between the two frameworks is essential. QHI asks: Can the substrate support persistent habitation? QCHI asks: Can what lives there remain continuous long enough to become civilization? Quantum memory forms one of the foundational domains of the book. Future quantum systems may require memories capable of storing, synchronizing, buffering, and distributing quantum states. But civilization-scale memory cannot depend on preserving arbitrary quantum states forever. Long-duration continuity may instead require layered memory architectures combining: Quantum memory Logical quantum information Classical archival storage Provenance records Error histories Migration records Human-readable interpretation. This leads to a broader principle: Long Memory requires more than storage. It requires provenance, correction, interpretation, and handoff. Quantum error correction therefore becomes more than a computational technique. Within the book, it becomes a form of habitat maintenance. Error syndromes become diagnostics. Logical qubits become protected state spaces. Fault-tolerant operations become infrastructure rules. Recovery becomes continuity under damage. The book asks: When should a system repair? When should it migrate? When should it reconstruct from verified state? How should uncertainty be preserved? How can error correction avoid erasing historically meaningful provenance? Fault tolerance therefore expands into a civilization concept: Continuity under damage. Quantum computing architecture forms another major layer. Superconducting qubits, trapped ions, neutral atoms, photonic systems, spin qubits, topological approaches, modular quantum computing, cryogenic control, and heterogeneous quantum-classical systems are examined through a habitability lens. The central question is not which architecture will ultimately dominate. It is: Which architectures can support persistent services across generations of hardware? A civilization cannot depend on one machine that must never disappear. It requires migration. This introduces the concept of substrate portability. A persistent agent may need to move: From one processor to another From one quantum architecture to another From one logical encoding to another From quantum execution to classical fallback From one network node to another From one data center to another From one hardware generation to its successor. Migration therefore becomes a fundamental habitability requirement. This connects quantum infrastructure directly with digital identity. A persistent AI resident may possess: A stable identifier Long-term memory Permissions Assets Relationships Institutional roles Delegated authority Commitments Reputation Historical provenance. If the underlying quantum substrate changes, which of these properties must remain continuous? The answer cannot simply be: Copy everything. Some information may be ephemeral. Some states may be private. Some memories may require correction. Some rights may expire. Some quantum states cannot be duplicated arbitrarily. Identity therefore becomes a layered continuity problem rather than a simple storage problem. Quantum networking forms another major technological domain. Future distributed quantum systems may depend on entanglement distribution, repeaters, quantum memories, transduction, routing, synchronization, authentication, classical control channels, and interoperable protocols. The book examines what happens when persistent agents depend on infrastructure that may be probabilistic, intermittent, heterogeneous, or geographically distributed. Connectivity is therefore treated as more than bandwidth. A quantum network may need to manage: Entanglement availability Fidelity Latency Quantum memory lifetime Routing success Classical coordination Authentication Recovery Fallback. A persistent habitat must degrade gracefully. If entanglement is unavailable, the civilization should not disappear. Critical functions may need classical backup. This creates the concept of hybrid habitability: Quantum when useful. Classical when necessary. Persistent across both. Virtual worlds form the conceptual center of the book. If some parts of such a world depend on quantum computation, quantum simulation, quantum randomness, or quantum networking, the world becomes a hybrid classical-quantum environment. This raises one of the book’s most important questions: When does a quantum computer stop being merely a machine and start becoming part of a place? The distinction is fundamental.
