Title: From Open Data to AI-Powered Digital Twins: The TPDC’s READY Framework for the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau
Abstract: Abstract:The Qinghai-Xizang Plateau, a pivotal regulator of global climate and hydrological cycles, hosts intricate multi-sphere interactions under accelerating global changes. Unlocking its full scientific potential requires not only open data sharing but also intelligent, AI-ready data governance. The National Tibetan Plateau Data Center (TPDC) has established a leading open-data ecosystem, hosting over 8,400 datasets (62% fully open access) totaling 674 TB, and implementing systematic FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) principles through automated lifecycle management, peer review, DOI assignment, and CC-BY licensing.To advance from open data to AI-powered digital twins, TPDC has pioneered the READY framework (Richness, Ethics, Accessibility, Diversity, Yield), bridging geoscience data with AI-driven discovery through three transformative systems: (1) AI-Ready Data Governance & Semantic Automation, implementing cross-sphere quality control and ethics reviews, while utilizing NLP and knowledge graphs for automated metadata generation and semantic annotation; (2) AI-Ready Data Engineering, achieving multi-modal spatiotemporal anchoring and cross-scale alignment to build hierarchical Earth system models, notably treating uncertainty as a ‘first-class object’; and (3) AI-Ready Data Service, shifting from auxiliary analysis to a model-oriented continuous data supply, creating a dynamic loop that supports foundation model training and enables integrated prediction-decision making.. These capabilities are strengthened by integrating data from the Second Tibetan Plateau Scientific Expedition and Research (STEP), historical archives, and international collaborations (e.g., NSIDC, ICIMOD, WMO), ensuring global interoperability and scientific robustness.TPDC’s data governance framework has underpinned over 8,000 SCI publications, enabling critical insights into climate adaptation, cryosphere-related hazards, and sustainable pathways. Ultimately, TPDC is committed to realizing the vision of ‘probing the past, assessing the present, and preparing for the future,’ providing robust, multi-scale predictions to support sustainable development and ecological security.Keywords: National Tibetan Plateau Data Center (TPDC); Qinghai-Xizang Plateau; AI-Ready Data; READY Framework; Digital Twins; FAIR Principles; Earth System ScienceReferences:Li, X., Cheng, G., Wang, L., Wang, J., Ran, Y., Che, T., Li, G., He, H., Zhang, Q., Jiang, X., Zou, Z., & Zhao, G. Title: Lessons from the Minab tragedy: protecting education in the age of AI-assisted warfare
Abstract: "The destruction of the Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab, Iran, on February 28, 2026, should force the international community to confront a painful truth: even the most technologically advanced militaries remain capable of catastrophic errors when civilians are insufficiently protected. This article aims to elaborate on lessons learned from Minab and similar tragedies, hoping that although the scientific community cannot by itself prevent wars, it can influence how evidence is gathered; technologies are developed; and accountability is pursued." On February 28, 2026, what began as an ordinary school day at Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School ended in unimaginable tragedy when United States and Israeli missiles "according to multiple public reports and ongoing investigations", struck the school grounds, causing the collapse of large sections of the building and trapping hundreds of children, teachers, and staff beneath the rubble. According to multiple independent investigations, at least 168 people were killed, many of them young students between the ages of seven and twelve [1][2][3][4][5][6][7][8].The school, known for serving children from the local community, was filled with students attending classes when the attack occurred. Witnesses described scenes of panic as explosions shook the area. Teachers reportedly rushed to protect their pupils, guiding them toward safer parts of the building and attempting to contact parents. Moments later, additional strikes reportedly hit the vicinity, turning the school into a scene of destruction and chaos. Rescue workers, emergency personnel, and local residents immediately began searching through the debris. Images and videos from the aftermath showed shattered classrooms, torn schoolbooks, children's backpacks, and desperate efforts to locate survivors. Families gathered outside the ruins, hoping for news of their children, while hospitals struggled to cope with the large number of casualties and injuries. Due to the distasteful and offensive real images of this catastrophe, an AI generated picture of Shajareh Tayyebeh elementary school before and after bombardment is shown in Figure 1 to virtually describe the level of crime and destruction.Figure 1. AI generated by ChatGPT [9].The tragedy sparked widespread grief across Iran and drew international attention. Human-rights organizations condemned the loss of civilian life and called for independent investigations into the circumstances of the attack. Several groups argued that schools are protected civilian sites under international humanitarian law and that all parties to a conflict must take every possible precaution to prevent harm to children. For the people of Minab, the attack left scars that extend far beyond the physical destruction of a school building. Classrooms that once echoed with laughter and learning became symbols of loss. Parents mourned children whose futures were cut short, classmates grieved friends they would never see again, and an entire community struggled to come to terms with the scale of the devastation.The Minab school tragedy stands as a painful reminder of the human cost of armed conflict. Regardless of political disputes and military objectives, the deaths of so many children underscore the profound consequences that war can have on civilians. As investigations and debates continue, the memory of the students, teachers, and families affected by the attack remains a powerful call for accountability, protection of civilians, and the pursuit of peace.The reported destruction of a school in Minab, Iran, and the deaths of large numbers of children have drawn international attention to the vulnerability of educational institutions in conflict zones. While investigations and public accounts continue to examine the circumstances of the incident and questions of responsibility, the event highlights a broader and well-documented concern: the devastating impact of armed conflict on children and their access to education. Schools serve not only as centers of learning but also as places of safety, social development, and community cohesion. When educational facilities are damaged or destroyed during military operations, the consequences extend far beyond the immediate casualties. Survivors often experience long-term psychological trauma, interrupted education, displacement, and reduced access to essential social services. International humanitarian law provides special protections for civilians and civilian infrastructure, including schools. Numerous international organizations have documented the increasing risks faced by children in conflict-affected regions and have called for stronger measures to prevent attacks on educational facilities. Such incidents raise urgent questions regarding civilian protection, accountability, and compliance with established legal norms [1,3].The reported Minab tragedy certainly illustrates how a single event can affect an entire generation [7-8]. Families, friends, educators, healthcare workers, and local communities bear the burden of recovery long after media attention fades. Figure 2 is a painting by an Iranian artists drawn in memory of the innocent children who have lost their life in this tragedy [10]. Beyond the immediate loss of life, the destruction of educational environments can undermine social stability and hinder long-term development. For researchers, policymakers, and humanitarian organizations, incidents involving schools underscore the importance of systematic data collection, independent investigation, and evidence-based policy responses. Understanding the factors that place children at risk during armed conflict is vital for developing effective prevention strategies and strengthening international mechanisms for civilian protection.of political perspectives, the protection of children and educational institutions remains a universal humanitarian imperative. Continued research, transparent investigations, and global cooperation are necessary to reduce the chance of similar tragedies and ensure that schools remain places of learning rather than casualties of war. The tragedy is not simply a story about one school. It is a warning about the growing gap between the sophistication of modern weapons and the reliability of the information systems that guide them. Military planners increasingly rely on vast streams of intelligence data, satellite imagery, automated analysis, and algorithm-assisted decision-making. These technologies promise greater precision and fewer civilian casualties. Nevertheless, the events in Minab demonstrate that precision is meaningful only when the underlying information is accurate and continuously verified. A missile can strike within meters of its intended coordinates and still produce a humanitarian disaster if the coordinates themselves are wrong. Reports surrounding the Minab strike suggest that the school stood near facilities associated with Iran's Revolutionary Guards and that historical information about the area may have influenced targeting assessments. Whether future investigations ultimately attribute the disaster to outdated intelligence, procedural failures, technological shortcomings or human error, the broader lesson remains the same: civilian protection cannot be delegated to assumptions embedded in databases.This challenge extends beyond the Middle East. Around the world, governments are investing heavily in artificial intelligence, autonomous systems and data-driven military planning. Advocates often emphasize speed, efficiency and operational advantage. Far less attention is devoted to the consequences of incorrect data, degraded intelligence or flawed classification systems. When errors occur, they can be amplified by the very technologies designed to improve decision-making. The deaths of children in Minab should therefore be viewed not only as a humanitarian tragedy but also as a policy failure. International law already requires belligerents to distinguish between military objectives and civilian objects and to take all feasible precautions to minimize civilian harm. The question is whether existing accountability mechanisms are keeping pace with rapidly evolving military technologies.The growing integration of artificial intelligence into military decision-support systems raises an additional challenge for International Humanitarian Law. The legal principle of proportionality requires commanders to determine whether the anticipated incidental civilian harm would be excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage expected from an attack. This assessment is inherently qualitative, context-dependent, and ultimately a matter of human legal judgment rather than algorithmic optimization. AI systems may assist by processing large volumes of intelligence or identifying potential military objectives, but they cannot independently evaluate the moral, legal, and contextual considerations that proportionality requires. Moreover, AI does not merely provide neutral information. By determining which information is highlighted, how confidence levels are presented, and how rapidly decisions are expected to be made, AI systems actively reshape the conditions under which human judgment is exercised. Automation bias, opaque model behavior, embedded biases in training data, and increasing operational tempo may unintentionally narrow the deliberative space required for careful legal assessment. Ensuring meaningful human control therefore requires more than retaining a human "in the loop"; it requires designing AI-supported decision processes that preserve independent legal judgment, transparency, and accountability.Three reforms deserve urgent consideration. First, countries should adopt stricter independent review procedures for targets located near schools, hospitals, and other protected civilian sites. Second, military investigations involving large-scale civilian casualties should be transparent and subject to external scrutiny. Third, governments developing AI-assisted targeting systems should be required to disclose how such systems are validated, audited, and monitored for error.The children who died in Minab will never benefit from these reforms. However, their deaths should compel policymakers, military leaders and researchers to examine whether current practices are adequate for an era in which a single targeting mistake can extinguish hundreds of futures in a matter of seconds. Scientific and technological progress is often celebrated for expanding human capability. The true measure of that progress, however, is whether it also expands human responsibility. Minab reminds us that the answer remains uncertain. The consequences of attacks on children extend far beyond the immediate death toll. Every classroom contains a reservoir of future human potential that cannot be measured at the moment of loss. Among the students killed in Minab may have been future scientists, physicians, engineers, teachers and innovators whose contributions could have benefited not only their own communities but humanity as a whole.Scientific progress depends on the emergence of talent from diverse social, economic and geographical backgrounds [11]. History repeatedly demonstrates that transformative discoveries often come from unexpected places. The next breakthrough in cancer treatment, renewable energy, climate adaptation, artificial intelligence or public health may originate from a child attending a school far from the world's major research centers. When conflict destroys educational opportunities or claims young lives, society loses not only individuals but also the knowledge, creativity and leadership they might have contributed. The effects are cumulative. Beyond those who perish, surviving classmates may experience trauma, displacement and interruptions to their education. Schools may close, teachers may leave, and families may become reluctant to send children to class. The resulting decline in educational attainment can persist for decades, reducing the number of students who ultimately enter higher education, research and innovation. In this way, a single attack can reverberate through an entire generation. For the global scientific community, the protection of children and educational institutions is therefore not solely a humanitarian concern. It is also an investment in humanity's future intellectual capacity. Every child denied the opportunity to learn represents a possibility lost; every school destroyed narrows the pipeline through which future discoveries emerge. The cost of such violence cannot be calculated only in lives lost today, but also in knowledge, solutions, and progress that the world may never realize.Although the scientific community cannot by itself prevent wars, it can influence how evidence is gathered, how technologies are developed, and how accountability is pursued. For this purpose, several avenues may be proposed as follows:The global research community could support an independent, internationally governed system that documents attacks on schools, universities, hospitals, and other civilian institutions. Using satellite imagery, geospatial analysis, open-source intelligence, and forensic methods, such a network could provide rapid, evidence-based assessments of incidents. Reliable documentation can reduce misinformation, preserve evidence, and support future accountability processes.Scientists, engineers, and legal scholars should collaborate in developing internationally recognized AI assurance frameworks for military decision-support systems. These frameworks should include: auditable workflows documenting how AI contributes to operational decisions; system cards describing intended use, limitations, uncertainty, training data, and known biases; continuous monitoring for concept drift, performance degradation, and changing operational environments; independent verification that AIassisted systems remain compatible with International Humanitarian Law throughout their operational life cycle rather than only during initial deployment.The scientific community has historically shaped norms in areas such as nuclear weapons, biotechnology, and climate science. Similar leadership could help establish norms for AI-assisted warfare.Researchers in geospatial science, remote sensing, and information systems could help maintain verified, continuously updated maps of schools, universities, and other protected civilian sites. If integrated into military planning systems worldwide, such databases could serve as an additional safeguard against accidental targeting.Compared with investment in weapons development, relatively little research funding is devoted to understanding and preventing civilian casualties. Governments, foundations, and academic institutions could support multidisciplinary research involving: conflict studies, artificial intelligence, human rights law, data science, risk assessment, psychology, and trauma recovery. The goal would be to identify systematic ways to reduce harm before military operations occur.Even during periods of geopolitical tension, scientific cooperation often survives when political dialogue breaks down. International scientific organizations such as the International Science Council and agencies within United Nations frameworks can help maintain channels of communication between countries in conflict. Although scientific diplomacy cannot prevent every war, it can create relationships and trust that reduce misunderstandings and encourage de-escalation.The scientific community can advocate for schools and universities to be treated similarly to internationally protected cultural and humanitarian sites. This could include: enhanced monitoring, rapid international investigations after incidents, stronger legal protections, greater political consequences for violations.Prevention is crucial, but so is recovery. Scientists, universities, and funding agencies can provide scholarships, remote learning opportunities, research fellowships, and educational support for children affected by conflict. This helps ensure that the loss of educational opportunity does not become a second tragedy following the initial violence.States developing AI-assisted targeting technologies should ensure that Article 36 reviews under Additional Protocol I extend beyond conventional weapons to encompass the entire AI-enabled decisionsupport process. Because machine-learning systems may evolve after deployment through changing data distributions and operational conditions, legal review should be an ongoing rather than one-time process. Scientists can contribute methodologies for continuous validation, uncertainty estimation, and independent auditing [12][13].Although existing international laws prohibit the targeting of civilian infrastructure, and places such as schools and hospitals, a major problem, particularly in recent years, is that these laws are being flouted openly by governments with little to no consequences. So, while it is important to develop regulations related to the design and use of AI, scientists, engineers, legal scholars, and politicians also need to make sure their governments follow the existing rules. In addition, scientific organizations should collaborate with international bodies investigating attacks on educational institutions by providing technical expertise in digital forensics, satellite imagery, geospatial analysis, and data verification.The scientific community cannot determine where wars are fought, but it can influence how knowledge is used within them. Scientists have helped humanity split the atom, map the genome, and explore distant planets. The same ingenuity should be directed toward a more immediate challenge: ensuring that advances in technology reduce, rather than amplify, the risk to children caught in conflict. Protecting schools is not only a humanitarian obligation; it is a commitment to preserving the minds that will shape humanity's future.

Title: Opening ecological data to reduce bias and strengthen AI in ecology
Abstract: In 1985, Richard Stallman introduced copyleft, a licensing principle that allows source code to be used, modified, and redistributed provided that the same freedoms are preserved in derivative works (Stallman, 1985). Although developed for software, copyleft offers a useful analogy for ecological research, where data, metadata, and analytical code should be accessible and reusable under clear licenses. Similarly, our ability to understand and address ecological challenges such as biodiversity loss, species range shifts, land degradation, and climate change depends on ecological knowledge being open where ethically appropriate and otherwise responsibly accessible. Such knowledge should also be managed according to the FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) and established domain standards such as Darwin Core and Ecological Metadata Language (Wieczorek et al. 2012, Wilkinson et al. 2016). Despite substantial progress in open science (Dwivedi et al. 2022), many key ecological datasets (e.g., national ecological inventories, biodiversity records, and high-spatial- and temporal-resolution remote-sensing data) remain proprietary or available only with restricted access (e.g., requiring formal approval). These gaps are substantial: Large-scale analyses of hundreds of millions of ecological records reveal persistent taxonomic, geographic, and temporal biases (Meyer et al. 2015, Daru and Rodriguez, 2023). Much of the scientific literature also remains behind paywalls, while open-access publication fees can create barriers for researchers with limited funding (Rocchini and Neteler 2012). This paradox, that is, publicly funded knowledge becoming inaccessible to the public, constrains who can participate in ecological research and which ecosystems, regions, and perspectives are ultimately represented. AI does not create this problem but can amplify it by embedding data biases in models reused at scale, while closed training data limit independent scrutiny (Koch et al. 2022). AI for ecology encompasses task-specific machine-learning and computer-vision models, as well as foundation models, including large language models (LLMs). These systems differ in scale, purpose, and accessibility, but all depend on the quality, documentation, and governance of the data used to train and evaluate them. By integrating diverse data sources, AI can transform ecological research. However, when data, code, or model-development processes cannot be independently inspected, existing knowledge gaps and biases may be transferred into ecological inference. Appropriately open, reliable, and interoperable ecological data, together with transparent and auditable AI infrastructures, are therefore essential for robust, equitable, and epistemically sound ecological research. The expansion of AI in ecological research intensifies the need for transparent and well-documented knowledge. Bias is not unique to AI: statistical, mechanistic, and machine-learning models can all inherit limitations from their data and assumptions. AI can increase the scale, opacity, and reach of these effects (Han et al. 2023). Currently, many applications in ecology use task-specific AI models trained for bounded prediction or classification problems (Pichler and Hartig 2023). These models are often trained on specialized aggregated ecological repositories (e.g., biodiversity data from the Global Biodiversity Information Facility [GBIF]), climatic variables (e.g., from WorldClim and ERA5), or land-use and land cover change mapping (e.g., from satellite imagery). In contrast, the rise of foundation models, including LLMs used for the automated synthesis of scientific literature, code generation, data processing and analysis, requires massive cross-domain training sets that are difficult to build from scratch. Consequently, models trained on skewed, geographically biased, or inaccessible datasets can systematically misrepresent under-sampled regions and reflect long-standing inequities in ecological knowledge. When training datasets are inaccessible, their composition is also difficult to inspect, making gaps in the representation of regions, languages, taxa, or perspectives harder to detect and evaluate. Thus, LLMs are not necessarily more biased than task-specific AI models, but their biases can be harder to trace and hence propagate across a wider range of users, tasks, and applications. In ecology, both task-specific and generic models inherit the limitations of the data used to train them. For example, species-recognition models inherit taxonomic imbalances in training images (Koch et al. 2022), whereas LLMs can process ecological information rapidly but may perform poorly on specific tasks. Gougherty and Clipp (2024) found that LLMs often struggled to extract pathogen-incidence values and sometimes inferred that all individuals were affected when no incidence value was reported. Similarly, Dorm et al. (2026) showed that LLMs performed poorly in generating species range maps and offered only limited improvement over random guessing in threat classification. Comparable effects have been observed in other AI domains, where imbalances in training data have produced systematically poorer model performance for underrepresented groups (Birhane, 2022). Together, these examples illustrate how unbalanced training data can transfer existing knowledge gaps into model outputs, highlighting the importance of identifying, documenting, and reducing such biases before models are applied beyond their validated domain. AI models can furthermore introduce subtler epistemic risks (Loru et al. 2025), including the confident fabrication of ecological information, the misrepresentation of species-trait responses to environmental gradients, and the generation of unsupported ecological interactions or spatial patterns. In ecological applications, documented limitations already include errors in quantitative information extraction and uneven performance across tasks (Gougherty and Clipp, 2024, Dorm et al. 2026). For these reasons, responsible openness and transparent governance of ecological data and metadata are vital, because the reliability of specialized models and large-scale synthesis depends on whether foundational ecological resources can be appropriately accessed, documented, and independently evaluated. Reproducible evaluation therefore requires practical commitments. Ecological AI studies should provide standardized documentation describing where their training data came from, which taxa, regions, and environmental conditions they cover, how the model is intended to be used, and its known limitations. Established tools such as datasheets for datasets and model cards can support this documentation (Gebru et al. 2021). Models should also be evaluated across taxa, regions, languages, and environmental conditions, and data, code, prompts, model weights, and independent evaluation sets should be released where ethically, legally, and technically possible (Maasri et al. 2022, Smith et al. 2024). In order to improve data exchange and utilization, general principles and standards for the creation, verification, and sharing of data should be established while respecting the owners and creators of specific databases. Any restrictions and access procedures should also be documented. Public initiatives such as the Minerva LLM (Orlando et al. 2024) illustrate the value of transparent, language-specific model development, but openness alone does not ensure ecological or cultural validity across regions. AI also changes the politics of openness by creating a risk that openly shared data and open-source code are incorporated into proprietary models without reciprocal access, attribution, credit, or participation for the researchers, developers, and communities who produced them. In public and public/private programs such as GenAI4EU (2025), adequate funding should mean sustained support for data curation, digitization of legacy records, targeted collection in documented gaps, local skills and infrastructure, and independent auditing, not only model development. Funders, publishers, scientific societies, and research institutions should recognize data curation as a research output and require transparent documentation and evaluation. Collaboration should connect local communities and data holders to national infrastructures, international repositories, and standards bodies. Identifying and reducing bias in AI development, enabling robust validation, and sustaining open infrastructures all depend fundamentally on the availability of high-quality, representative, and well-documented ecological data. Where data are scarce, uneven, or unreliable, transparency becomes especially important for identifying gaps and assessing their consequences (Titley et al. 2017). Open data and governance policies must therefore be accompanied by dedicated funding for targeted data collection, the digitization of legacy records, curation, metadata preparation, quality control, local computational infrastructure, training, and equitable collaboration, particularly in under-sampled regions. Such investments are necessary to prevent openness from disproportionately benefiting institutions that already possess the resources needed to exploit shared datasets. Openness should not, however, imply unrestricted public release. Precise locations of threatened species, Indigenous and local knowledge, and data governed by consent or legal agreements may require spatial generalization, controlled access, embargoes, or community authority (Tulloch et al. 2018). Data should instead be as open as possible and as protected as necessary, combining FAIR data stewardship with the CARE principles (Collective Benefit, Authority to Control, Responsibility, and Ethics) where Indigenous or community-governed data are involved. International coordination among funders, ecological societies, repositories, publishers, data providers, and model developers is also needed to establish interoperable standards for data collection, annotation, documentation, sharing, and controlled access. Differences in the quality, resolution, and accessibility of ecological datasets should be explicitly documented and considered during model development and evaluation rather than remaining hidden (Dwivedi et al. 2022). Without shared standards and a commitment to responsible openness, ecological AI risks becoming fragmented, opaque, and shaped primarily by actors with the greatest computational and data resources. The practical priorities that we highlight are the following. Ecologists, AI researchers, funders, journals, repositories, and ecological societies should: audit geographic, taxonomic, temporal, and, where relevant, linguistic gaps in AI training and evaluation data, and quantify their effects on model performance; fund targeted data collection and the digitization of legacy records where these gaps have meaningful consequences; require machine-readable metadata and licenses, provenance records, uncertainty documentation, datasheets for datasets, and model cards; maintain independent benchmark datasets stratified across regions, taxa, sensors, and environmental conditions; and ensure that data-producing communities have access to computational infrastructure, training, credit, and decision-making roles rather than being treated solely as data providers (Wilkinson et al. 2016, Smith et al. 2024). Ecological research stands at a decisive crossroad: As AI reshapes how we observe and interpret the natural world, the openness and responsible governance of our data, models, and publications will determine whether this transformation is equitable and scientifically robust. Unrepresentative datasets, or data and models that cannot be independently evaluated, risk narrowing ecological insight, reinforcing global disparities, and introducing epistemic distortions that degrade our collective understanding of ecological systems. A well-governed, participatory, and inclusive ecological knowledge system, open where possible and protected where necessary, supported by public LLM research, auditable domain-specific models, and genuinely accessible publishing practices, is crucial to ensure that AI becomes a tool for discovery and justice rather than distortion. Just as copyleft preserved the freedoms to use, modify, and share software, responsible openness can free environmental science from informational silos while respecting legitimate restrictions. In the age of AI, openness is not only a technical requirement but an ethical obligation: Shared and responsibly governed knowledge is the foundation of collective solutions. Title: How Many Biopsies Are Enough? Rethinking Biopsy and Surveillance Strategies for Barrett's Esophagus in Asia
Abstract: The diagnosis and surveillance of Barrett's esophagus (BE) in Asia remain areas of uncertainty and heterogeneity, largely due to regional variations in clinical practice and the lack of established guidelines. In contrast to Western countries, where BE management is guided by standardized protocols, evidence from Asian populations is limited, particularly regarding the diagnostic yield of biopsies for intestinal metaplasia (IM) and the determination of surveillance strategies for BE. Most Western guidelines recommend systematic random biopsies when columnar-lined esophagus (CLE) is identified on endoscopy, applying the Seattle protocol to detect IM, given its well-established association with esophageal dysplasia and adenocarcinoma (EAC) [1, 2]. Accordingly, histologic confirmation of IM is considered essential for the diagnosis of BE and is considered the foundation of surveillance strategies. In contrast, many Asian guidelines, including those in Japan, do not require histological IM for the BE diagnosis. This contributes to uncertainty with regard to the prevalence of IM and the standardized surveillance protocols in Asian BE cohorts. A recent nationwide survey in Japan conducted in 2024, involving 804 endoscopists, evaluated real-world practices in the diagnosis and surveillance of BE. The results revealed substantial inconsistencies, particularly the very low adherence to the Seattle protocol, reported at only 0.6%, and the limited use of biopsies specifically intended to detect IM, which were performed in just 6.0% of cases [3]. Similar findings have been reported in previous surveys, indicating that Asian endoscopists generally perform fewer biopsies, largely due to practical and resource limitations [4, 5]. Together, these findings reveal a lack of uniform biopsy practices and highlight the need for careful consideration of their implementation. In this issue, Tsai et al. conducted a large retrospective study to evaluate the diagnostic yield of random biopsies for detecting IM in Asian patients, addressing the scarcity of data on both biopsy yield and the required number of biopsies [6]. A total of 117,526 consecutive esophagogastroduodenoscopies (EGDs) were retrospectively screened. Among 5963 EGDs, 3135 patients (5.1%) were diagnosed with CLE, endoscopically diagnosed BE. Analysis of 4675 EGDs with 8994 biopsies revealed an overall IM detection rate of 35.1% per endoscopy, with significantly higher yields in long-segment CLE (74.8%) compared with short-segment CLE (32.9%). A single biopsy detected IM in 26% of cases, whereas three biopsies increased detection rates comparable with the Seattle protocol. Among patients initially negative for IM, repeat endoscopy modestly increased detection, mainly at the second examination. These findings demonstrate the critical impact of biopsy number on IM detection and support the need for pragmatic biopsy strategies specifically for Asian populations. The authors' recommendation of obtaining three biopsies represents a practical and clinically relevant approach that bridges the gap between ideal Seattle protocol adherence and routine clinical practice. Given its comparable efficacy and greater simplicity, this approach may be a more acceptable alternative biopsy protocol for Asian endoscopists. Nevertheless, an unresolved question remains: Is a three-biopsy strategy sufficient for long-segment CLE in Asian patients? Despite its strengths, the study should not be interpreted as evidence that three biopsies are adequate in all patients, as IM is unlikely to be uniformly distributed within CLE. The observed plateau in yield after three biopsies may reflect the predominance of short-segment BE in Asians rather than a true plateau of sampling. Although long-segment BE (LSBE) is less prevalent in Asia than in Western countries, emerging evidence from Japan suggests that the risk of neoplastic progression in LSBE may be comparable. In a recent Japanese prospective registry study, a 10-year follow-up revealed an EAC incidence in LSBE cases, 1.01 (0.57–1.73)%/year, similar to that reported in Western countries [7]. Another nationwide, multi-institutional study showed that cancer risk steadily increases with length of BE, with EAC incidence in Japanese LSBE patients comparable to Western data [8]. In such patients, the risk of progression to neoplasia from IM is substantial, and a three-biopsy strategy potentially risks undersampling. These findings indicate that LSBE in Asia should not be considered low risk and may require more robust strategies. Importantly, it should be noted that this study was retrospective, and variation in endoscopists' experience has influenced biopsy numbers and potentially technical performance. The other concern is the study's follow-up methodology, which is based on chart review and telephone interviews rather than systematic surveillance or BE registry. Furthermore, no systematic use of narrow-band imaging, acetic acid, magnification endoscopy, or artificial intelligence was incorporated. Recent BE practice is rapidly shifting toward image-enhanced endoscopy (IEE) and targeted biopsy, and the role of random biopsies will continue to be debated. Multiple studies have already demonstrated that advanced imaging technologies improve IM and dysplasia detection compared with random sampling. IEE has demonstrated utility in differentiating neoplastic from nonneoplastic lesions through detailed assessment of mucosal and vascular patterns, enabling real-time optical diagnosis and facilitating targeted biopsy. Targeted biopsy allows selective sampling of suspicious areas, thereby improving diagnostic yield while reducing the number of biopsies required. Nevertheless, this approach is highly operator-dependent and may be less reliable in less experienced hands, causing interobserver variability. Importantly, IEE and pathological examination serve as complementary roles, and histological diagnosis remains the gold standard for definitive diagnosis and for guiding clinical management. Therefore, rather than representing mutually exclusive strategies, a combined approach with careful mucosal inspection with IEE, targeted biopsy, and selective random sampling may currently represent the most pragmatic strategy. Looking ahead, the increasing adoption of artificial intelligence-assisted endoscopy may further enhance lesion detection, potentially shifting the paradigm away from extensive random sampling. From this perspective, the most relevant question for the future is not simply “how many biopsies are needed,” but rather “how many are required after careful, high-quality endoscopic assessment.” Another important discussion point raised is the need to develop BE surveillance protocols. There is currently no standardized accepted surveillance protocol in Asia, and surveillance intervals vary among institutions and countries. This lack of consensus hampers the development of evidence-based surveillance recommendations tailored to Asian populations. In this study, IM detection was independently associated with male sex, older age, longer CLE length, and a higher number of biopsies [6]. Addressing these gaps is essential for optimizing BE surveillance and improving early detection of neoplasia. Identifying high-risk subgroups within the Asian BE population, based on factors such as smoking, obesity, or other risks, will be important. Although chronic GERD is considered the primary causal risk factor for EAC based on Western data, previous studies have shown that up to 40% of patients with EAC have no history of chronic GERD [9]. In the aforementioned study in Japan, patients who developed EAC were significantly more likely to have a history of smoking [7]. Robust, population-specific data are needed to inform more individualized surveillance and biopsy strategies. Another particularly valuable aspect of this study is its discussion of follow-up strategies for patients with suspected BE but negative IM on initial endoscopy. Although most guidelines specify surveillance intervals for nondysplastic BE according to segment length, they often fail to address whether, and how, patients without IM on initial biopsy should be followed. In this regard, the study assessed whether repeat endoscopy improves the detection of IM in patients who were IM-negative at index endoscopy. Among 1772 IM-negative patients, IM was detected at the second endoscopy in 24.2%. If all IM-negative patients underwent a second endoscopy, an estimated 428 additional IM cases would be identified, increasing the additional yield of 16.9%. Based on these results, the authors recommend a repeat endoscopy for patients initially negative for IM. Their recommendation is both timely and clinically meaningful. This aligns with the 2022 American College of Gastroenterology guideline, which states that a repeat examination may be reasonable given that the yield for detecting IM on a second endoscopy can be 25% or higher, whereas further examinations beyond this are unlikely to be beneficial [1]. By incorporating this concept into an Asia-focused strategy, the present work fills an important gap in clinical guidance. What, then, should be the way forward? Management of BE in Asia requires pragmatic, data-driven approaches and establishment of refined guidelines. Most importantly, prospective, population-based registries with standardized biopsy and surveillance protocols are needed to define the true natural history of BE in Asia. Given the lower prevalence of LSBE, surveillance may be better to move beyond uniform models toward more refined, risk-adapted strategies. As the epidemiology of BE continues to evolve, standardized, evidence-based surveillance strategies will be essential to guide future studies and improve early neoplasia detection. In this context, the biopsy strategies proposed in this study provide an important reference point, enabling meaningful comparisons across studies. Equally important is the recognition of the need to optimize the quality of endoscopic examination. Key quality indicators, including adequate inspection time, measures to enhance neoplasia detection, and adherence to biopsy protocols, play a central role in improving diagnostic yield [10]. Ultimately, such practical, evidence-based approaches have the potential to shape the future of BE research and patient care in Asia. The authors have nothing to report. Title: Research & Research Data Management: 1. Introduction - Welcome to the Research Revolution
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Abstract: In this foundational video, you'll discover why Research Data Management (RDM) is far more than administrative busywork—it's a practical skill that directly improves every aspect of your research workflow. Rather than viewing RDM as overhead, the video frames it as "research fluency": the ability to locate raw data, scripts, notebooks, and analysis context within minutes instead of days or weeks. The core problem is familiar to most research teams. A promising dataset is created through careful work, strong figures are published, and then a collaborator asks for validation: Where are the raw inputs? What's the processing trail?Suddenly, scripts are scattered across laptops, file names have been changed repeatedly, and critical preprocessing steps were done interactively but never recorded. What should be a one-hour handoff becomes a multi-week reconstruction—delaying publication, stressing the team, and weakening confidence in conclusions. This pattern happens across disciplines, from climate research to materials science, and it's largely preventable through forward planning. The video introduces four critical data layers that must be managed together: raw data (original measurements), processed data (cleaned and transformed outputs), metadata (the context that makes values meaningful—instrument settings, sample IDs, calibration status, units), and analysis code (the scripts and notebooks that generate results). When any layer is missing, reproducibility weakens; when two are missing, trust collapses quickly. You'll learn a practical seven-stage lifecycle that keeps you organized from start to finish: planning (what will you collect?), creation (experiments and measurements), processing (cleaning and transformation), analysis and interpretation (statistics, modeling, visualization), publication and sharing (packaging for others), preservation (keeping data accessible over time), and reuse (enabling future studies). The key insight is that RDM decisions made before the first measurement—naming conventions, folder structure, metadata templates, backup strategy—compound over time and reduce friction at every downstream stage. The video emphasizes two foundational documents: a Data Management Plan (DMP) that serves as your strategic map, and Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) that turn intent into repeatable action. Both prevent silent drift when teams rotate members or projects span long periods. Metadata receives special attention, because it's the invisible backbone of trustworthy science. A data table without context is like a map without labels. Good metadata captures what was measured, how, when, where, by whom, with what instrument, and under which conditions. The video stresses capturing metadata at the moment of work, using templates with required fields, and standardizing units, vocabularies, and notation. The FAIR principles—Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable—are presented as a practical framework, not just compliance checkboxes. Findable data uses persistent identifiers and rich metadata. Accessible data has a clear path to obtain it, whether open or controlled. Interoperable data uses shared formats and vocabularies. Reusable data includes enough provenance, method documentation, uncertainty notes, and licensing that others can apply it responsibly. A major theme is uncertainty and variability. No measurement is perfect, and the video explains the distinction between random error (estimated through replication) and systematic error (the more dangerous kind, from calibration drift or hidden biases). The message is clear: report uncertainty explicitly, link it directly to method documentation, and keep the full chain intact—from raw outputs through calibration logs, SOP versions, preprocessing decisions, code revisions, and quality-control flags. Looking forward, the video connects RDM to AI and machine learning in research. AI tools are entering labs rapidly, but they only work reliably on well-structured, documented data with clear provenance. Fragmented datasets amplify confusion; clean, quality-annotated datasets unlock genuine discovery. This reframes RDM as a readiness strategy for human-plus-AI science. The video closes with a practical seven-step roadmap: create a DMP, standardize SOPs, capture metadata in real time, document transformations clearly, report quality explicitly, publish through repositories with persistent identifiers, and preserve through trusted infrastructures. The advice is to start small, build through repeatable habits rather than heroic cleanups, and treat RDM as part of scientific stewardship—not because it's required, but because it extends your scientific impact far beyond your original project scope. This introduction sets the stage for the follow-on videos. As you move from this overview to specific domains—like documenting chemical synthesis experiments and recording purity assessment protocols—you'll apply these same foundational principles in concrete, hands-on contexts. You'll learn how to capture synthesis parameters (precursor materials, temperatures, reaction times, atmospheres), how to record characterization methods (instruments used, calibration states, detection limits), and how to link raw spectra, chromatograms, or microscopy images to the metadata that explains them. The habits you adopt for documenting one synthesis will scale when you document dozens; the templates you build now become your lab's foundation for reproducibility, collaboration, and impact. ----------------- The pictures have been generated using DeepAgent The voice has been provided by Elevenlabs The video was produced by using HeyGen

Title: THE BILLIONAIRE PROMISES vs. THE BREWTANIUS RECEIPTS: A Structural Invalidation of the Trillionaire Trajectory through Sovereign Engineering

Abstract: THE BILLIONAIRE PROMISES vs. THE BREWTANIUS RECEIPTS: A Structural Invalidation of the Trillionaire Trajectory through Sovereign Engineering I. Executive Statement: The Collapse of the Monopoly Hypothesis The economic historiography of the early 21st century has been dominated by a singular, pervasive, and largely unchallenged narrative: the "Trillionaire Trajectory." This economic theory posited that the future of human civilization—its energy grids, its labor force, its transport logistics, and its extraterrestrial expansion—would inevitably coalesce into the proprietary domains of a select few ultra-high-net-worth individuals. The assumption was that the capital requirements for generalized autonomy, humanoid robotics, and interplanetary colonization were so high that only those who had already captured the value of the Internet Age (Web 2.0) could afford to build the infrastructure of the Artificial Intelligence Age (Web 3.0/Industry 4.0). The primary avatars of this trajectory, Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos, spent two decades constructing market valuations based not on current revenue, but on the promise of these future capabilities. Tesla’s stock price is not a reflection of car sales; it is a call option on a future monopoly of autonomous transport. Amazon’s valuation is not merely about retail; it is a bet on the eventual privatization of the global and orbital supply chain. These valuations rely on the maintenance of technological bottlenecks—specifically the closed control of training data, proprietary energy interfaces, and vertical integration of manufacturing.1 However, a rigorous, exhaustive analysis of the technological landscape in 2025 reveals a fundamental structural correction. The "monopoly assumptions" underlying these valuations have been intercepted. They were not intercepted by a corporate competitor or a rival nation-state, but by a structural shift in the technological substrate itself, spearheaded by the "Brewtanius" initiative (led by Mark Anthony Brewer) and the CollectiveOS architecture.1 This report serves as a "receipts drop"—a forensic accounting of the divergence between the aspirational promises of the billionaire class and the deployed, timestamped, and physically verifiable technologies delivered by the Brewtanius initiative. The evidence suggests that while the billionaire class was busy hypothesizing a future of "optional labor" and "post-money civilization" while still charging subscription fees, a disabled Black veteran operating without a billion-dollar budget successfully engineered the "operating system for civilization".1 This is not a debate of personalities. It is a confrontation of architectures. The "Closed Loop" of the Monopolist, designed to extract rent from scarcity, has been out-engineered by the "Open Stack" of the Sovereign Engineer, designed to generate abundance through distributed governance. The following analysis details how the Brewtanius initiative delivered 94 published white papers, solved 17 UN global issues, and deployed a verifiable "Anti-Scarcity Stack" in a five-month sprint, effectively rendering the trillionaire trajectory mathematically impossible.1 II. The Epistemological Crisis of Autonomy: Probabilistic Promises vs. Provable Safety The valuation of Tesla and the reputational capital of Elon Musk are inextricably linked to the promise of Full Self-Driving (FSD). The prevailing economic theory suggests that by solving generalized autonomy first via a proprietary neural network, Tesla will accrue a monopoly on transport-as-a-service, generating software-margin profits on global logistics. This projection relies on a specific technological bet: that "end-to-end" neural networks—black boxes that map camera inputs directly to steering outputs—can achieve safety levels surpassing human capability through infinite data ingestion.1 The Brewtanius "Guardian Stack" has introduced a superior epistemological framework that invalidates this bet. It asserts that the current paradigm of "learning to drive" through pattern matching is fundamentally flawed because it conflates correlation with causation. A. The Failure of Correlational AI and the "Long Tail" Tesla’s FSD architecture is fundamentally correlational. It operates on the premise that with sufficient training data—petabytes of video ingested from the fleet—a neural network can "learn" the correct response to any driving scenario. This philosophy suggests that perception and control are distinct only in theory, but in practice, a unified neural net can absorb the complexities of the road through massive video ingestion.1 However, as evidenced by recent interventions and regulatory scrutiny, this approach suffers from the terminal "Long Tail" problem. When faced with a novel event—an overturned truck spilling unusual cargo, a pedestrian behaving erratically in a construction zone, or a chaotic intersection with contradictory signage—the system is forced to guess based on statistical similarities to past data. It does not understand why it should stop; it only knows that statistically, stopping is the likely output associated with similar pixel arrangements.1 Recent analyses of Tesla’s FSD intervention rates indicate a plateau in reliability. While performance improves in nominal conditions, the failure rate in edge cases has not improved exponentially as promised. This "black box" nature renders the system opaque to regulators. When a failure occurs, it is difficult to trace the specific parameter or weight responsible, leading to a cycle of "patching" rather than proving.1 B. The Guardian Stack: Sovereign Causal Perception In direct contrast, the Guardian Stack, delivered by the Brewtanius initiative, utilizes an architecture of Sovereign Causal Intelligence. This system moves beyond simple object detection to build a "theory of mind" for other road actors.1 Using the AION engine, the Guardian Stack models intent. It does not merely observe a pedestrian; it reasons. For instance, the system processes visual data to conclude: "That pedestrian intends to cross because they are looking at the bus stop across the street" rather than merely calculating a velocity vector.1 This moves the system from observing motion to understanding motivation, allowing it to anticipate actions before they manifest as physical threats. This causal layering addresses the epistemological deficit of the Tesla model. A correlational engine can predict that a car usually stops at a red light, but it cannot reason that a car must stop because crossing would violate the physics of collision avoidance. The Guardian Stack’s causal engine provides the "why" that the neural net lacks. C. Provably Safe Planning (PSP): The Mathematical Certainty The most significant divergence lies in the validation of safety. The Guardian Stack introduces Provably Safe Planning (PSP), a methodology that replaces statistical probability with mathematical certainty.1 Before the Guardian vehicle executes any maneuver—whether a lane change, a turn, or an acceleration—the system generates a formal mathematical proof that the action is safe under all predicted outcomes. If a plan cannot be proven safe, it is rejected. This utilizes formal verification methods similar to those used in aerospace and chip design, adapted for real-time robotics. The system does not ask, "Is this likely to be safe?" It asks, "Is it mathematically impossible for this trajectory to result in a collision given the current constraints?".1 D.
