Title: Four Laws of Therapeutic Dynamics
Venue: Journal of Occupational and Environmental Medicine
Abstract: Modern medicine enjoys a rich legacy of aphorisms. Ever since medical school, I have been taken with that tradition. The margins of many a notebook bear witness. Thirty years ago, these musings seemed whimsical. Ten years ago, I no longer thought they were so trivial; I started making gentle forays into the clinical literature. What follows is anything but a gentle foray; it is the strident prose of a physician who is hard-pressed to serve his patients or teach his students according to his conscience. Of all my aphorisms, the following four are incontrovertible. They are guideposts for any reader who feels the need to be a patient. They are a primer for any clinician trying to help a patient maintain healthfulness. They are the ammunition an occupational physician might use in protecting a work force from being savaged by that Byzantine, rapacious, chaotic demon, the American "health care system." The First Law: The Death Rate Is One per Person We are not meant to go gently into the unknown. But go we must; the issue is when. What's the most we can hope for? No science can answer that question with any certainty a priori-never for an individual who is well. The assumptions necessary to extrapolate from the past to predict your future are simply overwhelming. My personal philosophy rests on data, admittedly flawed, that promises an average life expectancy for our species that approaches 85 years. Anything beyond that is a bonus. So for me, the issue is to get my patient to age 85, smiling back at the journey and expecting to be comforted in passing when the moment arrives. If you share this philosophy, if you harbor not even a faint illusion of immortality, then you should also share my exasperation at the medicalization of advantaged America and my disgust at our callousness toward the disadvantaged. Advantaged Americans, like advantaged citizens of most industrialized countries, are nearly there; we are all likely to reach the age of 85 in reasonable health. If you ward off obesity and avoid tobacco and other noxious exposures, your chances are excellent. I'm not suggesting that at 85, like so many lemmings, we'll meet our makers. There will always be tragedies-statistical outliers, if you will-those will die before their time and those who linger beyond theirs. I am asserting that we can do no better than to arrive at 85, that most of us will make it, and that very few of us have anything to gain from the medical "advances" touted as lifesaving. Let's take "cancer" and "heart disease" as object lessons. Cancer has carried away many a loved one. But it is the specter of cancer that is the scourge. We are taught that "screening" and "aggressive" treatments are our salvation. Well, the truth is that only serendipity and the surgeon may make it more likely that some disease other than breast, prostate, lung, or colon cancer will carry you off at 85. No matter how we torture the data, no aggressive chemotherapeutic regimen increases that likelihood. That is not to say these cancers are rare. To the contrary, many of us will be afflicted with breast, colon, or prostate cancer at age 85. But few of us with cancer will die of that cancer; most will not even be aware of its presence. We will die, but we would have died anyway, with or without the cancer, at 85. Certainly there are tragedies-people who die before the age of 85 of cancer. They deserve all the compassion, palliation, and empathy we can muster. They do not deserve ineffective chemical heroics, nor do the rest who have cancer but have no change in life expectancy. Besides, succumbing to cancer at too young an age may not be just bad luck; these unfortunate people may harbor a genetic susceptibility, an Achilles' heel, that someday we'll learn to recognize before it's too late to attempt to protect their entitlement of 85 years. Today, any public "health" mandate for mammography, prostate-specific antigen assays, or screening of stools for occult bleeding is not up to the task. Then there's cardiology and cardiovascular surgery. In mid-century, coronary artery disease was a scourge-but it is no longer. In fact, we are living long enough to manifest the diseases of old age, such as cancer. Nonetheless, we the people are not disabused, and they, the experts, are permitted the hubris of generations past. Cardiologists and cardiovascular surgeons make a practice of designing and purveying interventions based solely on "first principles," eg, the latest widget to image the myocardium or do violence to the plaques in arteries. But the "first principles" are wrong. That is the inescapable conclusion of multicenter study after study-each extensive and expensive, and each bearing its acronym proudly (TIMI, TAMI, GISSI, GUSTO, ISIS, CASS, etc). Whatever minimal survival advantage is afforded the tiny but vaunted subset with major disease of the "left main" coronary artery is overwhelmed by the peri-invasive mortality that is the only other readily demonstrable effect on survival. Despite the futility of doing violence to the ischemic heart, modern American cardiology and cardiovascular surgery conspires to purvey well over 400,000 cardiac catheterizations, some 300,000 angioplasties, and a similar number of bypass grafts each year. Americans would be better off if we spared their coronary arteries all known surgical assaults forevermore! If you don't believe me, ask your favorite cardiologist to defend any variation on the dialogue shown in Fig. 1.Fig. 1: Template for a dialogue between a patient concerned about heart disease, and his or her physician.The readership of this journal is part of a modern advantaged industrial society. Aside from a few exceptions, such as the treatment of some infectious diseases with antibiotics, of congestive heart failure with certain medicines, and of cervical cancer and some lymphomas, medicine can offer nothing to improve one's likelihood of living longer. But we market the myth and ignore the corollaries. The disadvantaged die young, and we look away. And the elderly die inelegantly, badgered and dehumanized-and we participate. The Second Law: Never Poke a Skunk I, and many of my generation in medicine, lived a myth-to my own detriment, I still live it. I believe that any profession, and certainly medicine, is a meritocracy. Each individual is personally accountable for knowledge, soul-searching, self-criticism, and self-awareness. And each professional is answerable to peers on all these accounts. How else do we safeguard the person who assumes the most vulnerable of stations in our society, that of patients? This myth has eroded. There were always those physicians who fell short, and there will always be. But never before did falling short lead to career options in medicine to the degree that it does today! For two decades, the academy has been crawling with people who know more and more about less and less. They knew who they were, we knew who they were, and our students knew. I have decried the trend, but the patient did not suffer. Now there are people with medical degrees who don't even pretend to know more and more about clinically relevant phenomena. Rather they claim to know more and more about how best to serve "units" of care, and how best to organize "care givers." You can spot these anti-physicians by their shibboleths: "team players," "the good of the institution," he or she's a "good citizen," "must change to survive," "there's a new order," etc. They are the bloated, overpaid, self-congratulatory medical administration. Medical administration is no longer infrastructure. These "doctors" and their fellow travelers abound in the academy and out; they sell themselves as purveyors of truth, keepers of the key to a better future, and exemplars of nobility. No physician and no patient is a match for their self-service. To take them on, eyeball to eyeball, is to lose; we share neither language nor goal nor ethic. If only I could learn how to work comfortably around them, perhaps I could teach this essential skill. Someone more talented will have to take up the challenge and teach me. The Third Law: There Has Never Been a Quack Without a Theory Hubris. The scourge of the clinician since antiquity; to be so certain as to be unaware that you might be so wrong. In this century, how many tonsils were removed and thymus glands irradiated to stop pharyngitis from recurring? How many "retroverted" uteruses were removed to halt back pain? Radical mastectomies for cure? The list goes on and on, all examples of hubris. No wonder we all applauded when it became clear, only 30 years ago, that so many clinical inferences could be tested, even tested proactively. However, we are so enamored with the process that we have permitted distortions to set in that represent nothing more than New Age Hubris. It is easy to design studies and perform analyses leading to inferences that conform to some preconceived notion or promote some vested interest. Clinical medicine is being overwhelmed by the imperious P values that are imprimatur to a marketing exercise pursued with zeal by purveyors of techniques, pills, and facilities. To wit: I don't know a well-trained scientist who is willing to perform a controlled experiment on 1000 inbred mice in the hopes of detecting a few percent difference in some biological outcome. Do you? Would anyone fund such an experiment? Any scientist worth his or her salt would tell you that there is so much biological variability even in inbred mice that a small difference is not interpretable, even if it is unlikely to occur by chance. Larger differences are likely to be meaningful. But larger differences can be detected in experiments with far fewer mice. Nonetheless, every week, the "scientific" literature of clinical medicine offers up a conclusion based on a few percent difference in outcome when thousands or even tens of thousands of human beings are exposed to something that as many "controls" are spared. The authors avow confidence in the small difference because it is not likely to occur by chance more than one time in 20 (Probability [P] < 0.05). Smitten by this imperious P value, the lay press trumpets the inference. The lay press trumpets the inference even if it is the opposite of the inference trumpeted last week, or last month, or last year. Epidemiology is funded to degenerate into the scare of the week, the diet of the month, the drug of the decade. Much of this is another testimony to human foibles; it's nice to feel important and, in the academy, funding is credibility, if not power. But some of this may be more than human foibles. Some may be nefarious. When there is so much money at stake, the impartiality of science may be no match. "Peers" who review studies interpreted in a way that fosters their incomes and power are likely to suffer less dyspepsia than if the authors had offered a pejorative interpretation. That's human nature. But how about when drug companies contract other companies to undertake and analyze major studies of new drugs, often facilitating these studies by paying doctors to enroll patients, all in the quest of a P value that the Food and Drug Administration finds persuasive? That's a Faustian contract if ever there was one! Imperious P values stalk the overweight, the smokers, and those patients whose families are riddled with individuals who died an untimely death. Clearly we have much to learn about the plight of these people, and how best to advise, educate, palliate, and comfort. Today we urge them on in the Sisyphean task of reversing their "risk factors," laboring under the assumption that if they do so, their risks will diminish. And we ply them with drugs on the basis of study after study in which data has been tortured to assert uncertainty, or discern unconvincing minimal effects, or excuse the negatives. The fact is, oral hypoglycemics, treating mild hypertension, and-with exceptions such as some rare genetic defects-lowering cholesterol have not been shown to increase the likelihood that anyone will reach the age of 85. Thanks to imperious P values, "me too" antibiotics, analgesics, and other classes of drugs stand in rows as "samples" in nearly every clinic. Thrombolytics are the standard of care for myocardial ischemia even though they pale next to aspirin in risk/benefit. The cardiovascular enterprise is the standard-bearer of the American medical "high tech" sophism; since we can do it, it must be good and valuable. The American heart is not the only body part that suffers the "high tech" sophism and thereby supports an industry: regional back pain warrants neither imaging nor surgery; arthroscopic knee, wrist, and shoulder surgery is in quest of therapeutic validation, as is most sinus surgery, and on and on … Some of this, as in days of old, is perpetrated in the absence of data. Much is perpetrated in spite of the data-driven by the flow of moneys that enrich the surveyors but succor the ill not at all, and justified by the presence of imperious P values. The Fourth Law: Institutions Die; People Live I have lived through four distinct institutions of medicine: proprietary hospitals built on hubris, the golden but fleeting age of clinical investigation, the corruption of unbridled fees for any service declared "necessary," and now, the leveraging of the healthfulness of the advantaged American. I was too young to grasp the distortions of the proprietary hospitals fully. I came of age in that fleeting golden age of clinical investigation, which passed into legend by the 1980s. It was superseded by the age of the "interventionists" who took advantage of New Age Hubris to strut the stage, bloated with the largesse of Medicare. They silenced the clinicians, labeled them "second class," and dispersed them. The irony is that even though these clinicians abound today across the land, a sophisticated ministry to the ill and great American resource, they have no credibility even if they could find a voice; all medicine is tainted by presumption of conspiracy with the interventionists. Otherwise, medicine as a cottage industry could be championed: universal coverage by a single payer only for compassion, for ongoing counsel, for prescription of the few interventions available today that are supported by more than imperious P values, and for discerning those of value in the future. Instead, since 1992, we have moved in the opposite direction. Industrialists have subjugated the interventionists and now command the institution. "Saving money" is a euphemism for profit margin. Top administrators of even small hospitals and managed "care" companies are paid more than governors, senators, and even the president of the United States. "High tech" is marketed at bargain prices, worthless or not, and "providers" are pressured by "purveyors" to spend less and less time, or none at all, with "customers" and "clients." This new institution is Orwellian. It is transparently and avowedly self-serving. It deserves to die. No doubt it will, and soon. The question is whether it is the last institution of medicine. Nortin M. Hadler, MD Professor of Medicine and Microbiology/Immunology; University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill; Attending Rheumatologist; University of North Carolina; Hospitals Chapel Hill, NC

Title: Correction: Advanced phycocyanin detection in a south American lake using landsat imagery and remote sensing
Abstract: Algal blooms in oligotrophic lakes have become a growing concern for inland aquatic systems, where their frequency is increasing at an alarming rate (Feng et al., 2024). These lakes, once characterized by low nutrient levels and clear waters, are now vulnerable to the impacts of the triple planetary crisis of climate change, biodiversity loss and water pollution (Jenny et al., 2020;Mishra, 2023). These interconnected challenges have created conditions that exacerbate algal bloom, posing significant risks to aquatic ecosystems, water quality and human health (Igwaran et al., 2024).Among the most damaging blooms are those caused by cyanobacteria, also known as blue-green algae (Vadeboncoeur et al., 2021). Cyanobacterial blooms are especially dangerous because many species of this group produce toxins that can be harmful to aquatic life, terrestrial animals and humans (Chorus, I., & Welker, 2021;Moreira et al., 2022;Svirčev et al., 2022). These blooms are characterized by the presence of both general pigments, such as chlorophyll-a, and more specific pigments, such as phycocyanin, a marker for cyanobacteria (Konik et al., 2023). Phycocyanin is not only crucial for the photosynthetic processes of cyanobacteria but also serves as a valuable indicator to monitor their presence and growth (Almuhtaram et al., 2021). Detection of this pigment has become essential for tracking bloom dynamics and assessing water quality in affected lakes (Binding et al., 2021). Rising global surface temperatures, driven by climate change, have created increasingly favorable conditions for the growth and persistence of cyanobacterial blooms (Zepernick et al., 2022). Warmer waters favor stratification of lakes, reducing water circulation and creating nutrient-rich environments in the upper layers where cyanobacteria thrive (Chorus, I., & Welker, 2021). In addition, warmer temperatures can increase the metabolic rate of these algae, further accelerating the formation of blooms (Wu et al., 2024). The cumulative effects of climate change, combined with nutrient enrichment from agricultural runoff and urbanization, have intensified the frequency and severity of these toxic blooms, turning once pristine oligotrophic lakes into sites of ecological concern (Sivarajah, 2020;Devlin & Brodie, 2023).The need for advanced monitoring and mitigation strategies is more urgent than ever, as harmful algal blooms threaten not only aquatic biodiversity, but also the sustainability of freshwater resources for human use (Ahmed et al., 2022;Kazmi et al., 2022). Remote sensing technologies, especially those capable of detecting phycocyanin, are increasingly important for early detection and management of these blooms (Zahir et al., 2024). On the other hand, we acknowledge the complexity of inland water optics, including the influence of inherent optical properties that can introduce uncertainty into reflectance-based estimates. Additionally, the use of multispectral satellite data particularly from the Landsat series is limited by its relatively broad spectral bands, which can hinder the accurate detection of narrow absorption features, such as those associated with phycocyanin. A wide range of indices have been created and evaluated, from those adapted from agricultural and terrestrial vegetation applications to combinations of spectral bands specifically designed to detect primary productivity in aquatic environments (Luo et al., 2023). For example, spectral indices such as Surface Algal Bloom Index (SABI) (Alawadi et al., 2010) and Flotation Algal Index (FAI) (Ma et al., 2021) have been used in Lake Villarrica to determine the spatial distribution of Chl-a, while Green Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (GNDVI) and Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) have been applied to measure chlorophyll concentration in the aquatic system of Lake Laja (Rodríguez-López et al., 2020). Despite these advances, significant challenges remain. Many indices do not perform optimally in aquatic ecosystems other than those for which they were initially developed and validated (Lukhabi et al., 2023). This is because conditions in different lakes are influenced by a variety of factors, including geographic, meteorological, and physicochemical characteristics (Melese & Debella, 2023).It is therefore essential to fill these gaps by developing methods that are more accurate site-specific based on the predominant optical characteristics of the aquatic system under study.Statistical techniques, such as linear regression, are commonly used to estimate water quality parameters (Gad et al., 2023;Adjovu et al., 2023). For example, Rodríguez-López (2020) developed models to estimate chlorophyll concentrations in six lakes in south-central Chile. In a subsequent study (Rodríguez-López et al., 2021), it was shown that combining regression techniques with remote sensing data could achieve the same objective, allowing the study of spatial and temporal variability in these aquatic systems. The integration of statistical methods with data from a variety of sources including in situ water quality monitoring and satellite observations can improve the ability to monitor and manage aquatic vegetation (Mukonza & Chiang, 2023;Batina & Krtalić, 2024). Compared with nonlinear models or analytical approaches, linear regression offers the advantages of simplicity, interpretability, and computational efficiency, which are valuable when establishing baseline predictive models for water quality. This, in turn, will contribute to the conservation and sustainable management of these critical natural resources. In Chile, species responsible for harmful algal blooms, mainly cyanobacteria, have been reported in lakes such as Villarrica, Laguna Grande de San Pedro, Vichuquén and Laja (Rodríguez-López et al., 2020;Rodríguez-López et al., 2023;Yépez et al., 2024). Therefore, the objective of this work is to develop statistical models to estimate algal pigments by combining water quality data with satellite observations.This lake system located at 39°18'S latitude and 72°05'W longitude is one of the most studied Chilean lakes due to its environmental, economic and social importance (Rodríguez-López et al., 2022). Its basin has multiple uses including tourism and agriculture. In addition, it has two important cities in the Araucanía Region on its banks: the city of Villarrica and the city of Pucón. A secondary water quality standard has been implemented for this lake that monitors the parameters of Chl-a, nitrogen and phosphorus nutrients and water transparency, however, every summer an algal bloom appears that extends over the largest surface of the lake and lasts for several months during the year (Rodríguez-López et al., 2023). Limnological parameters, including water temperature (°C), Chlorophyll-a (µg/L), Phycocyanin (µg/L), turbidity (NTU), and dissolved oxygen (ppm), were recorded during monitoring campaigns conducted by the Dirección General de Aguas (DGA) of Chile between 1989 and 2024. The data, collected at seven monitoring stations as detailed by Rodríguez-López et al. (2023), initially covered the four stations from 1989 to 2009. However, from 2009 onwards, probably due to resource constraints, measurements were only made in summer and spring. The monitored parameters included surface temperature (measured using the standard thermometry method 2250 B of the NCh 2313 compendium), surface chlorophyll-a (Chl-a, using the fluorometric method), total phosphorus (determined by the standard method 4500 P B, 22nd edition, EAM), total nitrogen (measured using the standard method 4500-N C, 22nd edition, EAM), and water transparency (assessed by Secchi disk depth, SDD). At each station in the lake, water samples were collected from five different depths using a 5 L Niskin bottle. These samples were stored in a thermal container. These samples were stored in thermally insulated boxes, kept cold at about 5°C on ice, before being transported to a collection center for analysis. Chemical analyses were performed at the DGA chemical laboratory, accredited according to Chilean standard NCh ISO 17025 of 2005 by the Instituto Nacional de Normalización. (Vanhellemont, 2020;Vanhellemont et al., 2016). In this study, two correction approaches were used: the default Dark Spectrum Fitting (DSF) algorithm (Vanhellemont, et al., 2018;Vanhellemont, 2019, Vanhellemont, 2020) and the earlier Exponential Extrapolation (EXP) method (Vanhellemont and Ruddick, 2014;Vanhellemont and Ruddick, 2015;Vanhellemont and Ruddick, 2016). Corrected Rrs bands for water and some spectral indices were derived from the ACOLITE output. These included individual bands, various band ratios, and additional spectral indices, which were subsequently used as input variables in the next steps for phycocyanin prediction. The bands used ranged from the blue to the shortwave infrared region (B, G, R, NIR, SWIR) and a total of 11 band ratios and 17 spectral indices were calculated. These variables were selected based on expert criteria and an extensive literature review focused on spectral indicators related to water quality, chlorophyll concentration, algal blooms, and nutrient levels in aquatic environments that could be related to phycocyanin (Viso-Vázquez et al., 2021;Wang et al., 2022;Rodríguez-López et al., 2023;Magrí et al., 2023;Lyu et al., 2023;Choi et al., 2023). The surface reflectance values (ρs) of each indicator were extracted in a 3 × 3 pixel matrix per sampling point (Rodríguez-López et al., 2023). The extraction sites were located entirely over open water, free from coastal influences, floating vegetation, and shadows. Although Figure 1 does not display the precise locations of the sampling points due to the map scale, they are situated well away from the coastline. Importantly, both the sampling points and the extraction pixels were free of clouds and fog. This extraction was carried out in QGIS 3.40 software (QGIS Development Team, 2024) and the area of interest (Roi) was downloaded from the Chilean Geospatial Data Infrastructure (IDE-Chile, https://www.ide.cl/) accessed on 04 September 2024.Table 1 show the spectral indices obtained and its specific algorithm. Building upon previous work (Rodríguez-López et al., 2024 PC), we developed linear regression models to estimate concentrations of the pigment phycocyanin (FCA). In this study, a broader set of explanatory variables was employed, derived from the processing of satellite imagery and incorporating both spectral bands and vegetation indices (see Section 2.3). Due to the limited volume of data available at individual stations (usually < 90 data points), we aggregated all observations across stations to construct generalized models rather than site-specific ones.To identify the variables most strongly associated with FCA, we first computed pairwise Pearson correlation coefficients between all candidate predictors and the dependent variable. Only those variables exhibiting statistically significant correlations (pv < 0.05) were retained for model development.Regression models were then constructed using three variable selection techniques: stepwise selection (Efroymson, 1960), backward elimination (Kutner et al., 2005), and forward selection (James et al., 2023), to determine the most parsimonious and explanatory model configuration. These approaches iteratively assess combinations of predictors based on established statistical criteria, such as the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) and Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), to optimize the balance between model complexity and explanatory performance.While linear regression was chosen for its high degree of interpretability a critical objective for understanding the environmental drivers of phycocyanin its suitability was formally evaluated. We conducted direct comparative analysis against a set of common non-linear machine learning models, including Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, Support Vector Regression, and a multi-layer perceptron Neural Network (Rodríguez-López et al., 2023). This analysis was designed to empirically determine whether the substantial loss in model interpretability associated with these more complex algorithms would be justified by a statistically significant improvement in predictive performance.To assess the generalization performance of the candidate phycocyanin (FCA) regression models and mitigate the risk of overfitting inherent (Cohen & Jensen, 1997) in using model-fit statistics alone (such as AIC or in-sample R 2 ), we employed k-fold cross-validation (with k=10) (Mahmood & Khan, 2009). This procedure provides a robust assessment of predictive capability on data unseen during model training, which is particularly critical given the aggregation of observations across sites (see Section 2.4).To more rigorously test model stability and generalizability, several advanced procedures were implemented. First, we conducted Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV), the most stringent form of cross-validation for a dataset of this size. Second, bootstrap validation with 1,000 iterations was performed to generate 95% confidence intervals for performance metrics, providing a robust measure of model stability. Third, temporal validation was executed by training the model on earlier chronological data and testing it on more recent observations to explicitly assess its predictive power on future, unknown conditions. Finally, the selected ordinary least squares (OLS) model was benchmarked against regularized regression techniques (Ridge, Lasso), which penalize complexity to directly diagnose and prevent overfitting. The final model was selected based on the optimal trade-off between predictive accuracy (maximizing R² and minimizing RMSE) (Preacher, 2006), model parsimony, and consistent, robust performance across this entire suite of validation protocols.Finally, to ensure that the assumptions underpinning linear regression were met, diagnostic checks were performed on the selected model. Title: Guest editorial: Marketing technologies and development in Africa
Venue: African Journal of Economic and Management Studies
Abstract: Africa stands at an extraordinary inflection point in its economic and technological trajectory. With the world's youngest population – median age of 19 years compared to the global average of 30 – and mobile phone penetration exceeding 80% in many countries, the continent is experiencing a digital marketing renaissance that is fundamentally reshaping how businesses engage with consumers, how governments deliver services and how markets function (Han et al., 2023). This transformation is not merely an adoption of Western digital practices; rather, it represents a unique evolution where necessity breeds innovation, leapfrogging traditional infrastructure limitations to create distinctly African solutions to African challenges.The confluence of widespread mobile connectivity, youthful demographics and entrepreneurial dynamism has created fertile ground for marketing technology adoption across the continent. Mobile money transactions in Sub-Saharan Africa exceeded $701bn in 2022, demonstrating the region's leadership in financial technology innovation (Takyi, 2024). E-commerce adoption, while still nascent compared to developed markets, is growing exponentially, with platforms adapting to local payment preferences, logistics challenges and consumer behaviors (da Costa, 2022). Digital marketing investments by small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are yielding measurable performance improvements, with studies documenting substantial increases in sales and customer engagement following the adoption of digital channels (Deku et al., 2024).However, this digital transformation unfolds against a backdrop of persistent challenges. Infrastructure gaps, regulatory uncertainties, cybersecurity concerns and digital literacy deficits create friction in technology adoption pathways (Sagala and Őri, 2024). Trust remains a critical mediating factor in consumer acceptance of digital transactions, particularly in contexts where corruption and service quality inconsistencies have historically eroded confidence in formal institutions (Han et al., 2023). The interplay between technological capability, institutional trust and consumer behavior creates a complex ecosystem that demands nuanced scholarly investigation.This special issue of the AJEMS brings together six empirical studies that illuminate different facets of marketing technology adoption and impact across African contexts. These papers span multiple countries – Nigeria, Somalia, Ghana, Egypt and South Africa – and examine diverse technologies including self-service systems, mobile wallets, e-commerce platforms, immersive virtual reality applications, hotel automation and smartphone branding strategies. Collectively, they advance our theoretical understanding of technology acceptance in developing markets while offering practical insights for managers, policymakers and entrepreneurs navigating Africa's digital transformation.What emerges from these studies is a portrait of African consumers who are simultaneously pragmatic and aspirational – seeking technologies that solve immediate problems while also enhancing their social status and quality of life. These studies reveal that trust, perceived usefulness and ease of use remain foundational to technology adoption, but these factors operate through culturally specific mechanisms. Corruption mitigation emerges as a unique driver of self-service technology acceptance in Nigeria. At the same time, lifestyle compatibility proves crucial for mobile wallet adoption in Somalia, and hedonic value significantly influences online shopping behavior in Ghana.As we navigate through these six contributions, we explore how they collectively advance three critical conversations in the marketing technology literature: (1) the contextual adaptation of technology acceptance models to African institutional environments, (2) the role of trust and institutional quality in mediating technology adoption and (3) the sectoral diversity of digital transformation across B2C, B2B and service industries. Each paper makes a distinctive contribution while reinforcing common themes that speak to the broader dynamics of marketing technology diffusion in emerging markets.The six papers in this special issue are organized thematically to facilitate a coherent narrative about marketing technology adoption across different sectors and consumer segments in Africa. We begin with foundational technologies – self-service systems and mobile payments – that address basic transactional needs while building digital literacy and trust. We then progress to consumer-facing e-commerce platforms that leverage these foundational technologies to enable new shopping behaviors. Next, we explore cutting-edge immersive technologies that represent the frontier of marketing innovation, followed by an examination of automation in the hospitality sector, which demonstrates the integration of technology in service delivery. Finally, we conclude with an examination of brand relationship dynamics in the smartphone industry, illustrating how technology products themselves become objects of emotional attachment and loyalty.This progression from foundational to frontier technologies and from transactional to relational outcomes mirrors the actual evolution of digital marketing ecosystems in African markets. It also reflects increasing levels of consumer sophistication and the maturity of technological infrastructure required for successful implementation.We begin this special issue with Anka and Shamim's (2026) groundbreaking study on the adoption of self-service technology (SST) in Nigerian fuel stations. In this context, technology adoption intersects with institutional challenges in particularly revealing ways. This paper deserves the opening position because it tackles a fundamental question that underlies all subsequent discussions of marketing technology in Africa: How do technologies gain acceptance in environments where institutional trust is compromised?Nigeria's fuel distribution sector has long been plagued by corruption, including fuel adulteration, meter manipulation and inconsistent service delivery. These practices have eroded consumer confidence and created transactional friction. Anka and Shamim's (2026) study demonstrates that SSTs – automated fuel dispensing systems that reduce human intermediation – are valued not merely for their convenience but for their capacity to mitigate corruption. Using PLS-SEM analysis of data from 233 Nigerian consumers, the authors reveal that willingness to use SST positively correlates with customer trust, corruption mitigation and customer intimacy.The study's most compelling finding is the mediating role of corruption mitigation in the relationship between SST willingness and customer intimacy. This suggests that technology adoption in African contexts cannot be understood solely in terms of functional attributes (ease of use and usefulness) but must also consider institutional quality factors. When consumers perceive that technology reduces opportunities for corruption, they develop stronger trust, which in turn enhances their emotional connection with the service provider. This finding extends TAM by incorporating institutional governance variables – a theoretical contribution with implications far beyond the fuel sector.From a practical standpoint, this study offers fuel station operators and policymakers a roadmap for technology-enabled service improvement. By positioning SSTs as anti-corruption mechanisms rather than merely efficiency tools, marketers can tap into consumer frustrations with existing systems and position technology as a solution to institutional failures. This framing may accelerate adoption rates and enhance brand differentiation in competitive markets.The Nigerian fuel station context also provides an ideal starting point for this special issue because it represents a high-frequency, high-stakes transaction environment where trust deficits have direct economic consequences. If SSTs can succeed in building trust in this challenging context, the findings offer optimism for technology adoption in other sectors facing similar institutional challenges across Africa.Moreover, this paper introduces the concept of “customer intimacy” as an outcome variable, moving beyond simple adoption intentions to explore the more profound relational consequences of technology use. This sets the stage for subsequent papers in the collection, which examine how technologies shape not only transactions but also relationships, emotions and identities.Following naturally from the discussion of foundational trust-building technologies, Mukhtar and Barre's (2026) study examines the adoption of mobile wallets in Somalia. In this context, mobile money has become the de facto financial infrastructure due to limited banking penetration and ongoing institutional challenges. This paper occupies the second position because it extends the conversation on trust and technology acceptance into the mobile financial services domain, which represents perhaps Africa's most significant contribution to global fintech innovation.Somalia presents a particularly instructive case for research on mobile wallets. With a fragmented formal banking infrastructure and a population accustomed to mobile money for remittances, the country has leapfrogged traditional payment systems. However, as Mukhtar and Barre (2026) demonstrate through their analysis of 321 respondents using PLS-SEM and SPSS, adoption is not automatic even in environments where mobile payments are ubiquitous. Their multidisciplinary model, which integrates the TAM and UTAUT frameworks, reveals that attitude, lifestyle compatibility, perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness directly influence adoption intentions. Meanwhile, facilitating conditions, Internet quality, security and trust operate through attitude as a mediator.The finding that lifestyle compatibility emerges as a significant direct predictor of adoption intention is particularly noteworthy. In the Somali context, where mobile wallets must integrate with existing social practices around money management, gift-giving and family support, technology adoption is not merely a rational calculation of utility but a question of cultural fit. This aligns with emerging research on technology adoption in collectivist societies, where individual decisions are embedded in social networks and obligations (Solomon and Allen, 2023).Equally important is the finding that security and trust do not directly influence adoption intention but work through attitude formation. This suggests that Somali consumers have developed pragmatic attitudes toward mobile money – accepting certain security risks as inherent to the technology while valuing its lifestyle benefits. This risk-benefit calculus differs from patterns observed in developed markets, where security concerns often directly inhibit adoption. The resilience of Somali mobile money adoption despite security concerns speaks to the compelling value proposition these services offer in contexts with limited alternatives.From a managerial perspective, this research suggests that mobile wallet providers in Somalia and similar markets should prioritize lifestyle integration and ease of use in their marketing communications over security messaging. While security infrastructure must be robust, marketing efforts should focus on demonstrating how mobile wallets seamlessly fit into daily routines, social obligations and aspirational lifestyles.This paper also makes an important methodological contribution by proposing and validating additional constructs beyond the original TAM and/or UTAUT models. The inclusion of lifestyle compatibility and Internet connection quality reflects the researchers' sensitivity to local contextual factors that standard technology adoption models may overlook. This contextualization of theory is essential for advancing our understanding of technology diffusion in diverse African markets.The progression from SSTs in Nigerian fuel stations to mobile wallets Title: Keith Moser. Fake News in Contemporary Science and Politics: A Requiem for the Real?
Abstract: Keith Moser’s book Fake News in Contemporary Science and Politics configures a transdisciplinary rhetoric of how deceptive content circulated by media channels has catastrophically created a pervasive “hyperreality” that not only sanctions itself stealthily but also obfuscates all truth claims. Moser understands this “hyperreality” as a false epistemic truth that attacks humanity in the form of a tide of “infodemic crises” in today’s digital era. Moser also emphasizes the alarming nature of this hyperreality, which manufactures a counterfeit reality capable of generating counter-facts that deny the very existence of objective truth.This book is of indispensable interest not only to those who subconsciously recognize the perils of the self-postulated truth fallacies that authorize themselves in this modern technological globe but to humanity in its entirety. With a sense of urgency, it elucidates how the omnipresence of fake news and conspiracy theories within scientific and political domains endanger the Anthropocene and reflects the dire consequences of living in a post-truth digital world, in which the norms of factuality are compromised. Moser takes a lethal step by going beyond scholarly convention and proving how world leaders driven by capitalist ideology hegemonize truth by capitalizing technology to cater to their selfish intentions. Primarily, he grounds his analysis on Jean Baudrillard’s theories of hyperreality, which postulates postmodernism as the “diagnosis” of the problem of hyperreality rather than the root-cause of it, leading to a “complete disappearance,” “effacement,” or “disfiguration of the totality of human relations” (6–8). Structurally, the book is divided into five chapters, which individually contain the “abstract,” “keyword,” “introduction,” “body,” “conclusion,” and “reference” sections, making it comfortable for the reader to effectively peruse the laboriously researched project.The “Introduction” demonstrates the ubiquity of fake news and conspiracy theories by emphasizing the real-life consequences of the “pervasive misrepresentation” or what Moser refers to as the “infodemic” or stimulated hyperreality that vitiates human ability to distinguish truth from falsehood. In this regard, he cites examples of how Big Carbon or alt-right media outlets, which, despite factual truth, encourage the denial of the hazards of global warming and anti-vaccination movements to satisfy their short term “myopic” monetary narrative (2). However, Moser’s focus on the economic motives behind these movements, while significant, might oversimplify the complex interplay of social, psychological, and cultural factors that also contribute to the spread of misinformation. Moser further explores how postmodern autocratic leaders like Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin exploit this simulated reality to destabilize democratic institutions, suppress dissent, and consolidate power.Another reason that Moser provides for the increasing hold of fake news and conspiracy theories is what he calls “late capitalism.” Moser claims that late capitalism, which has changed its focus from being product-oriented to consumer-oriented, has created a commodity fetishism that tyrannically produces a “commercial simulacrum” of “hyperreal fantasies” (7, 5). Moser’s analysis of late capitalism as a driving force behind the proliferation of fake news and conspiracy theories is insightful because it places needed emphasis on the relationship between economic determinism and media authenticity.Chapter 2, “Climate Change Denial: An Ecocidal, Parallel Universe of Simulation,” delves further into the problem of climate change denial that jeopardizes global health resulting from an obvious lack of any mitigating action. Drawing on Baudrillard’s critique of the post-factual “rift between evidence and truth” created by hyperreal echo chambers, and Jean-François Lyotard’s theory on the influence of corporate actors in research funding, Moser underscores the role of far-right populist leaders who, with their “anti-science, post-factual rhetoric,” propagate climate change as a hoax, thereby constructing an “ecocidal, parallel universe of simulation” that diverts public attention from the reality of “anthropogenic climate change” (15). Moser makes a compelling argument that the hyperreality created by various meta-narratives and conspiracy theories provide counterevidence against truth itself (16). For instance, Moser asserts that Big Carbon turned to tobacco companies to “greenwash reality” to fund their commercial interests. He also cites the Global Warming Petition Project as an example of absurd “knowledge” that casts doubt on human-caused climate damage (22). This, Moser claims, is possible by bribing researchers who thus produce false facts to “orient research” for their personal interests of the corporate sources or the “wealthiest,” thus “peddling pseudo-science to the public” (18–20). While Moser’s application of Baudrillard and Lyotard offers a sharp critique of the mechanisms behind climate change denial, one might question whether these postmodern frameworks fully capture the complexity of the issue. For instance, Baudrillard’s focus on hyperreality might obscure the very real psychological, social, and political factors that drive individuals and communities to reject scientific evidence. Moreover, while Lyotard’s critique of corporate influence is pertinent, Moser could also have explored how social media algorithms and echo chambers contribute to the proliferation of misinformation.Another facet worth mentioning in this chapter is Moser’s unabashed attack on well-known political leaders who actively distort truth and mislead the public by leveraging their positions of power and privilege. Owing to various policies and the withdrawal from the 2015 Paris Agreement, he audaciously critiques political leaders such as Trump, Bolsonaro, and Abbott, who, through post-truth discourse, contribute to a hegemonic effort to bypass rational thought and overtly promote a distorted hyperreality (34). With great urgency, Moser concludes the chapter with a pressing and forceful assertion that “if the forces of obscurantism prevail, [human society] will have signed [their] own death warrant soaked in the ubiquitous blood of alternative facts” (46). Moser’s critique is persuasive and timely, especially in light of these leaders’ environmental policies and their withdrawal from the 2015 Paris Agreement. While the author’s argument effectively underscores the existential threat posed by climate change denial, it also raises awareness about the rhetorical effectiveness of such apocalyptic warnings.Chapter 3, “COVID-19 Vaccine Hesitancy: The Ongoing, Hyperreal Saga of a Deadly Epidemic and Infodemic,” examines the phenomenon of COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy among people who challenged scientific research that cautioned against the dangers of the pandemic as a hoax, refused to get vaccinated, and consequently lost their lives. In this vein, Moser claims that this hesitancy is due to the “deadly effects of anti-science simulacra that decimated the human population” (53). He explores how misinformation, such as the debunked myth linking the COVID-19 MMR vaccine to autism, fueled public distrust in vaccination (58–59). Moser’s analysis opens new avenues for a deeper exploration of the psychological mechanisms that make individuals more susceptible to such myths. For instance, he might consider the role of cognitive biases, such as confirmation bias, which can lead individuals to seek out and believe information that aligns with their preexisting views, even when that information is demonstrably false.Moser furthers his argument by drawing parallels between vaccine hesitancy and skepticism toward other major epidemics, attributing this resistance to anti-science rhetoric, media sensationalism, and misinterpreted metanarratives (60, 73). He also discusses how certain faith-based perspectives, which view the pandemic as divine retribution, exacerbated the spread of disinformation, further entrenching individuals in hyperreal filter bubbles (83). This argument is relevant in highlighting the intersection of religion and misinformation while critiquing faith-based perspectives for spreading disinformation. This argument offers an insightful perspective of the role of religion in the pandemic, recognizing that faith can be both a source of disinformation and a powerful force for public health advocacy.In Chapter 4, “Alternative Facts Trump Reality: The Spectacular Anatomy of an Insurrection,” and chapter 5, “The Baudrillardian Discourse of the Good: Putin’s False Flag Operation to Denazify Ukraine,” Moser intensifies his attack on autocratic leaders like Trump and Putin engaging in a parhessia of how the emergence of post-truth politics has eroded the foundation of democratic societies. Moser critically analyzes Trump’s “Stop the Steal” metanarrative, his cultivated “celebrity image,” and the coup d’état attempt on January 6, 2021, as primary evidence supporting his argument. He asserts that Trump’s violence resulted in unwarranted casualties representing what Moser terms a “manufactured” “insurrection,” characterized by “alternate planes of (hyper-) reality” designed for political gain. Moser argues that this event was the culmination of “four years of a purely simulacral” form of governance (95).Once again, Moser uses Baudrillard’s concept of hyperreality as a potent tool for deconstructing the superficial layers of Trump’s capitalist strategies. He fervently describes Trump’s manipulation of truth as a form of “cosmetic surgery on the real,” creating an “optical illusion” in which Trump is portrayed as the victim rather than the oppressor (99, 110). Such a depiction strikingly conveys the artificiality of Trump’s narrative construction while also highlighting the disorienting effects of post-truth politics. On a similar tangent, Moser argues that Putin’s “digital iron curtain” and his justification for the invasion of Ukraine are predicated on a binary narrative that pits absolute good against evil, thereby distorting reality to legitimize his actions (139). In both cases, Moser draws correspondences between how Trump and Putin use digital platform to enforce their pretentious victimhood by validating their own false versions of truth. While both engage in post-truth tactics, Putin’s control over Russian media and the state’s repressive apparatus differs significantly from Trump’s more decentralized approach, which relies heavily on social media and grassroots mobilization. Acknowledging these distinctions could provide a more nuanced understanding of the global landscape of post-truth politics. Nevertheless, both chapters conclude with a call to action, urging readers to resist the tyranny of fake news and further take responsibility for combating the spread of disinformation instead of “impotently watching the dark clouds of obscurantism cover the planet in the age of (dis-) information” (168).All in all, Moser’s book is valuably incisive for readers interested in exploring the relationship between media authenticity and the influence of autocratic leaders who control public perception by generating false realities. With efficacy, Moser creates crucial awareness of the dangers of fake news in today’s technologically driven world and offers potential remedies, such as inoculation theory, media literacy, evidence-based knowledge, along with news legislation to diagnose the malaise of fake news that plagues contemporary human society. Although, as he claims, these solutions do provide a ray of hope to tackle the problem of manufactured “hyperreality” they also invite further critical inquiry concerning their practical implementation within sociopolitical contexts where educational access is unevenly distributed. This highlights a potential limitation in Moser’s approach, as it presumes a level of epistemic agency that may not be universally accessible.Undoubtedly, the implementation of evidence-based knowledge offers a robust foundation for epistemic inquiry and the identification of Moser’s concept of “hyperreal news,” raising important questions about who will assume responsibility for such an undertaking. This approach also opens up new avenues for guiding epistemic exploration, particularly within the Anthropocene–Technocene nexus, which intersects with the disciplines of Media Studies, Sociology, Anthropology, and Technology. Additionally, building on Moser’s central assertion that media, particularly television, serves as a pivotal platform for either guiding or misleading the public, this observation presents a promising avenue for further examination of, for instance, the intersection of morality and epistemology in shaping and sustaining constructed realities within the context of fake news. This argument also underscores the profound influence of media in shaping collective realities. This observation could be further developed to investigate the role of emerging technologies—such as artificial intelligence and deepfake videos—in perpetuating or combating hyperreality. Exploring these dimensions would enhance the relevance of Moser’s work in addressing future challenges posed by technological advancements.While Moser’s arguments may occasionally appear repetitive due to his frequent references to the dangers of hyperreality and the suggested mitigation strategies, this does not diminish the significance of the issues he raises. His openness to transdisciplinary dialogue is efficacious and impactful, making Fake News in Contemporary Science and Politics a critical contribution to understanding the complexities of living in a post-truth world. Indeed, his work challenges readers to confront the epistemic and ethical implications of a society increasingly governed by manufactured realities and offers a thought-provoking framework for navigating the uncertainties of the post-truth era.

Title: Book Reviews
Venue: JAWRA Journal of the American Water Resources Association
Abstract: TIPON: Water Engineering Masterpiece of the Inca Empire , Kenneth, R. Wright , ASCE Press , 1801 Alex Bell Dr., Reston, Virginia 20191-4400 . 2006 . 153 pages. $56. ISBN 0-7844-0851-3 . Author Kenneth R. Wright and his collaborators have delighted and inspired the water resources community with their paleohydrological work in Macchu Picchu. Now they turn to another, perhaps lesser-known, marvel of Inca engineering: the Tipon archeological site in the Cusco region of Peru. In 12 short chapters, this new book blends perspectives from a number of fields, including archaeology, history, civil engineering, hydrology, hydraulics, climatology, agriculture, architecture, construction, and geology. These various interlocking perspectives cannot be neatly separated. For example, Chapter 3, “Ancient Climate” parallels reconstructed paleoclimate with the sequence of pre-Inca empires and Andean agriculture, placing Tipon in its physical, sociological, and political context. The chapters, although related to each other, are somewhat independent. A reader could choose to browse or skip some and read others in depth, without losing essential information. Chapters 1 and 2 provide overviews of Tipon’s features. Chapters 4 through 9 examine various features in more detail, always including the cultural context: the Central Terraces, Hydrology, Canal System, Hydraulic Engineering, Buildings and Structures, Outer Wall and Cruzmoqo (a mountain summit structure with military and religious significance). Chapter 10 is a general introduction to Inca design and construction. Chapter 11 (contributed by G.L. McEwan) provides an overview of pre-Inca and Inca history and culture. Finally, Chapter 12 (by Ruth M. Wright) is a walking tour of the site; some readers may be fortunate enough to visit Tipon; others can trace the tour on a map, cross-reference the book’s many photos, and imagine being there in person. The author is a practicing engineer and applies familiar methods to estimate irrigation water requirements for the agricultural terraces, precipitation supply to the region, rates of ground water and surface water delivery, and flow rates in the hydraulic structures. The author’s collaborators include current experts on the Inca; the reference lists includes sources as recent as 2005. As a starting point for further research, the references are heavy on archaeology and culture (Inca and pre-Inca), but also include works on paleoclimatology as well as modern-day standards for water quality and hydrologic/hydraulic design. The book is nicely designed for either casual browsing or thorough reading. The page space is approximately evenly divided between text and a variety of graphical material. Attention to typography (typeface, line length, word and line spacing) and the use of frequent subheadings make the text very readable. Each chapter begins on a right-hand page, with a preview box on the left-facing page; a casual reader could learn a great deal by flipping through the book and reading these 12 preview boxes: “A Perfect Setting,”“Work Begins,”“The Inca Learned From the Past,” etc. Every page contains at least one graphical image; these include ground-based and aerial photography, maps, quantitative graphs, historic sketches, and contemporary scale drawings. Image captions are grouped at the bottom of pages, providing a clean, uncluttered look even for page spreads with a half a dozen images; clever geometric icons connect the captions to their respective subjects. Readers who are familiar with Wright Water Engineers’ spectacular Macchu Picchu calendar series – and expecting more of the same – might find the small black-and-white photos disappointing. These photos, however, illustrate the ideas developed in the text and become more impressive after closer study. A cover worthy of a “coffee-table book” and eight pages of color plates begin to satisfy the desire for scenic beauty while keeping the book’s price economical. Although it refers to several centuries of scholarship, this is not a scholarly book. The writing style is informal, even conversational [for example: “...just who built (the outer wall) represents a question that has not yet been answered. More about that later.”] The author’s stated aim is to “provide modern engineers and casual tourists alike with an appreciation of the Inca civilization through the analysis of the works they left behind.” The technical details are appropriate for anyone with undergraduate-level training in hydraulics and hydrology. The author’s genuine enthusiasm and admiration of the ancient engineers are contagious. Tipon is recommended for anyone who wishes to appreciate and celebrate the accomplishments and importance of water engineering in a global and historical context. Kaye L. Brubaker Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering University of Maryland College Park, Maryland 20742 Wetland Systems to Control Urban Runoff , Miklas, Scholz . Elsevier , Radarweg 29, P.O. Box 211, 1000 AE, Amsterdam, The Netherlands . 2006 . 333 pages. ISBN 0-444-52734-6 . While wetlands are gaining popularity for treatment of stormwater and wastewater, there is still a great deal to learn about how these systems operate as part of a treatment train. Traditional treatment processes and design are well understood, but this knowledge is only slowly leaking into the use and design of wetlands and other sustainable urban drainage systems (SUDS; also known as best management practices, BMPs, in the U.S.). Miklas Scholz takes on the formidable task to develop a wide ranging book in scope and audience. Wetland Systems to Control Urban Runoff attempts to bridge this gap in knowledge with a book aimed at students, researchers, and professionals to comprehensively discuss the science, design, operation, and performance of traditional and wetland systems. The author writes clearly to provide a succinct summary of traditional treatment processes and performance analysis of different wetland systems. The beginning of the book (Chapters 1-5) briefly reviews and orients an unfamiliar reader to basic water and wastewater chemistry, sewage treatment, and common pollutants found in streams and stormwater. A large part of the book (Chapters 6-23) focuses on different treatment components and the accompanied processes. Preliminary and primary treatment units, such as screening units, settling tanks, coagulation and flocculation techniques, and clarifiers are described (Chapters 6-11) and include design considerations and details. Logically, the next several chapters (Chapters 12-23) review secondary and tertiary treatment processes and waste disposal considerations. Each of these chapters is short and concise, which aids in readability and the use of this book as a reference resource. This overview effectively summarizes the main mechanisms and concepts of the processes of a traditional waste/wastewater treatment system. The reader should seek another source if a detailed explanation of this material is needed, although good sources are not indicated within the text. Throughout the chapters on treatment processes, infrequent mention is made of how a specific process is connected to a wetland system aside from that it functions before or after the wetland in the treatment train. Chapter 16 considers constructed wetlands, specifically typical chemistry and biology within wetlands, and types of wetlands. However, strong connections are not drawn between this chapter and the rest of the book. The first 23 chapters read as a refresher of a treatment textbook. The chapters that follow (Chapters 24-31) describe several different SUDS experiments, and read as stand-alone journal articles based on the previous work of Scholz. There is no segue between these two distinct parts in subject matter or style. The case studies analyze different experimental scenarios, such as wetland systems to treat stream water, roof runoff, and road runoff. These studies are current, informative, and demonstrate the key elements for pollutant removal; interestingly, several of the case studies showed that the presence of vegetation did not significantly increase pollutant removal for subsurface flow wetlands (Chapter 26). Chapters 28 and 30 evaluate different model and assessment tools for SUDS. These two chapters are the most useful, as they provide a tool for choosing the technology that would be best for a proposed application and methods to efficiently monitor and evaluate SUDS performance. Despite the background of treatment science, several case studies, and modeling tools that are given in this work, there is a missing link: how to implement wetland systems into traditional treatment facilities in an innovative and practical way. Many of the case studies are at the laboratory scale and specific to stormwater applications. The question remains as to how the laboratory results scale to a treatment facility, particularly with regards to ensuring effluent quality throughout the year and over time. From my reading, Scholz does not fully achieve the lofty ambition to provide a comprehensive text for students, researchers, and practitioners on the science and incorporation of wetlands into treatment practices. Thus, Treatment Wetland by Kadlec and Knight (CRC Press, 1996) remains the reigning text on the science, design, and performance of wetland systems. However, this book is a step in highlighting the usefulness of wetland systems as a unit within the treatment train of stormwater and wastewater. This work is useful to graduate students and researchers and will hopefully entice more study and literature on connecting our depth and breadth of knowledge of traditional treatment practices with emerging SUDS technologies. Batzer and Rebecca Sharitz ( Editors ). University of California Press , 2120 Berkeley Way, Berkeley, California 94720 . 2006 . 568 pages. $60. ISBN 978-0-520-24777-2 . Seventeen authors, mostly affiliated with universities, contributed to the 12 chapters of Ecology of Freshwater and Estuarine Wetlands. The chapters and sections are well organized and arranged; the book essentially comprises a series of review articles, each averaging about 40 pages. Chapter 1 provides a very brief introduction and foundation for all of the chapters. The following three chapters cover the physical features of wetlands, including geomorphology, soils, and hydrology. Chapter 2 describes how landscape influences hydrology and other conditions that lead to the occurrence of wetlands. Later in the chapter the properties of wetland soils are explained, followed by a description of features unique to depressional, nondepressional, and estuarine wetlands. Chapter 3 builds on this foundation and considers a wide range of topics in hydrology, including vadose (soil water) flow, phreatic (ground water) flow, wetland water budgets, hydropatterns, and effects of land use. Chapter 4 provides a bridge between wetland plants and animals and their relationship to abiotic factors, with excellent photographs, descriptions, and references. Chapters 5 through 8 describe the core of wetland ecology, moving from bacteria to plant ecology, and on through the interaction of animals and wetlands. Chapter 5, the longest at 60 pages, integrates and synthesizes the relationship among bacteria, biogeochemistry, and hydrology. This relationship creates, perhaps, the foundation upon which most other wetland ecological processes occur. In the first part of Chapter 6, general concepts of plant ecology are covered and the second part provides specific characteristics of plant communities and their dynamics in a wide range of wetland types. Chapter 7 presents similar treatment for wetland animals, which have received less attention in past research and literature; this chapter, therefore, gives a unique review concerning wetland ecology. Finally, Chapter 8 builds upon the pervious chapters by describing wetland systems and introduces the potential effects of global change. Evidence presented supports the significance of algal periphyton in the biotic dynamics of wetland ecosystems. The last section of the book focuses on applied wetland ecology. This section opens with a chapter on wetland regulation and policy, which at first glance seems to have little to do with ecology. The relationship, however, becomes clear in the later parts of the chapter, where wetland delineation and functional assessment are reviewed. Chapter 10 provides a very readable account of approaches and pitfalls to wetland restoration, with many case studies. Chapter 11 covers “flood-pulsing” systems, which refer to riverine and floodplain wetlands. When compared to the large diversity in the types of wetlands, it seems unusual to single out this group. Flood-pulsing systems, however, do exhibit a unique oscillation between aquatic and terrestrial habitat, with much of the recent research carried out by the contributing authors. Finally, the book concludes with a review of how changing global climate will affect wetland ecology and function, and recommends methods for future management. The style of each chapter varies because the multiple authors have a wide range of experiences and backgrounds. Most of the chapters succeed in providing an up-to-date, detailed review of current knowledge and research questions. A few chapters, however, make a greater attempt to explain fundamentals. For example, Chapter 3 partly focuses less on recent research and more on hydrological concepts by presenting equations that describe soil-water properties, vadose flow, phreatic flow, and very basic models of evapotranspiration. It reads like an introductory textbook on hydrology, but lacks examples, explanations, and limitations of how these equations and models can be applied to wetland systems. Additional resources will be needed by interested readers who lack experience in hydrology. Several important topics in wetland hydrology are generally omitted, including past and recent literature that relates to ground-water interaction/surface-water interaction, hyporheic flow in riverine wetlands, surface-water hydraulics, and the dynamics of water storage. In contrast, the chapter on wetland restoration is especially stimulating, informative, and useful. Several tables and concept boxes provide guidance on wetland restoration that includes the collective wisdom of years of success and failure. Concerning content, the closest book on the market today is Mitsch and Gosselink’s Wetlands, originally published in 1986 and now in its Third Edition (published in 2000). Wetlands contains many of the same topics and has experienced great success as a college textbook. Wetland Ecology by Keddy (2004) covers similar ground as Ecology of Freshwater and Estuarine Wetlands, but takes a more generic and traditional approach toward ecological principles. Wetland Soils, edited by Richardson and Vepraskas (2000) focuses on soils and hydrology in much greater detail. Similarly, Chapter 9 of Ecology of Freshwater and Estuarine Wetlands gives only a very brief summary of delineation and functional assessment when compared to Tiner’s more practical and applied Wetland Indicators (published in 1999). According to the editors, Ecology of Freshwater and Estuarine Wetlands was written to provide a textbook for college-level wetland ecology courses. The variable detail and differences in style among chapters will likely make it difficult to use as a textbook. Although it could fill the need for a seminar-style graduate course, it serves more as a reference book. Nonetheless, this volume will be valuable to serious students of wetland ecology and professional wetland scientists who need to quickly find and assess recent research and understand the basics of ancillary topics.
