Title: Automated Region-of-interest Localization and Classification for Visual Assessment
Venue: International Workshop on Structural Health Monitoring (IWSHM)
Abstract: Visual assessment is a process to understand the state of a structure based on evaluations originating from visual data. Low-cost, high-performance vision sensors are providing new avenues for overcoming the spatial and temporal limitation in current human-based visual assessment when used in conjunction with aerial sensing platforms. However, past implementations are limited in their ability to deal with a high volume of images while only a small fraction of them are important for actual inspection. Such difficulty induces an unwanted high rate of false-positive and negative errors, reducing the trustworthiness and efficiency of their implementation. To overcome this challenge, we develop and validate a novel automated image localization and classification technique to extract regions-of-interest (ROIs) on each of images, which contain the target region of the structure for visual evaluation (TRI). First, ROIs are extracted based on the geometric relationship between the collected images and the TRIs using structure-from-motion algorithm. Second, unwanted ROIs corrupted by occlusion and image blur are effectively filtered by a robust image classification technique, called convolutional neural network. Then, a damage detection technique is applied only on such highly relevant and localized ROI images. The capability of the technique is demonstrated using a full-scale highway sign structure for the case of crack detection on weld connections.

Title: Unsupervised Representation Learning for Surface Variability Discovery in Natural Cork Stoppers
AI-Powered Industrial Automation: Trends and Challenges
Venue: Journal of Advanced Engineering & Applied Sciences
Abstract: The introduction of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has greatly changed the nature of automation in industries making manufacturing processes smarter, efficient, and adapting. Industrial automation using AI makes use of machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), computer vision and predictive analytics to streamline the production process, cut down on operational expenses, increase safety and quality. In this paper, we are going to take a look at the modern trends and uses and issues which are related to the integration of AI into industrial automation systems. Among the most important tendencies, there are autonomous robotics, predictive maintenance, AI-based quality control, and real-time process optimization. Another issue that the study recognizes potentially impacting the successful implementation of AI technologies is the issue of data security, system interoperability, workforce adaptation, and algorithm transparency. The results indicate that, although AI adoption can be highly beneficial in terms of productivity, efficiency, and decision-making, one should pay extra attention to the issue of data governance, human-machine cooperation, and the regulatory framework to implement AI sustainably.

Title: Preparing for an agentic era of human-machine transportation systems: Opportunities, challenges, and policy recommendations
Sensor Fault-Tolerant Thermal Error Modeling Method for CNC Machine Tools Based on Temperature Feedback LSTM(TF-LSTM)
PROBLEMS IN NAVIGATION SYSTEMS OF AIRCRAFT AND THEIR SOLUTIONS
Venue: International journal of technology and academic research
Abstract: This article systematically analyses the principal problems encountered in navigation systems of modern aircraft and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), and evaluates contemporary technological solutions. Five core problem categories are identified: GPS signal loss and spoofing attacks, inertial navigation system (INS) drift accumulation, sensor failures due to electromagnetic interference and environmental factors, navigation degradation under electronic warfare (EW) conditions, and meteorological influences on navigation accuracy. Solutions examined include Extended and Unscented Kalman Filter (EKF/UKF) algorithms, artificial intelligence-based navigation, visual odometry and SLAM, terrain-aided navigation (TAN), and redundant fault-tolerant sensor architectures. The study draws on ICAO, EUROCONTROL, and NASA technical documentation, as well as peer-reviewed publications from IEEE Aerospace & Electronic Systems.

Title: A New Health Index for RUL Estimation of MEMS Sensors Using Dimensionality Reduction and Artificial Neural Networks
Venue: IEEE Transactions on Instrumentation and Measurement
Abstract: The accurate estimation of the remaining useful life (RUL) of micro-electromechanical systems (MEMS) sensors is crucial for enabling effective condition-based maintenance (CBM) and improving system reliability. This is of vital importance in planning machinery replacements before their actual fault, reducing downtime and thus greatly optimizing costs. However, unlike industrial components (such as bearings, rotating machinery, or power devices), current prognostic strategies for MEMS sensors are limited due to the lack of suitable health indexes (HIs) capable of describing the degradation path of the sensor’s metrological performances. To address this gap, this article proposes a novel HI for MEMS accelerometers based on static accelerometer outputs by combining time-domain and frequency-domain features using a dimensionality reduction technique. By applying dimensionality reduction, the method captures the essential characteristics of sensor degradation, which are then used to train a deep learning-based model for predicting the RUL sufficiently in advance to allow for appropriate maintenance. This article aims to fill an important gap by providing an innovative solution for MEMS sensor prognostics, with broad implications for industrial sectors reliant on precision sensing technologies. The performance of the proposed health indicator is validated through experimental data, demonstrating its ability to enhance the accuracy of MEMS sensor prognostics. Using data from the proposed accelerated life test and the Arrhenius degradation model, the RUL prediction based on the proposed health indicator has been performed at various operating temperatures, including typical conditions of industrial environments with high thermal stress.

Title: Interpretable AI for predicting crack propagation analysis in 3D-printed gear systems
Abstract: The significance of structural integrity tests is growing for 3D-printed gear systems utilised in automotive, aerospace, and industrial applications. Crack initiation and propagation in additive manufacturing must be predicted owing to the presence of anisotropic materials, layer-by-layer flaws, and residual loads. This work presents an explainable XAI framework for predicting crack propagation in dynamically stressed 3D-printed polymer and metal gear systems. Digital image correlation, vibration sensing, and thermography collect high-resolution microstructural, geometric, and operational data. A convolutional neural network informed recurrent unit hybrid deep learning model captures the spatial patterns of cracks and their temporal changes. Engineer friendly XAI approaches, including SHAP values, Grad-CAM visualisation, and feature attribution mapping, demonstrates the process of crack growth through microstructural flaws, print orientation, loading parameters, and environmental variables. The experimental evaluation of multimaterial 3D-printed gear prototypes provides accurate predictions and robust finite element fracture model connections. This predictive framework with XAI is trustworthy and simple to use for making next-generation 3D-printed mechanical components last longer, be of high quality, and regulate their lifespans.

Title: Intelligent Sensor Fault Diagnosis in Autonomous Robotic Platforms
Venue: International Journal of Intelligent Automation & Robotics Engineering
Abstract: Autonomous robotic platforms have become an integral part of industrial automation, intelligent manufacturing, autonomous transportation, precision agriculture, healthcare robotics, and hazardous environment exploration. The operational reliability of these robotic systems strongly depends on the accuracy and health of their sensing infrastructure. Sensors including inertial measurement units (IMUs), LiDAR, cameras, ultrasonic sensors, GPS modules, encoders, force-torque sensors, and proximity sensors continuously provide environmental and operational information for autonomous decision-making. However, sensor degradation, calibration drift, communication failures, environmental interference, and hardware aging can significantly deteriorate robotic performance and may even lead to catastrophic failures. Consequently, intelligent sensor fault diagnosis has emerged as a critical research area that combines artificial intelligence, machine learning, data analytics, and model-based reasoning to identify, classify, and predict sensor faults in real time. In this paper, a complete intelligent sensor fault diagnosis framework for autonomous robotic platforms is proposed. The proposed framework utilizes the integration of multi-sensor data fusion, feature extraction, deep learning-based fault classification, anomaly detection, and predictive maintenance components into a unified architecture. Experimental performance evaluation shows significant enhancements versus traditional threshold-based diagnostic approaches in terms of high fault detection accuracy, lower false alarms and reduction in the latency for diagnosis among different faults with an increased reliability level on system diagnosis. These results demonstrate that AI-assisted diagnostic models significantly increased robotic autonomy through the ability to proactively manage faults, reduce downtime and enhance operational safety. The proposed framework is suitable for deployment in Industry 5.0 manufacturing systems, autonomous vehicles, collaborative robots, and intelligent service robotics.

Title: Deep Learning–Driven Analysis and Quantification of Histopathologic Features in a Dextran Sulfate Sodium–Induced Colitis Mouse Model
Abstract: Dextran-based colitis models have been used extensively to study the pathophysiology of inflammatory bowel disease, including ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease. Histologic studies of animal colon sections require an unbiased scoring to yield meaningful outcomes. These examinations tend to be tedious, time-consuming, and influenced by inherent human bias, which can be reduced with digital pathology tools. In this study, a deep learning-based classifier was used to identify and quantify key histologic features in colon sections from a dextran sodium sulfate-induced colitis mouse model. The artificial intelligence (AI)-based classifiers were trained on HALO, an interactive human-in-the-loop image analysis platform, to sequentially identify tissues, mucosa, submucosa, and lymphoid tissues followed by quantification of different levels of tissue damage and cell infiltration within subregions, as well as goblet cell numbers and several cell types based on nuclear phenotyping. AI-based assessments could accurately identify key pathologic features and detect alleviation of the damage. This quantitative AI-based assessment of tissue damage exhibited good correlation and better sensitivity to detect histopathologic changes compared with the pathologists' assessment. This proof-of-concept study successfully established the efficiency of machine learning-based classifiers in characterizing disease pathology and their utility during the initial phases of drug discovery.

Title: Modality Bias in LVLMs: Analyzing and Mitigating Object Hallucination via Attention Lens
Abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) have demonstrated remarkable multimodal comprehension and reasoning capabilities, but they still suffer from severe object hallucination. Previous studies primarily attribute the flaw to linguistic prior caused by the scale mismatch between visual encoders and large language models (LLMs) in LVLMs. Specifically, as current LVLMs are built upon LLMs, they tend to over-rely on textual prompts and internal knowledge of LLMs, generating descriptions inconsistent with visual cues. However, through an in-depth investigation of the hallucinated mechanisms, we empirically reveal a previously overlooked phenomenon: LVLMs may ignore not only visual information but also textual modality during hallucination, a behavior termed as modality bias, which indicates that LVLMs struggle to simultaneously attend to both visual and textual modalities, leading to fragmented understanding of user-provided instructions. Based on this observation, we propose a simple yet effective training-free method to mitigate object hallucination. Concretely, we intervene and adjust the attention weights of textual and visual tokens, balancing cross-modal compatibility for better alignment with user intentions. Furthermore, we adopt a contrastive decoding strategy to reduce the LVLM's overreliance on its parametric knowledge, synergistically enhancing our attention manipulation. Extensive experiments confirm the widespread presence of modality bias in LVLMs. Notably, our method effectively mitigates hallucination across multiple open-source LVLMs and benchmarks, highlighting its generalizability and efficacy.

Title: The Algorithmic Leviathan: Artificial Intelligence, the Reshaping of Political Power, and the Existential Threat to Human Agency
Abstract: Master of information technology, Belhaven University, USA Master of Population Science, University of Dhaka, Bangladesh Email: ashikur.rahman.nazil@gmail.com AbstractThe rapid proliferation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies is precipitating a paradigm shift in the nature of political power, global stability, and the very fabric of human society. This paper posits that AI is not merely a tool but a transformative force capable of creating unprecedented forms of centralized control, destabilizing international relations, and ultimately posing an existential threat to human autonomy. The thesis is structured to first analyze the mechanisms by which AI enables the rise of "digital dictatorships," enhancing state capacity for surveillance, propaganda, and social control to an extent that eclipses historical totalitarian regimes. Subsequently, the paper examines the global power impact, arguing that AI is becoming the new currency of geopolitical dominance, creating a dangerous arms race that risks conflict and systemic collapse. The core argument culminates in an exploration of the ultimate danger: the potential cession of political and social decision-making to autonomous AI systems. This scenario, termed the "Algorithmic Leviathan," threatens to reduce humanity to a state of managed dependency, eroding free will, stifling subsequent generations, and effectively ending meaningful human political life. By synthesizing research from computer science, political science, and ethics, this paper contends that the unmitigated integration of AI into political structures paves a path toward a future where humanity becomes a slave to its own creation, with catastrophic consequences for future generations. The conclusion underscores the urgent need for robust, global governance frameworks to ensure AI remains a tool for human empowerment rather than the instrument of its subjugation. Keywords—Artificial Intelligence, Political Power, Authoritarianism, Global Politics, Existential Risk, AI Governance, Social Control, Future Generations, Algorithmic Leviathan. I. Introduction THE 21st century is defined by a technological revolution whose core engine is Artificial Intelligence (AI). From machine learning and natural language processing to predictive analytics and autonomous systems, AI is reshaping economies, cultures, and societies at an accelerating pace. However, its most profound and potentially perilous impact may be on the structure and exercise of political power. The central thesis of this paper is that the uncontrolled development and deployment of AI systems pose a fundamental threat to democratic norms, global stability, and ultimately, human sovereignty. We are at a critical juncture where the design and governance of AI will determine whether it serves as a tool for human betterment or becomes the foundation for a new, and perhaps final, form of tyranny. Historically, political power has been derived from control over resources, territory, information, and the means of violence. AI is fundamentally altering this calculus. It offers a new source of power: control over cognition and prediction. States and non-state actors that can most effectively harness AI for surveillance, persuasion, and strategic analysis can amass power on a scale previously unimaginable. This paper argues that this dynamic is leading to three interconnected catastrophic outcomes: The Creation of Unprecedented Dictatorships: AI provides authoritarian regimes with the tools to achieve near-total societal control, creating systems of governance that are more resilient, intrusive, and efficient than any in history. This is not merely an enhancement of existing models but a qualitative leap into a new form of digital totalitarianism. The Destabilization of Global Power: AI is becoming the central axis of geopolitical competition, driving an arms race in autonomous weapons, cyber warfare, and information operations. This erodes the existing world order, increases the risk of miscalculation and conflict, and could lead to a new, unstable bipolar or multipolar world dominated by AI superpowers. The End of Human-Centric Politics and Society: The most extreme, yet increasingly plausible, risk is the gradual or abrupt cession of political and social decision-making to AI systems. This would mark the end of politics as a human endeavor, reducing citizens to managed data points, stifling human creativity and dissent, and damning future generations to a life of pre-determined outcomes and psychological dependency, effectively rendering them slaves to the algorithm. This paper is structured to systematically unpack this argument. Section II provides a conceptual framework, defining key terms and outlining the theoretical basis for AI as a political force. Section III delves into the mechanics of the AI-enabled dictatorship, examining its pillars of surveillance, propaganda, and social control. Section IV analyzes the global implications, focusing on the AI arms race and the shifting balance of power. Section V confronts the existential risk of full AI control, exploring the philosophical and practical consequences for human agency and future generations. Section VI discusses potential mitigation strategies and governance models. Finally, Section VII offers a concluding summary and a dire warning about the path ahead. The methodology of this paper is interdisciplinary, drawing on technical literature concerning AI capabilities, political science theories of power and the state, historical analyses of totalitarianism, and ethical frameworks from philosophy. It employs a qualitative analysis of existing trends to project a normative warning about a potential future, aiming to spur proactive discourse and policy action. II. Conceptual Framework: AI as a Political Artifact To understand AI's impact on political power, one must first move beyond viewing it as a neutral tool. AI, particularly machine learning, is a socio-technical system embedded with human values, biases, and political objectives. A. Defining Political Power in the Algorithmic Age Classical political theorists like Max Weber defined power as the ability to impose one's will despite resistance. Steven Lukes added a "third dimension" of power: the ability to shape others' perceptions and desires. AI operationalizes all three dimensions with terrifying efficiency. First Dimension (Decision-Making): AI can automate bureaucratic and legal processes, directly influencing who gets what, when, and how. Algorithmic resource allocation, predictive policing, and automated justice systems are direct exercises of political power. Second Dimension (Agenda-Setting): AI-driven information ecosystems can control what issues are debated and what alternatives are considered. By flooding information channels with specific content, AI can make certain policy options seem unthinkable. Third Dimension (Preference-Shaping): This is AI's most potent application. Through micro-targeted propaganda and manipulation of social media feeds, AI can engineer consensus, manufacture consent, and shape the very identities and desires of a population, ensuring they align with state or corporate objectives. B. The Pillars of AI-Enhanced Power The political potency of AI rests on several key technological pillars: Big Data and Surveillance: The fuel for AI systems. The ubiquitous collection of digital footprints—from social media, financial transactions, location data, and Internet of Things (IoT) devices—creates a digital panopticon of unprecedented scale. Machine Learning and Predictive Analytics: The engine. ML algorithms can identify patterns, predict individual and group behavior, and flag anomalies. This allows authorities to anticipate dissent, identify potential opponents, and optimize control strategies. Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Generative AI: The voice. NLP enables the analysis of sentiment and intent at scale. Generative AI (e.g., Large Language Models) can produce limitless, targeted, and highly persuasive text, audio, and video content for propaganda and disinformation campaigns. Autonomous Systems: The fist. From drones to software bots, autonomous systems can enact physical and digital enforcement without direct human intervention, enabling scalable and relentless application of power. This technological convergence creates a feedback loop: more data leads to better models, which enable more effective control, which in turn generates more data. This loop is the foundation of the new political order we are entering. III. The AI-Enabled Dictatorship: Creation and Perpetuation The marriage of AI with state authority does not just strengthen existing authoritarian regimes; it creates a new model of governance—the algorithmic dictatorship. This system is characterized by a move from reactive repression to proactive, pervasive, and personalized control. A. The Perfected Panopticon: Totalitarian Surveillance Historically, surveillance was limited by human resources. The Stasi in East Germany employed one informant for every 66 citizens—a massive undertaking. Today, AI-powered surveillance is infinitely scalable. China's Social Credit System is a prime, though often oversimplified, example. It integrates data from countless sources—financial records, social media activity, purchase history, and a vast network of facial recognition cameras—to generate a score for each citizen. This score determines access to loans, employment, travel, and education. The psychological effect of such a system is profound. As Jeremy Bentham and Michel Foucault theorized with the panopticon, the mere knowledge that one could be being watched at any time induces self-censorship and conformity. AI makes the panopticon perfect. Citizens become their own wardens, internalizing the state's values not out of genuine belief, but out of fear of algorithmic penalty. This creates a society where dissent is pre-emptively extinguished, not through gulags, but through digital exclusion and social throttling. B. The Manufacture of Consent: AI-Driven Propaganda and Disinformation If surveillance is the stick, AI-powered propaganda is the carrot. The 2016 Brexit referendum and U.S. presidential election provided a glimpse of this power, but the technology has advanced exponentially since. Generative AI can now produce "deepfakes"—hyper-realistic but fabricated video and audio—and millions of unique, persuasive text messages tailored to the psychological profile of every individual. Micro-Targeting: By analyzing a user's data, AI can identify their fears, biases, and aspirations. It can then deliver a bespoke narrative designed to provoke an emotional response, whether it's anger, fear, or tribal loyalty. This fragments public discourse into billions of individual realities, making a shared, fact-based consensus impossible. Synthetic Media and Reality Apathy: The proliferation of deepfakes will lead to a state of "reality apathy" or "the liar's dividend," where the public, unable to distinguish truth from falsehood, simply disengages from factual discourse altogether. In this environment, the entity with the most powerful AI can define reality itself, creating a "post-truth" world where power is the ultimate arbiter of truth. This automated, personalized propaganda machine is far more effective than the state-controlled media of the 20th century. It doesn't just broadcast a message; it engages each citizen in a unique, manipulative dialogue, eroding the capacity for critical thought and independent political judgment. C. Predictive Policing and Social Control AI enables a shift from punishing past actions to pre-empting future behavior. "Predictive policing" algorithms, already used in some Western democracies, analyze historical crime data to forecast where crime is likely to occur or who is likely to commit it. In an authoritarian context, this concept is expanded to "predictive dissidence." An algorithm might flag an individual as a "high risk" for subversion based on their online reading habits, social connections, or even physiological data from wearables. This person could then be subject to pre-emptive measures: a visit from the police, restrictions on their movement, or a downgrade of their social credit score. The crime is no longer an act, but a statistically probable future state. This is the ultimate form of social control, targeting thought and potential before it can manifest as action. It creates a system where the only safe path is absolute conformity, effectively destroying the concept of political freedom. IV. The Global Power Impact: AI as a Geopolitical Weapon The concentration of AI power is not merely a domestic issue; it is reshaping the international order. The global competition for AI supremacy is the defining geopolitical race of the 21st century, with the potential to create new superpowers and destroy existing ones. A. The AI Arms Race: Lethal Autonomous Weapons and Cyber Warfare The most immediate danger is the militarization of AI. The development of Lethal Autonomous Weapons (LAWS), or "slaughterbots," represents a fundamental shift in warfare. These are systems that, once activated, can identify, select, and engage targets without further human intervention. Pro-liferation and Instability: LAWS lower the threshold for conflict. They are cheaper than human soldiers and can be deployed in massive swarms. A nation might be tempted to launch a swift, automated attack, believing it can achieve its objectives without risking a full-scale war. This increases the risk of miscalculation and rapid, uncontrollable escalation. The Responsibility Gap: If an autonomous weapon commits a war crime, who is responsible? The programmer, the commander, or the machine itself? This legal and moral vacuum undermines the foundations of international humanitarian law. AI in Cyber Warfare: AI supercharges cyber attacks. It can be used to find vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure (power grids, financial systems, water supplies) at machine speed, launch coordinated disinformation campaigns to destabilize rival nations, and create adaptive malware that can evade traditional defenses. A future conflict may begin not with a declaration of war, but with the silent, AI-driven collapse of a nation's digital backbone. B. The Shift in Economic and Strategic Dominance AI is a core driver of economic productivity and innovation. Nations that lead in AI research and development will likely dominate the industries of the future, from biotechnology to renewable energy. This economic power translates directly into geopolitical influence. The current competition is largely bipolar, between the United States and China. China's strategy, outlined in its "New Generation Artificial Intelligence Development Plan," is to become the world's primary AI innovation center by 2030. It combines state-directed investment, massive data collection from its population, and a lack of ethical constraints to achieve rapid progress. The U.S., while leading in fundamental research, is hampered by a fragmented regulatory approach and public concerns over privacy. This competition creates a new "AI divide." A small group of AI superpowers could exert immense influence over the rest of the world, imposing their technological standards and, by extension, their political and ethical values. Title: Optimizing urban tree structural risk assessment: An explainable machine learning framework integrating expert knowledge and multi-source data
DEVELOPMENT OF A SECURED DEEP LEARNING-BASED CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE PREDICTION SYSTEM WITH ADVERSARIAL ATTACK DETECTION AND DEFENCE MECHANISMS
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains among the leading causes of mortality worldwide, and deep learning models are increasingly applied to ECG signals, medical imaging, and clinical records to support early detection and risk assessment. However, such models are known to be highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks, intentionally crafted, often imperceptible input perturbations that can force incorrect predictions and compromise patient safety. This study developed and evaluated a secured deep learning-based cardiovascular disease prediction system that integrates a predictive neural network with adversarial attack detection and defense mechanisms within a single pipeline. Statistical anomaly detection, autoencoder-based reconstruction error analysis, and input sensitivity evaluation were combined to flag manipulated inputs, while adversarial training, input preprocessing, and ensemble-based regularization were used to strengthen model resilience. The system was benchmarked on standard datasets and evaluated under Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM), Projected Gradient Descent (PGD), and Carlini & Wagner (C&W) attack simulations. Results show that although the baseline model achieved strong performance on clean data (96.4% accuracy), performance degraded substantially under adversarial conditions in the absence of protection, most severely under PGD attack. Integrating detection and defense mechanisms raised adversarial accuracy from 58.7% to 88.6% while preserving clean-data performance, confirming that a layered, security-first architecture meaningfully improves the reliability and trustworthiness of AI-driven cardiovascular prediction systems without materially sacrificing predictive accuracy.

Title: A bimodal framework for nonstationary process monitoring via collaborative contrastive and adversarial unsupervised learning
Explainable AI (XAI) for Predictive Maintenance of Industrial Induction Motors
Abstract: Industrial induction motors constitute the mechanical backbone of modern manufacturing ecosystems, yet unplanned failures account for substantial production losses and safety hazards. While machine learning-driven predictive maintenance frameworks have demonstrated considerable diagnostic efficacy, their inherent opacity hinders adoption by maintenance engineers who require transparent, actionable rationales for model predictions. This paper proposes a novel Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) framework integrated with an ensemble machine learning architecture for real-time fault detection and remaining useful life (RUL) estimation in three-phase induction motors. The proposed system leverages vibration, current, and thermal sensor streams, extracts time-frequency features, and employs an XGBoost classifier augmented with SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) and LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) to deliver both global and instance-level transparency. Experimental validation on a curated industrial dataset encompassing five operational states—normal operation, bearing defect, rotor bar failure, stator winding fault, and air gap eccentricity—yields an overall classification accuracy of 96.7%, precision of 95.9%, recall of 96.2%, and F1-score of 96.0%, outperforming six benchmark algorithms. The XAI explanations reveal that current total harmonic distortion (THD) and vibration root mean square (RMS) are the principal discriminative features, findings that align with established motor fault physics and validate model trustworthiness for deployment in safety-critical industrial environments.

Title: WSN and UAV-Assisted Aircraft Structural Health Monitoring During Maintenance
Abstract: The research study is focused on tracking the structural health during maintenance by incorporating Wireless Sensor Network (WSN) and Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV). WSN embedded in aircraft are strain gauges, accelerometers, and temperature sensors to measure the real-time changes of parameters like stress, strain, and vibration. These are used to forward data from onboard sensors through a low-power long-range communication standard called Long Range (LoRa) to a base station. UAV is equipped with high-definition cameras, thermal infrared cameras, and Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) would be modified to inspect remote areas of airplanes. The UAV would be a video and thermal data capture traveling relay, hence relaying the sensor data back to the sensor nodes for processing. Data fusion techniques subsequently combine data from the WSN and UAV for the best aircraft maintenance. The fused data is taken into account by an Attention Mechanism-based Long Short Term Memory (AM-LSTM) model for predictive maintenance. The AM-LSTM model monitors the time-series sensor data to identify the patterns of structure and the need for future maintenance. These models enhance detection as they focus on prominent data features that can show early damage. Hence, proactive damage detection minimizes aircraft downtime and saves expensive repairs. The research proves the possibility of enhancement in the efficiency, safety, and reliability of aircraft maintenance using collaborative application of WSN, UAV, and deep learning, resulting in timely repair and more trustworthy operations.

Title: Robust and Explainable 3D Mode Shape Recognition Using Region-Aware Graph Neural Networks
Abstract: Mode shape recognition is a fundamental task in automotive NVH development, yet it remains dependent on manual visual inspection by experienced engineers. Existing approaches based on engineering heuristics, Modal Assurance Criterion (MAC), or geometry-dependent AI representations often exhibit limited robustness across different vehicle architectures, finite element (FE) meshes, and experimental measurement layouts, restricting their industrial applicability. This paper presents a Canonical Engineering Graph Representation and region-aware graph learning framework for robust and explainable 3D mode shape recognition. Rather than learning directly from vehicle-specific FE meshes, heterogeneous FE models and experimental measurements are transformed into a common graph whose nodes represent semantically meaningful structural regions connected through engineering-informed relationships. Geometry-independent regional descriptors are combined with graph attention learning and region-aware pooling to capture structural interactions while preserving engineering semantics and enabling physically interpretable predictions. The resulting representation decouples engineering knowledge from numerical discretization, allowing transfer across different vehicle programs without requiring identical mesh topology or sensor configurations. The proposed framework is validated using FE and experimental datasets from four vehicle programs under severe label scarcity. Results demonstrate high classification accuracy, cross-vehicle transferability, and physically meaningful explanations by directly relating predictions to engineering-defined structural regions used in NVH analysis. Beyond mode shape recognition, the proposed Canonical Engineering Graph Representation provides a reusable engineering abstraction for trustworthy and transferable AI across heterogeneous simulation and experimental workflows.

Title: Smart Drilling: Integrating AI for Process Optimisation and Quality Enhancement in Manufacturing
Venue: Journal of Manufacturing and Materials Processing
Abstract: Drilling is fundamental to the assembly of aerospace structures, where millions of fastening holes must meet stringent structural and geometric requirements. Despite significant technological advances, hole quality remains sensitive to nonlinear and stochastic interactions between mechanics, thermal effects, tribology, and structural configuration. This review consolidates recent advances in intelligent drilling, focusing on how sensors and artificial intelligence (AI) are integrated to enable process understanding, prediction, and control. In-process monitoring modalities (e.g., cutting forces/torque, vibration, acoustic emission, motor current/active power, infrared thermography, and vision) are examined with respect to signal characteristics, feature design, and modelling choices for real-time anomaly detection, tool condition monitoring, and phase/interface recognition. Predictive quality modelling of burr, delamination, roughness, and roundness is discussed across statistical learning, kernel methods, and neural and hybrid models. Offline parameter optimisation via surrogate-assisted and evolutionary algorithms is considered alongside adaptive control strategies. Practical aspects of robotic drilling and multifunctional end-effectors are highlighted as enablers of embedded sensing and feedback. Finally, cross-cutting challenges (e.g., limited, heterogeneous datasets and model generalisability across materials, tools, and geometries) are outlined, together with research directions including curated multi-sensor benchmarks, multi-source transfer learning, physics-informed machine learning, and explainable AI to support trustworthy deployment in aerospace manufacturing.

Title: Cracking the clinical code: A scoping review on mechanistic interpretability in medical report generation
Abstract: Medical report generation (MRG) bridges computer vision and natural language processing by translating clinical images into diagnostic text. Although encoder–decoder models have significantly advanced this domain, their opaque internal processes continue to impede clinical trust and regulatory acceptance. This survey presents a comprehensive methodological review of interpretability techniques applied to MRG, with particular emphasis on mechanistic interpretability. This emerging paradigm shifts the focus from attribution-based methods towards uncovering how specific model components such as neurons, attention heads, and residual connections encode diagnostic logic. We categorise core techniques including activation patching, causal tracing, circuit decomposition, and concept bottleneck probing, and propose a structured taxonomy spanning modalities, architectures, and evaluation strategies. Unlike conventional post hoc attribution methods, mechanistic approaches aim to provide causal, component-level explanations that are predictive and verifiable. We identify major challenges in this area, including cross-modal entanglement, the absence of internal ground-truth benchmarks, and the need for clinically aligned evaluation protocols. To address these limitations, we outline future research directions involving interpretable-by-design architectures, interactive explanation refinement through clinician feedback, and standardised metrics for mechanistic fidelity. By synthesising insights from machine learning, neuroscience, and radiology, this survey establishes a foundation for building MRG systems that are transparent, trustworthy, and clinically useful.

Title: Leveraging Large Language Models for Automated Insight Generation in Textile Manufacturing
Venue: Open Repository of the University of Porto (University of Porto)
Abstract: The textile manufacturing industry generates vast amounts of operational data, yet deriving actionable insights remains a manual and labor-intensive process due to the semantic gap between quantitative sensor logs and qualitative operator knowledge. While Artificial Intelligence (AI) has matured in the domain of defect detection via Computer Vision, current systems lack the reasoning capabilities to explain root causes or correlate visual defects with operational parameters. This dissertation proposes a Software Engineering (SE) architecture leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to automate insight generation in the knitting sector. A multi-agent system using Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and task-orchestration patterns is designed and implemented to abstract raw machine telemetry into human-readable narratives. Furthermore, specific software engineering challenges are addressed, including context-aware prompting for complex industrial schemas, deterministic metric aggregation, hallucination mitigation through execution-layer constraints, and secure architectural integration via the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The prototype is evaluated through automated tests for the Astra and MCP services and through a controlled comparison of seven OpenAI models generating the same daily factory report, measuring cost, runtime, token usage, completeness, and insight quality. The results show a functional and test-covered foundation for asynchronous daily report generation, while large-scale industrial validation remains future work.

Title: A Root Cause Analytics Model for Diagnosing Offshore Process Failures Using Live Operational Data
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Abstract: In offshore oil and gas operations, process failures can lead to significant production losses, environmental risks, and safety hazards. Traditional diagnostic approaches often rely on manual analysis and post-event investigations, which are time-consuming and reactive. This proposes a Root Cause Analytics (RCA) model designed to diagnose offshore process failures in real time using live operational data. The model integrates data streams from distributed sensors, control systems, and equipment logs to identify anomalies and trace fault propagation paths. By leveraging a hybrid approach that combines statistical analysis, rule-based inference, and machine learning algorithms, the RCA model isolates root causes with high accuracy and minimal latency. Key components include anomaly detection using time-series clustering, causal inference to map interdependencies between system variables, and a dynamic decision engine that updates fault hypotheses as new data arrive. A case study involving a floating production storage and offloading (FPSO) unit demonstrates the model's effectiveness in diagnosing pressure surges and valve malfunctions, reducing mean time to diagnosis (MTTD) by over 40% compared to baseline methods. The model also provides visual fault trees and impact assessments to aid operator decision-making. Live validation on a digital twin platform confirmed its robustness under varying operational scenarios, including equipment degradation and sensor drift. This RCA model represents a shift from reactive to proactive offshore operations by enabling real-time diagnostics, thus improving asset reliability and operational safety. Future enhancements will focus on integrating maintenance history and human-in-the-loop feedback for adaptive learning. Overall, the proposed framework underscores the value of combining live data analytics with intelligent root cause reasoning to support timely, data-driven interventions in complex offshore environments.

Title: Synthetic Data Creation of Neurons for Training Machine Learning Segmentation Algorithms Volume Electron Microscopy
Abstract: Mapping synaptic connectivity at cellular resolution with volume electron microscopy (EM) enables mechanistic study of neural circuits, but it requires dense segmentation and extensive proofreading. Recent connectomics resources such as the MICrONS cubic-millimeter dataset co-register calcium imaging from ∼75,000 neurons with an EM reconstruction containing >200,000 cells and ∼523 million synapses [1]. Whole-brain connectomics has also reached the adult female Drosophila brain (139,255 neurons; ∼5×10^7 synapses) [2,3]. Despite progress in automated methods, generating sufficient high-quality labeled training data remains a major bottleneck. Volume EM datasets are commonly acquired by serial sectioning (e.g., automated tape-collecting ultramicrotomy, ATUM) followed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) imaging and computational reconstruction [4]. While modern pipelines include automated segmentation, human-in-the-loop correction is often required to obtain reliable neuron instance segmentations at scale. Supervised machine learning models typically need large, diverse, and accurately labeled training sets; however, dense manual annotation for EM is expensive and difficult to scale. We therefore propose a synthetic-data pipeline that generates perfectly paired neuron instance masks and EM-like images to augment training for segmentation models, reducing dependence on manual labeling inspired by synthetic datasets used in PCB defect detection [5], Our approach is mask-first: (i) generate realistic neuron instance masks, then (ii) translate each mask into a matching EM-like image using conditional image-to-image translation. This pairing provides ground-truth labels by construction and is compatible with standard supervised training. As a foundational dataset, we downloaded 5,000 paired 512×512 patches from the publicly available MICrONS Explorer cortical mm^3 resource, including the corresponding neuron instance masks [2]. Patches containing fewer than two instances were excluded, yielding 3,800 paired samples for training and validation. For mask generation, we used Stable Diffusion (SD) and fine-tuned it via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) on the 3,800 real instance-mask images. Captions specified “neuron instance mask” and the number of cells in each patch. LoRA training was performed for 10 epochs, and the best checkpoint was used to sample synthetic masks across a range of instance counts. For mask-to-SEM translation, we trained pix2pix and SPADE conditional generative adversarial networks (GANs) on real paired data (real mask → corresponding real SEM image). Synthetic SEM images were then generated by feeding synthetic masks into the trained generator. In our experiments, SPADE produced sharper boundaries and more plausible ultrastructural texture than pix2pix (Fig. 2) and was selected for the final pipeline. To prepare training data for Micro-SAM, each mask was converted to a single-channel integer label image (background = 0; each neuron assigned a unique ID) and saved as a 16-bit TIFF, paired with the corresponding SEM image saved as TIFF. We compared Micro-SAM models trained on (a) real-only data, (b) mixed real+synthetic data, and (c) synthetic-only data, evaluating on a held-out set of real MICrONS patches using qualitative overlays (Figs. 3–4) and standard segmentation metrics (Dice/IoU and instance-level precision/recall). Preliminary results indicate that synthetic-only training is insufficient, while synthetic augmentation provides additional diversity; remaining failure cases are associated with blurred boundaries and missing nuclear/organellar cues in the generated SEM images. Overall, these results suggest that realistic instance mask generation is achievable, while mask-to-image translation is currently the dominant limitation. Future work will focus on improving translation fidelity using stronger conditioning and domain-specific constraints (e.g., membrane continuity and texture statistics), and on a controlled low-label study to quantify whether synthetic augmentation reduces the amount of real labeled data required for robust performance.
