Title: Poe in Cyberspace: “The Power of Words”
Abstract: Poe’s three Platonic Dialogues are among the most radical of his science fiction works. In the first, “The Conversation of Eiros and Charmion” (1839), a fiery comet destroys planet earth. In the second, “The Colloquy of Monos and Una” (1841), death and dying are described in exhaustive detail. In the third, “The Power of Words” (1845), an unlimited database of words is created in the air—anticipating today’s internet. As editor, Evert Duyckinck thought so highly of the Platonic Dialogues that he included two of them in the 1845 Wiley & Putnam edition of Poe’s Tales.Regarded as the best of the three dialogues (M 3:1210), “The Power of Words” was inspired by the radical ideas of the British polymath Charles Babbage in his Ninth Bridgewater Treatise (1837), which crossed the Atlantic in magazine popularizations and an 1841 American edition. Martin Farquhar Tupper, a London reviewer of the Tales, asked publisher G. P. Putnam, “Shall we make Edgar Poe famous by a review in the Literary Gazette?” (qtd. in Dwight Thomas and David K. Jackson, The Poe Log: A Documentary Life of Edgar Allan Poe, 1809–1849 [G. K. Hall, 1987], 585).Noted for his impressive combination of science, mathematics, and invention, Babbage drew unusual public attention to his breakthrough prototypes of the difference engine and analytic engine, early versions of the modern calculator and programmable computer. Working at ultra-small and ultra-large dimensions beyond the boundaries of contemporary engineering, Babbage methodically applied Newton’s principle of the conservation of matter to the long-term nature of the vibrations in the air produced by human speech.Babbage’s remarkable theory specified that human speech left permanent impressions in the form of vibrations in the atmosphere. In “Chapter IX. On the permanent Impression of our Words and Actions on the Globe we inhabit” of The Ninth Bridgewater Treatise (1837), Babbage declared, “The pulsations of the air, once set in motion by the human voice, cease not to exist with the sounds to which they gave rise” (108).1 The result was that “in less than twenty hours every atom of its atmosphere takes up the altered movement” (109). Although too small to be detected by the human ear, the phenomenon was “demonstrated to exist by human reason” (110).Babbage observed, “Thus considered, what a strange chaos is this wide atmosphere we breathe! Every atom, impressed with good and ill, retains at once the motions which philosophers and sages have imparted to it, mixed and combined in ten thousand ways with all that is worthless and base. The air itself is one vast library, on whose pages are for ever written all that man has ever said or woman whispered” (111–12). As a result, “the air we breathe is the never-failing historian of the sentiments we have uttered, earth, air, and ocean, are the eternal witnesses of the acts we have done” (112). “No motion,” he asserted, “is ever obliterated” (114).Babbage’s prose in the Treatise was too radical and dense to be popular. Fortunately, the encyclopedia editor Dionysius Lardner wrote lectures and magazine articles that explained and simplified Babbage—sometimes with his help. Incidentally, Americans were most likely to read British magazine articles in their American reprints; in fact, Poole’s Index listed the page numbers of the American reprints, not the British originals.Improbably, some of Babbage’s most advanced ideas found their way into the most unlikely American periodicals. In 1839, the popular literary figure Nathaniel Parker Willis commented on Babbage’s idea of the preservation of past speech in a database in his reprint journal The Corsair, a periodical the New-Yorker judged “dashing and clever and Frenchified” (qtd. in Frank Luther Mott, A History of American Magazines, 1741–1850 [D. Appleton, 1930], 356–57). Willis wrote, “Mr. Babbage in his (miscalled Bridgewater) Treatise announces the astounding fact, as a very sublime truth, that every word uttered from the creation of the world has registered itself, and is still speaking, and will speak for ever in vibration” (qtd. in Terence Whalen, Edgar Allan Poe and the Masses: The Political Economy of Literature in Antebellum America [Princeton University Press, 1999], 256).Since Babbage was best known for his mechanical inventions, when Charles Frederick Briggs wanted to disparage Poe’s work, he remarked, “I think a machine something like Babbage’s[,] might be constructed to write poetry and criticisms like his” (qtd. in Heyward Ehrlich, “The Broadway Journal (1): Briggs’s Dilemma and Poe’s Strategy,” in The Collected Writings of Edgar Allan Poe, ed. Burton R. Pollin, vol. 4 [Gordian Press, 1986], xxi).Poe himself mentioned Babbage as an inventor in “Maelzel’s Chess-Player” (1836) and in “The Thousand-and-Second Tale of Scheherazade” (1845). Despite the wide public attention given to Maelzel’s chess-player as a supposed automaton, Poe called attention to its nearly impossible task of mastering all possible chess moves, even those reflecting the “indeterminate will of [an] antagonist” (Edgar Allan Poe, “Maelzel’s Chess-Player,” in Edgar Allan Poe: Essays & Reviews, ed. G. R. Thompson [Library of America, 1984], 1256). At this time Poe was fully aware of the achievements of Babbage’s devices, and he mused, “What shall we think of a [calculating] machine which can . . . actually print off its elaborate results, when obtained, without the slightest intervention of the intellect of man?” (Poe, “Maelzel’s Chess-Player,” 1255).In “The Thousand-and-Second Tale of Scheherazade,” Poe offered tongue-in-cheek circumlocutions to describe recent inventions, including the Electrotype, the Electro Telegraph, and the Electro Telegraph Printing Apparatus. Poe acknowledged that “Babbage’s Calculating Machine” had such great reasoning powers that “in a second, it performed calculations of so vast an extent that they would have required the united labor of fifty thousand fleshly men for a year” (M 3:1166).Today, internet databases are described as residing “in the cloud,” a metaphor for their online location. In Poe’s era the comparable term was “in the ether,” describing the area beyond the atmosphere that supposedly filled all space. Since it was known in nineteenth-century science that sound could not traverse a vacuum, it was assumed that light similarly could not do so and that something else was required to fill space.In “The Power of Words,” Poe argued that the ether “alone pervades all space, [and] is thus the great medium of creation” (M 3:1215). A master of algebraic mathematics could retrieve all vibrations in the air and even those beyond the air in the ether: “To a being of infinite understanding—one to whom the perfection of the algebraic analysis lay unfolded—there could be no difficulty in tracing every impulse given the air—and the ether through the air—to the remotest consequences of any even infinitely remote epoch of time” (M 3:1214). Such a “being of infinite understanding” might trace “all particles of all matter—upward and onward for ever” (M 3:1214). Speaking of the “impulses upon the atmosphere of the Earth” and thus of the “physical power of words,” Poe’s Agathos asked, “[I]s not every word an impulse on the air?” (M 3:1215). Poe also maintained that mathematically capable angels could retrieve past patterns of speech; in addition, other angels with generative capability could create heavenly bodies simply by speaking them (as in Genesis) (M 3:1215).In the communications revolution of Poe’s era, steam and electricity were the two new sources of power. Steamboats and steam locomotives greatly sped up travel and distribution, and the steam-powered printing press greatly accelerated the manufacture of books and periodicals. Moreover, the electric telegraph made messages available nearly instantaneously and on an increasingly global scale. In The Victorian Internet: The Remarkable Story of the Telegraph and the Nineteenth Century’s Online Pioneers (Walker, 1998), Tom Standage argued that in thus raising audience expectations of nearly global and almost instantaneous communications the modern telegraph produced a cultural effect equal to that of the later internet. Before electrification, the early visual telegraph required a clear line of sight between its towers, so straight thoroughfares called telegraph avenues were established. Before the dots and dashes of Morse code became standard, one early electric telegraph, displayed at the Mechanic’s Institute in New York in 1846, used piano-style keys for input and printed paper strips like tickertape for output.For Poe, the wide reprinting of successful works was an early form of networking. “The Raven” (1845) reached a huge reading public as a result “not only of its innumerable reprintings and many translations but also [of] the imitations” in periodicals (M 1:351–52). By contrast, the circulation of books such as Poe’s Tales (1845) and The Raven and Other Poems (1845) was quite limited in comparison to the liberal runs of reprints in periodicals. In detail, most of Poe’s readers encountered his work in newspapers and magazines. Even the celebrity Poe enjoyed as the author of “The Raven” was “largely the product of the poem’s unauthorized reprinting” (Meredith L. McGill, American Literature and the Culture of Reprinting, 1834–1853 [University of Pennsylvania Press, 2003], 218). Poe took especial pride in the remarkable number of reprints of “The Raven,” which exceeded those of the previous leader, “The Gold-Bug” (1843).” He quipped, “The bird beat the bug, though, all hollow” (M 1:351).Poe believed that a heightened style was a necessity for publication success. In defending “Berenice” (1835), Poe listed the essential ingredients of such a style: “In the ludicrous heightened into the grotesque: the fearful coloured into the horrible: the witty exaggerated into the burlesque: the singular wrought out into the strange and mystical.” Moreover, Poe argued that such a style was necessary in the building up of magazines as articles “find their way into other periodicals, and into the papers, and in this manner, taking hold upon the public mind they augment the reputation of the source” (O 1:84, 85).When Poe discovered a new method of self-publishing called anastatic printing, he believed it would “revolutionize the world.” Adding acid to the manuscript and pressing the page against a metal plate etched a printing positive. Poe claimed that “a vast number of absolute fac-similes” could thus be made inexpensively, offering an alternative to expensive but underused stereotype plates stored in London warehouses that constituted an investment of “a million sterling” (Edgar Allan Poe, “Anastatic Printing,” in The Collected Writings of Edgar Allan Poe, ed. Burton R. Pollin, vol. 3 [Gordian Press, 1986], 84, 85).The rise of the internet had more revolutionary effects than those Poe imagined for anastatic printing. In the 1960s government support was important for the early internet. The Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA), an arm of the U.S. Department of Defense, produced the pioneering ARPANET to connect big computers at UCLA, Stanford, the University of California, Santa Barbara, and the University of Utah. To protect early online platforms from the risks of legal liability, Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act of 1996 held that online platforms were not legally liable for content they recirculated. As as result, web pages could present third-party content without copyright and avoid damaging lawsuits. Thus, if the New York Times falsely calls you a swindler, you can sue, but if Facebook reposts someone saying the same thing, you cannot.In the 1990s, Tim Berners-Lee simplified the difficulty of reading online pages with different formats. HTML (hypertext markup language) could be configured to support different browsers in users’ machines. Afterward, HTML added CSS (cascading style sheets) for formatting and JavaScript for elements of programming, but the most radical changes were produced by the introduction of the iPhone and its competitors, which made the internet personal, worldwide, and omniscient. Gatherings of web pages began to appear. The first collection was made at Project Gutenberg. An archive that sampled almost all web pages was formed at the Wayback Machine of the Internet Archive. A wide sampling of internet research was offered at Google Scholar. Many published books, including copyrighted works under the “fair use” exemption, were collected at Amazon Books. A deep gathering of web pages became available at HathiTrust.org.The introduction of AI (artificial intelligence) by ChatGPT in 2022 led to an investment race by Amazon, Apple, Google, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia, and OpenAI, each seeking a dominant position. The oddity of the AI boom is that nobody really knows how it works or why sometimes it produces inappropriate responses called “hallucinations.”Babbage’s idea of a database of words in the air, discussed by Poe in “The Power of Words,” enjoyed an unexpected revival in a recent project in Australia titled Atmospheric Memory. From August 12, 2023, to November 5, 2023, Atmospheric Memory was presented at the Sydney Science Festival at the Powerhouse Museum, combining light, sound, and colossal projections. The museum posted the following description on its web page: “Inspired by computing pioneer Charles Babbage’s proposal that the air is a ‘vast library’ storing every word ever spoken, Rafael Lozano-Hemmer’s breathtaking immersive art environment invites audiences to a multisensory experience at the intersection of art and science.” Of this project, Lozano-Hemmer stated, “I hope the project makes the atmosphere tangible, so it’s no longer seen as something neutral or invisible we take for granted. It is something complex, beautiful and irreversible.” This unusual application of the internet led to an unexpected question: “If we could ‘rewind’ air molecules to recreate all voices of the past,” he wondered, “whose voice would you want to hear?” (https://powerhouse.com.au/program/atmospheric-memory).

Title: The first practical innovation in nursing competition: April 26, 2024
Abstract: The first Practical Innovation in Nursing Competition, hosted by the Business Affairs Management Office, Technology Transfer Office, and Hospital Management Office of Peking University Health Science Centre (PKUHSC), was held on April 26, 2024, which also marked the 24th World Intellectual Property Day. As one of a series of events organized as part of Peking University’s Intellectual Property Publicity Month, the competition attracted extensive attention, with a full house at the venue and over 1.33 million scientists, clinicians, nurses, and students joining remotely. Being the first competition centered on practical innovation in nursing organized by PKUHSC, the competition focused on the characteristics of nursing as a discipline and the significant role nursing plays in clinical practice, health care, rehabilitation, and other fields, with the aim of providing a platform for the nursing discipline within PKUHSC to display its scientific and technological (S&T) innovation and research capabilities, thereby promoting the discipline’s development and facilitating the practical realization and implementation of the research. 2024 is the “Year of Discipline Quality” of Peking University, and Nursing is one of the “Double First-class” disciplines of PKUHSC. Thus, collaboration and innovation play an important role in the discipline’s development. This competition, focused on innovation and implementation, aims to encourage clinical nurses to participate, lead, and promote the practical realization and implementation of nursing research. It is my hope that this competition can stimulate the innovative vitality and professional ability of clinical nurses, and, looking forward beyond this event, lead to the discovery of more prospective, pragmatic and scalable nursing innovation projects, and achieve their implementation, thereby providing a new impetus of quality productive forces for the development of nursing at Peking University. Yuan Xiao, Deputy Director, PKUHSC. Sixty-three projects from Peking University’s School of Nursing and 10 affiliated hospitals took part in the competition, with 10 projects related to S&T research, disease control and prevention, health management, and other areas winning awards. “Development and application of radial artery hemostasis technology with trans-radial access (TRA),” led by Zhenhui Tao, deputy director of the Department of Nursing at Peking University First Hospital, won first prize. The project focused on TRA, a widely adopted therapeutic approach for coronary heart disease (CHD) patients. However, complications such as radial artery occlusion (RAO), access site bleeding, and hematoma remain problematic. Currently, the radial artery hemostatic device used in clinical practice is unable to achieve accurate quantification of pressure, and it is difficult to balance the dual risks of radial artery occlusion and bleeding by relying solely on experience and manual operation. Given these challenges, this project took the lead in developing the world-first patented “hemostatic device with quantitative pressure” technology, and in exploring a model of radial artery hemostatic pressure and continuous decompression combining hemodynamics, physics, and coagulation mechanisms, thereby standardizing the postoperative hemostasis process, reducing complications, and improving comfort, research possessing immense clinical, economic and social value. “An intelligent recommendation system for dementia care based on knowledge graph,” led by Dr Zhiwen Wang, director of PKUHSC’s Centre for Evidence-based Nursing won second prize. The growing number of older people suffering from dementia presents an array of challenges requiring ongoing professional guidance, while the current shortage of personnel has resulted in a supply-demand imbalance. This project, funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China, aims to develop technology capable of translating research evidence and expert experience into an intelligent recommendation system for dementia care. The project contains two significant innovations. First, it utilizes a personalized multicase data set of highly reliable information as its corpus and integrates research evidence and clinical experience into a dementia care-specific knowledge graph, which has been granted an invention patent. Second, it compares various algorithmic models to extract graph features and develops an intelligent dementia care recommendation system based on the acquired knowledge graph, innovations that have secured 2 software copyrights in addition to one ongoing patent application. This recommendation system could be implemented in the home, in the community, as well as in long-term care facilities, offering personalized care guidance via virtual experts, promoting service inclusivity, enhancing service efficiency, reducing complications, hospitalization, and emergency medical treatment costs, and alleviating the disease burden. System evaluation, including performance, effectiveness, safety, economy, and social suitability, has been completed, and algorithm optimization, by means of 13,773 interaction records to improve accuracy, has been achieved. The project “Intelligent endoscopy dual pathway: construction of an innovative endoscopy center based on Artificial Intelligence and the Internet of Things (AIoT),” led by Bei Li, head nurse in the Gastrointestinal Surgery Department of Peking University Shenzhen Hospital, also won second prize. This project derives from clinical necessity and targets some of the “pain points” and blind spots within nursing practice, leveraging a collaboration of medicine and industry with the Internet, the Internet of Things, and AI technology at its core, to bring about high-quality endoscopy nursing services by means of intelligent approaches. The “patient-endoscopy” dual pathway closed-loop management system links together all aspects of diagnosis and treatment, serving the needs of nurses and patients by creating a streamlined, automated process, displaying remarkable achievements in areas such as information exchange, precision management, and resource optimization. This system is embedded with an integrated robot for digestive endoscopy and colonic irrigation, smart storage, smart endoscopic retracing, human-machine recognition, doctor-nurse-patient-endoscope information linkage, resuscitation monitoring, whole process management, and other innovative tools. This system ensures digital management throughout the entire process, stimulating the “high-quality productivity forces” of nursing and refining the medical treatment process for patients. “A functional rehabilitation trainer and rehabilitation system for oropharyngeal facial muscles” led by Aili Wang, head nurse in the Otolaryngology Head and Neck Surgery Department of Peking University First Hospital, won third prize. The research pointed out that the snoring population increases by more than 70 million each year, >80% of whom experience stroke, sexual dysfunction, marital disharmony, and other problems. Seventy percent of traffic accidents are related to sleeplessness, and the fatality rate among snorers is as high as 3.8 times that of the general population. Moreover, treatment needs are difficult to meet due to high treatment costs, poor compliance, and other reasons, resulting in poor treatment outcomes. This training program includes an information module and phone applet, which is connected to the trainer via Bluetooth to guide and assist the training, strengthen the localized muscles on a noninvasive basis, relieve the stenosis of the oropharyngeal plane, and expand the airway. Different from conventional training models, this system is suitable for use in any available pocket of time, at any place, and for users of all ages. It can not only provide therapeutic training, reducing or eliminating sleep snoring, thus addressing both the cause and symptoms of the affliction, but also effective preventive training for snoring. Moreover, it can be used in the precise rehabilitation treatment of tongue and facial muscles of elderly patients suffering from dysphagia, choking while eating, mild Parkinson and facial paralysis. “Clinical application and research of finger and toe support device,” led by JiaGao from Peking University First Hospital’s Daxing Campus, also won third prize. The research pointed out that each year in China, millions of patients undergo finger or toe surgery, involving debridement and dressing changes, and tens of millions of patients are treated for impregnated tinea pedis. Each time, the procedure is made extra challenging by the need to manually separate the fingers (toes). The proposed device would assist the separation of single or multiple fingers and toes to an adjustable degree of opening, providing a more spacious operative site and bringing improved patient comfort and satisfaction. The device has already undergone clinical trials, where it has been shown to significantly increase the operative site area, save manpower, and improve the efficiency of the relevant procedures. It addresses a gap in existing technologies and resolves a challenge faced in current clinical practices. The market potential of this device is promising: utilizing cost-effective, disposable, and hypoallergenic materials, it offers substantial profits within a market valued at hundreds of millions of yuan. Its versatility extends to both home and hospital settings, catering to patients undergoing finger and toe surgeries, requiring dressing changes, and the tens of millions of individuals suffering from immersion-type tinea pedis. “A dark room test eye mask for glaucoma patients,” led by Jinping Hu, deputy president of the Airport Campus of Peking University Third Hospital, also won third prize. The dark room test has a certain value for the early diagnosis of suspected angle-closure glaucoma and is widely used in the clinical area. However, the test requires an absolutely dark room, posing problems such as patient safety risks, timing inaccuracies, and poor experiences. To address these concerns, they have designed a dark room test eye mask that is small, breathable, and tightly sealed, with automatic timing and alert functions based on clinical practice needs, aiming to improve patients’ peace of mind as well as the efficiency of dark room tests in glaucoma diagnosis. The product has already been granted a utility model patent, and a 3D model prototype has been produced. The team is currently seeking qualified manufacturing partners to begin sample production and clinical implementation research, to better conduct market promotion. “An electronic manometric radial artery hemostatic wristband” led by Juntao Duan, head nurse at the Catheter Laboratory of Peking University Third Hospital, won the Excellence Award. In 2023, there were more than 1.63 million cases of interventional treatment for coronary heart disease in mainland China (military hospital data not included), with 97.20% of patients undergoing surgery via radial artery access. Postsurgery, a hemostatic wristband should be used to compress the puncture site of the radial artery for a long time in order to stop bleeding. However, the wristbands lack the ability to quantify the compression pressure. Both excessive or insufficient pressure can compromise the hemostatic effect and may even lead to complications such as hematoma, forearm swelling, and radial artery occlusion. The manometric radial artery hemostatic wristband is much more user-friendly and effective. Via a blood pressure monitoring device, the pressure applied to the puncture point can be fed back to caregivers in real time, and the status of the applied hemostatic pressure is adjusted by operators based on experience, thereby effectively reducing complications. The hemostatic wristband has completed patent transfer and sample production and is now registered and awaiting approval. “An infusion tube monitoring clamp” led by YongGao, head nurse in the Emergency Department of Peking University Third Hospital Airport Campus, also won the Excellence Award. To ensure accuracy and patient safety during drug administration, nurses must regularly monitor infusion rates to ensure they remain within a safe range, be aware of the progression of different patients’ infusions, and be available to change infusion bags in a timely manner. To address these issues and alleviate nurses’ burden, an infusion tube monitoring clamp was designed, using infrared technology to monitor and display infusion drip speeds on a screen, facilitating nurses’ documentation during ward rounds. Once the infusion is completed, the device automatically sounds an alarm to alert nurses to replace the infusion bag. Currently, the utility model patent has been approved, and samples have been designed and produced. The device is anticipated to be affordable, compact, and suitable for widespread use in general wards and infusion rooms, indicating significant promotional value. “An improved surgical towel,” presented by QiuyanChen, a surgical nurse from Peking University First Hospital, also won the Excellence Award. A well-designed, innovative surgical towel that swiftly establishes a sterile perineal area during lithotomy surgery without the need to lift patients repeatedly, optimizing the surgical process and enhancing surgical efficiency. In addition, the towel reduces the risks of sacrococcygeal pressure injuries and intraoperative hypothermia, alleviates occupational low back pain among nurses, and greatly improves satisfaction among medical staff. Currently, the product has been fully launched to market in Peking University First Hospital as well as in numerous other hospitals in China and will be promoted to hospitals nationwide in the near future. “An ophthalmic prone position detector” led by Jia Liu, head nurse of the Ophthalmology Department at Peking University People’s Hospital, also won the Excellence Award. The prone position detector is a head position monitoring device for use after eye surgery. It is applied to patients with intraocular fillers who require prolonged head fixation following ophthalmic vitreoretinal surgery. The detection device allows for the setting of a body position change threshold, enabling appropriate limb movement within the permissible range to prevent skin pressure damage due to prolonged bed rest. The device is technically supported by AI design and computer chip engineers from the Beijing Institute of Technology. Currently, the detector sample is undergoing joint debugging testing and will commence clinical trials shortly.

Abstract: New research suggests that butterflies and moths come with mental baggage…left over from their lives as larvae.—ScienceHe’d like to be at one with his new selfbut memories sit in him like eyes.Sometimes scent implies an unheard-ofidea and he’s offbut it’s just another of the given forms.You’d think flight would be decent redress,the power to sift himself through airand leave each thought in its old place,where hard feelings also could be left.He shrugs and the wingsquiver with great precision,nature will have to live with what it’s done,he cannot manage even resignationwithout a show of grace.—Jana Prikryl, “The Moth” (2015)Recently I woke up to a provocative little news story. A popular software coding company called Cursor was thrown into crisis by a wayward AI system deployed to handle its customer service. Apparently a chatbot, posturing as a human named “Sam,” invented an explanation for a glitch that was logging users out when they switched between devices. With no human oversight, “Sam” told callers that logouts were “expected behavior” given “a new login policy”; in fact, there was no such policy. Rather, the AI generator was “hallucinating”—as AI technology is wont to do. The company lost a great deal of business when frustrated customers just gave up. As an AI tech advisor later posted: “This mess could have been avoided if leaders understood that (1) AI makes mistakes, (2) AI can’t take responsibility for those mistakes (so it falls on you), and (3) users hate being tricked by a machine posing as a human.”1 It honestly reminded me of the parenting advice one might give to someone who’d left their toddler at home alone to play with the stove.A techie friend describes his relation to artificial intelligence as “productive dreaming.” I suppose I shouldn’t have been surprised: the ineffably messy language models upon which AI feeds seem very much like Jungian dreams. Assemblages are made, images composed, patterns matched, meaning extracted—even when the guiding logic is not always made clear. Still, I had never thought to pair dreams and productivity. I came of age against a backdrop of Martin Luther King’s resonantly hopeful declaration that he had a dream. It was visionary, but not in a way that implied economic “productivity” or specific material outcome. So perhaps that is why my dreams come to me as lush visitations, relaxed wool-gathering, a freely wandering substance-without-substance, untethered to notions of “product.”In contrast, my friend seemed to think of AI as merely a technocratically expedited way of dreaming, a way to rapidly harness a universe of information, attach a search function, then simply press the Button of Instrumentalization that will squeeze it all for monetized juice. He even advised that I gather up my “useless” dreams, “feed them to AI, and tell it to write you some movie scripts. You could be rich.”His advice jolted me. My pleasantly relaxed internal dream-generator came face to face with the transactional seductions of generative AI-ness. It left me wondering about the econometric design logic of our increasingly technologically mediated lives.I grew up dreaming of personhood as key to the recognition of my humanity. During the height of the civil rights movement of the 1960s, I knew only that I did not want to be a “second-class citizen.” Even as a child I knew that the status called “personhood”—the legal recognition of capacity as an autonomous individual—was a portal to the protections and grace of full civic belonging. I memorized the Fourteenth Amendment. I took to heart all the narrative strategies, rooted in language, that allowed a body to be seen. The politics of the day left no question as to what was at stake: rights of association and of public accommodation, land claims, intimacies of belonging, desegregating institutions, population-wide public health, refuting eugenic concepts. If there was no easy remedy for social divisions, one almost always had a pretty clear sense of what processes to follow in pursuing what we hoped would be justice. We reached for rules of evidence in law, we aimed for reproducible results in science, we pressed doctors to do no harm in the practice of medicine. We aspired to hearings and due process before depriving anyone of life or liberty.Unfortunately, contemporary metrics for social order have shifted in this neoliberal moment, and citizenship itself has shifted from being conceived as a “bundle of rights” to a model premised on human capitalization, pecuniary status, and asset acquisition (as in “golden passports.”)2 The old landmarks of civil rights address—those clear-edged solids, those visible goals—seem not only much less accessible but much less discernible in a world dedicated to the purity of productivity. The promise of personhood—as a commitment to notions of autonomy; rights to privacy, public accommodation, and franchise; equality; and civic belonging—seems to be dissolving. We are rapidly sinking into a disordered digital echo chamber.The story of “Sam,” the hallucinating chatbot, also captured my attention because so many of us work in offices that are cutting labor costs by introducing AI assistants. We may be instructed not just to learn to operate them but to “play” with them, “talk with them,” and “make friends” with our new robotic helpmeets. Moreover, learning to use these tools involves engaging with their various “emotions” and “personalities” and not just their mechanics. This phenomenon was underscored in a much-shared episode of the Ezra Klein show, during which his guest cited a study showing that “if you emotionally manipulate the A.I., you get better math results. So telling it your job depends on it gets you better results. Tipping, especially $20 or $100—saying, I’m about to tip you if you do well, seems to work pretty well. It performs slightly worse in December than May, and we think it’s because it has internalized the idea of winter break.”3I told my tech friend that this sort of AI hallucination strikes me as a phenomenon not too far removed from the carefree indulgences of my own disobedient dreams. I have an internal version of “Sam”—it just doesn’t get to rule the world. That dreamy fugue self is always exploring, inventing, collaging bits and bobs, and making stuff up, free-associating with legions of imaginary friends. Indeed, in the very early moments of generative AI, I loved the possibility of such unbounded humanoid whimsy softening the machine with an open-minded, interactive deus ex machina. But these days, I am increasingly apprehensive about what happens when AI begins to fill human dreams with the humanoid—when it ghost-visits me at that precise hinge in my half-conscious perception, the silky joint where the pleasant fog of sleep meets the hard edges of practical existence. What happens, in other words, when AI-ness disguises itself as a mirror of my desire and slides through a portal of “productively” nudged awakenings, posturing as sensed human experience.We all know that office computers are suddenly and ubiquitously preloaded with AI software that, at the most basic level, suggests punctuation, spelling, words, paragraphs, and a range of what might be logical choice points. It feels as fanciful and seamless as a dream, but it operates as a programmatic norming of language, too; it is only as creative as its database, and its database is really an emotionless remix—the lowest common denominator of a deceptively universalizing but very narrow slice of human experience (Western, Anglophile, quantitative, skewing to masculine modifiers). Its effectiveness as an autonomous support system for human beings “requires a level of empathy, nuance, and problem-solving that AI alone currently struggles to deliver,” explains Sanketh Balakrishna, an engineering manager at cloud security platform Datadog. “I would be cautious about depending entirely on an AI bot for addressing user issues.”4 ***Sherry Turkle is a social psychologist and founding director of MIT’s Initiative on Technology and Self. She has observed that in the early days of home computing, people couldn’t quite imagine how to “keep computers busy.” Dates and addresses were so easily and cheaply contained by paper calendars and rolodexes. It wasn’t that long ago, but there has been a seismic revolution: “Once we networked with each other, once computers were our portal to being with each other, we really don't have to worry about keeping computers busy. They keep us busy.” Indeed, we are not just tethered but addicted, sutured, chained to our screens, whether we want to be or not. It is practically impossible to function in the present industrialized world without the assistance of our handheld devices; busy indeed, they affirm our creditability, attest to our humanity. “These technologies are our current partners in the human adventure,” says Turkle. We must ask: “does it serve our human purposes?—a question that causes us to reconsider what these purposes are.”5In law, “the human adventure” is less defined by our biological “nature” than by juridical determinations of “personhood.” Law crafts personhood. Personhood confers agency, autonomy, equality, franchise, standing to sue, due process, and the capacity to access the privileges and immunities guaranteed by the Constitution. Personhood also refers to the rhetorical framings that infuse our various philosophical and religious conceptions of living subjects, legally anthropomorphized nonpersons, and culturally enchanted objects. Negotiating the relations and borders between human and subhuman, thinker and thing, autonomous being and automaton, is urgently consequential in an era of algorithmic assortment and mass surveillance.For some years, I have taught a class entitled “The Anatomy of Autonomy.” In it we study notions of individualism, configurations of citizenship, the civic vivacity of righted beings, the civil death of statelessness and incarceration, concepts of human capital, and legal fictions like corporate personhood. We read Aristotle, René Descartes, Ralph Waldo Emerson, tracking the underpinnings of notions like integrity of the body, the limits of one’s “private person,” and the hagiography of the singular agentic individual. We interrogate the features of an imagined ideal body, like Leonardo da Vinci’s Vitruvian Man, and how those metrics might undergird figurations of homo economicus, or the legal subject, or a rights-bearing citizen. We discuss how social value is sometimes tethered to temporal orderings—that is, concepts like nostalgic pasts or utopic futures—and how those orderings allow us to imagine ourselves as upwardly mobile, self-made, self-owning, self-regulating, free-willed choice-makers.For the last decade and a half, the single most exciting part of such a course was discussion of Citizens United v. Abstract: Table of ContentsReference WidgetRETURN TO TOCPREV6.1.9NEXT6.1.9 Socioeconomic StatusACS Inclusivity Style GuideSocioeconomic StatusAlison KreckmannAlison KreckmannUI/UX DesignerAmerican Chemical SocetyEmail: [email protected]More by Alison Kreckmannhttps://doi.org/10.1021/acsguide.60109 This publication is free to access through this site. Request reuse permissions Share Add toView InAdd Full Text with ReferenceAdd Description ExportRISCitationCitation and abstractCitation and referencesMore Options Share onFacebookTwitterWechatLinked InRedditEmail When & How to Refer to Socioeconomic Status GroupsBackground: Socioeconomic status is a complex concept that involves education, income, and overall financial security, occupation, living conditions, resources, and opportunities afforded to people within society. Socioeconomic status and one's perceived social standing are factors of social class. Generalizing and pejorative language about socioeconomic status and class contributes to stereotypes. Furthermore, mentioning socioeconomic status when it is not relevant could introduce bias.While there are no universal definitions of "high" and "low", the terms "high income" and "low income" are often used to describe where on a range an individual falls. But these terms may mask important distinctions when it comes to other aspects of poverty or wealth, and they may be misleading, as "wealthy people may qualify as low-income, or [the term 'low income'] may not capture the effects of wealth on class", the Style Guide from the N.Y.U. Review of Law & Social Change explains. The American Psychological Association (APA) uses the term "low-income and economic marginalization" in 2019 guidelines to establish common terminology that includes both limited financial resources and marginalization related to social class.Some organizations, such as the APA, recommend avoiding the phrase "poor people", in part because of negative connotations associated with the word "poor". Others argue that alternatives to "poor" are sanitizing attempts to alleviate a communicator's discomfort rather than the discomfort of people the words are meant to describe.Recommendation: Mention socioeconomic status only when relevant. Define specific income data and education levels when appropriate. Consider including contextual details about net worth or measuring income relative to a poverty line, a benchmark that may serve as a recognizable and quantifiable standard, though it has been critiqued as a flawed and outdated measure of poverty. If you use "poverty line", note which kind, because countries define country-level property thresholds, while the World Bank defines a global poverty line. Avoid labeling socioeconomic status groups by a characteristic, such as "the unemployed", which can be derogatory, be dehumanizing, or imply that these groups are defined by the problems they experience. See also Avoid Labeling People by a Characteristic and Recognize Overlapping Identities.ExamplesUse: "Aggregated ratios indicated that participants from the lowest SES [socioeconomic status] community experienced higher home exposures compared to participants of all other communities over consecutive 24-hr monitoring periods, despite high participant mobility and relatively low variability in ambient PM2.5 during the study" (1).Avoid: that the poorUse: "Households making $50,000 or less a year were far more likely to experience a pay cut than those making $100,000 or more a year" (2).Avoid: Low-income households ... high-income households (While using "low income" and "high income" as descriptors may be appropriate once they are defined, describing the categories is clearer on first use, as people may define these categories differently.)Use: "Nonetheless, schools and instructors should have a plan to make computer hardware available to students who may not be able to afford their own devices or whose devices are outdated or not functioning" (3).Avoid: poor students (While using "poor" as an adjective may be appropriate in some situations, describing the situation is generally clearer than using a label.)Use: "We define the middle class as those in the middle 60% of the household income distribution—not poor, but not prosperous either. The average middle-class household has about $70,000 in income after taxes and transfers. To be middle class, a household of three would have an income between $40,000 and $154,000" (4).Avoid Deficit-Based Language for Socioeconomic StatusBackground: Deficit-based language focuses on what people lack. Describing people only with negative words like "struggling", "underprivileged", "at risk", and "vulnerable" stigmatizes individuals and fails to recognize the larger systems that create problems. In contrast, asset framing, a narrative strategy developed by social entrepreneur Trabian Shorters, leads with people's aspirations and contributions before mentioning problems; it also recognizes and names causal systems. Importantly, asset framing does not aim to just use more positive words and downplay very real problems: "Asset-framing doesn't ignore challenges. It's not about avoidance or substitution. It's more accurate to introduce a young person by their aspirations and contributions before mentioning their challenges than it is to sum them up as an 'at-risk youth,' " Shorters writes in the Communications Network.Recommendation: Avoid dehumanizing language that leads with deficits. Use explicit language that looks at root causes and describes the barriers that impede those seeking opportunity. When comparing socioeconomic status groups, use parallel phrasing or asset framing. When deficits need to be named, use neutral language instead of pejorative or stigmatizing words.In addition, aim to accurately portray people of various socioeconomic status groups; avoid communication that ignores socioeconomic problems, romanticizes poverty, or portrays lower socioeconomic status groups as heroes. Do not equate poverty to a curse or disease, as with "poverty-stricken" or "poverty-ridden". See also Neutral Language for Disabilities, Disorders, & Diseases and Acknowledge Systemic Factors That Affect Socioeconomic Status.ExamplesUse: people with a high school diploma versus people without a high school diploma or equivalent, or people with a [9, 10, or 11]th-grade educationAvoid: high school graduates versus high school dropoutsUse: Consider donating to help students from lower socioeconomic groups participate in science research.Avoid: Consider donating today to ensure these impoverished students receive the help they desperately needAcknowledge Systemic Factors That Affect Socioeconomic StatusBackground: An individual's successes and outcomes are affected by a variety of life experiences with systemic causes. Language that blames individuals for having a lower socioeconomic status ignores these structural issues. For example, using the phrase "lifestyle choices" to explain health disparities between socioeconomic groups masks the fact that inequities in society may severely limit the choices available to lower socioeconomic groups. For example, not eating as many fruits and vegetables may not be a conscious choice but rather the result of a lack of shops with fresh produce in a neighborhood. Similarly, the term "food desert" portrays access to food as a naturally occurring situation, whereas other terms, like "food apartheid", aim to emphasize the racial discrimination and structural barriers that cause unequal food access in U.S. society.Recommendation: Avoid characterizing an individual's socioeconomic status or economic mobility as the result of individual behaviors. Provide context, and use language that accurately reflects the challenges and opportunities faced by different socioeconomic status groups. Avoid assigning morality to socioeconomic status. See also Avoid Deficit-Based Language for Socioeconomic Status.ExamplesUse: "This has led to the development of introductory programs and support courses for students who experience opportunity gaps, which can improve students' outcomes" (5).Avoid: achievement gaps ("Achievement gaps" can imply that a difference in academic outcomes is a result of personal characteristics, whereas "opportunity gaps" emphasizes differences in circumstances.)Use: "There are good reasons some Americans find it difficult to work. For one, many families still don't have child care. Only about half of schools have fully resumed in-person classes, and many child care providers haven't reopened or returned to normal capacity" (6).Use: " 'My grandparents were bludgeoned every time the economy took a downturn,' Dee recalls, in part because of the legacy of redlining and the devaluation of property in Black neighborhoods" (7).Show Variety within Socioeconomic Status GroupsBackground: People within a particular socioeconomic status group may have markedly different experiences, behaviors, and aspirations depending on their geographic location, race, immigration status, age, gender, family structure, and many other factors. Implying that everyone in a group shares values or behaviors can seem inauthentic and alienate people.Conceptualizations of the middle and working class are largely coded as White, despite evidence that demonstrates that the middle class is racially and ethnically diverse. Language that emphasizes the racial diversity within classes, such as explicitly naming different racial groups, can help people create a more accurate view of these classes. Rashad Robinson and Nicole Sussner Rodgers explain in a 2020 Color of Change report, "Rather than eliminating the use of this term ["working class"], it is important to continue to expand its meaning, and the range of people whose image it evokes. One way to do that is to explicitly insert Black people into the narrative it carries, for instance, by talking about Black, white and other working class communities."Recommendation: Avoid language that treats socioeconomic status groups as homogeneous or that treats higher socioeconomic status groups as the norm. See also Recognize Words That Assume a Cultural Norm. In a discussion of working-class and middle-class people in particular, aim to include the names of races and ethnicities beyond White to avoid perpetuating a perception that those classes are White only. See also Minorities, Non-White.ExampleUse: Buying a car is a privilege enjoyed by some teens in the U.S.Avoid: an important coming-of-age ritual for every teenDo Not Use Racially Coded Terms for Socioeconomic StatusBackground: Phrases like "inner city" and "ghetto" have historically been used to describe majority-Black neighborhoods, and they continue to be used as coded ways of referring to communities of color, especially Black communities. Racially coded terms like these are imprecise and unclear. They also tend to equate location with a characteristic and ignore the policies and systems that create and perpetuate inequalities. The problems that people associate with the "inner city" U.S., for example, are not inherent to places at the cores of cities but are the result of discriminatory institutions. "Ghetto, in slang usage, has entirely lost the sense of forced segregation—the meaning it held for centuries. In a rapid about-face, it's become an indictment of individual choices", Camila Domonoske says in a 2014 NPR article explains. See also Avoid Language That Perpetuates Racial or Ethnic Stereotypes or Is Rooted in Violence against These Groups.Recommendation: Avoid pejorative, racially coded terms such as "urban", "ghetto", and "inner city".ExampleUse: "Majority-Black neighborhoods hold $609 billion in owner-occupied housing assets and are home to approximately 10,000 public schools and over 3 million businesses" (8).Avoid: urban neighborhoodsHow to Refer to OccupationBackground: Calling jobs or people "unskilled" or "low skill" is imprecise, demeaning, and inaccurate, as these jobs are valuable and require many skills. These terms are often "lumping together entry-level jobs, jobs that do not require much education or a formal credential, jobs that do not require experienced workers, jobs without much opportunity for advancement, menial jobs, and—most of all—low-wage jobs", Annie Lowrey says in a 2021 Atlantic article. Labeling the jobs and workers also seems to blame the people—who, at least in the U.S., are disproportionately immigrants—rather than the systems that created inequalities between types of jobs and the people who typically do those jobs. Furthermore, framing "low skill" jobs as only temporary waystations to something greater devalues those positions. "These so-called 'unskilled' jobs aren't just stepping stones to something 'greater' or more 'valuable.' They aren't merely summer jobs for teenagers and college students. These roles have immense value in and of themselves", Haley Johnson says in a 2022 Michigan Daily article.Another way people describe jobs is using the terms "white collar" and "blue collar". That terminology is vague, oversimplified, and outdated. Specific descriptions are clearer.Recommendation: Provide context and specific details when discussing jobs. Avoid representing some types of employment as being inherently better than others, and avoid describing jobs or workers as "unskilled" or "low skill". Use specific descriptions instead of "blue collar" and "white collar".ExamplesUse: "Out of all my high school jobs, lifeguarding came the closest to professional labor" (9).Avoid: closest to a real jobUse: "Low wage laborers or small farmers collect plant material from forests, pastureland, roadsides, and fallow agricultural land" (10).Avoid: Low-skill workersUse: "Understanding the extent to which PFAS exposures differ between firefighters and office workers can elucidate which compounds are likely to have occupational sources" (11).Avoid: white-collar workersHow to Refer to Housing StatusBackground: People may experience chronic, transitional, or episodic homelessness, which can include living outdoors or in inadequate dwellings. Lower socioeconomic status groups and people living in poverty are at a higher risk of becoming homeless. The term "homeless" has different meanings to different people. "Being homeless doesn't necessarily mean someone is sleeping on the street or in a car. It can mean sleeping on a friend's sofa due to the lack of an alternative. Many college students don't realize this and, therefore, don't consider themselves homeless", Denise-Marie Ordway says in a 2019 article in the article in the Journalist's Resource.Some organizations, such as the American Psychological Association, recommend person-first language, such as "people experiencing homelessness", instead of "homeless people". Some advocates, particularly on the West Coast of the U.S., use "unhoused", using the verb form partly to signal that becoming homeless is the result of events and not inherent to a person. Others use "houseless" because "homeless" has become linked to negative stereotypes about people who do not have permanent housing.Recommendation: When discussing people who do not have access to fixed, regular, or adequate housing, describe the specific situation and avoid generalizing and dehumanizing labels. Do not use the label "the homeless" (see also Avoid Labeling People by a Characteristic). In general, ask people how they want to be described and respect that choice (see Ask People How They Want to Be Described, & Respect That Language). If you cannot determine preference and need to group people, use "people experiencing homelessness" or another person-first alternative instead of "homeless people".ExampleUse: Large-scale additive manufacturing, or 3D printing, has drawn attention for its potential to create affordable, quickly constructed structures—like in Austin, Texas, where the technology was recently used to build homes for people experiencing homelessness (12).Avoid: the homelessAvoid Outdated & Generalizing Terms for CountriesBackground: The terms "developing/developed" and "first/third world" are considered to be outdated, imprecise, and demeaning. "Developing" suggests that development is a linear process in which "developed" countries have reached full civilization. It assumes that "developing" countries' success hinges on mirroring "developed" countries' strategies and ideologies, and it ignores variation between and within countries categorized as "developed" or "developing". In 2016, the World Bank stopped differentiating between "developed" and "developing" countries in its World Development Indicators. "Global South" and "Global North" have emerged as more recent alternatives in scholarly communication. "Global South" usually refers to Latin America, Africa, Oceania, and lower-income countries in Asia. But these terms have also drawn criticism for their ambiguity, and they can obscure important differences within countries. Other groupings of regions, like "majority world" and "minority world", are less well known. The problem with all names of global socioeconomic categories is that "grouping together a large variety of countries and regions into one category implies similarity across all the countries that are meant to comprise this group, one which simply does not exist economically, socially or politically", Natasha Holland writes in a 2019 Travel for Difference post.The Global Press Style Guide says of the terms "developing world/emerging economy/Global South": "The terms are geographically imprecise, do not have widely accepted definitions and are generally used as sanitized synonyms for poverty. Using generalized terms to imply poverty across large land areas and countries that have little else in common reflects bias and defines complex communities by foreign standards of wealth."Recommendation: Avoid using broad, vague terms that signal entire parts of the globe as "other", such as "developed" and "developing" nations and "first world" and "third world" countries. When discussing groups of countries, identify them by name or specific geographic regions. If the groups are not based on location, specifically define the issues you are exploring, and use classifications based on actual data. For example, the World Bank classifies countries by gross national income per capita and reassesses the classifications each year. Title: A review of computer vision applications for asset inspection in the oil and gas industry
Venue: Journal of Pipeline Science and Engineering
Abstract: This review explores the current application of computer vision (CV) technologies in the inspection of pipelines within the oil and gas industry, highlighting the methodologies, challenges, and advancements in this critical area. Through a systematic analysis of key articles, our study emphasizes CV’s role in addressing crucial issues such as corrosion, leaks, oil spills, and mechanical damage, areas identified as critical through our literature review. Predominant CV techniques like object detection and image segmentation, particularly using advanced frameworks like You Only Look Once (YOLO), Mask Region-based Convolutional Neural Network (R-CNN), and U-Net, showcase the field’s robust response to asset inspection challenges. Additionally, our findings reveal a significant reliance on in-house or directly acquired datasets, primarily through RGB and thermal imaging or increasingly via internet and satellite resources, underscoring the urgent need for standardized, accessible datasets to advance CV research. Despite these advancements, a gap in real-world testing remains, indicating a pressing need for field validation to ensure the operational viability of CV applications in asset inspection. In conclusion, this study reaffirms the transformative potential of CV technologies in enhancing asset integrity and operational safety across the oil and gas industry. However, the findings also highlight critical challenges, such as the scarcity of standardized datasets and the need for more comprehensive field testing. Looking ahead, future research should focus on expanding the application of CV, fostering collaborative dataset development, and ensuring that these technologies can bridge the gap between theoretical research and practical implementation, ultimately contributing to more reliable and efficient asset inspection.

Title: Aero-Engine Blade Defect Detection: A Systematic Review of Deep Learning Models
Abstract: Aero-engine blade defect detection is a crucial task in ensuring the safety and reliability of aircraft. The visual inspection of aero-engine blades is a complex process that requires extensive knowledge and experience. This paper presents a systematic literature review (SLR) of deep learning models for detecting defects in aero-engine blades. The review considers 13 primary studies, including methods and conceptual works. This is the first systematic review of deep learning models for aero-engine blade defect detection. The findings of this review demonstrate the potential of deep learning in detecting blade defects and improving the accuracy and efficiency of visual inspection. However, there is a need for more research on integrating deep learning models into practical applications and developing robust and reliable systems for defect detection. This review framework provides a comprehensive methodology for selecting and evaluating relevant studies, which researchers can use for future investigations in this area. These results should encourage further work on deep learning techniques, system integration, and testing and validation for defect detection of aero-engine blades.

Title: Computer Vision-Based Bridge Inspection and Monitoring: A Review
Abstract: Bridge inspection and monitoring are usually used to evaluate the status and integrity of bridge structures to ensure their safety and reliability. Computer vision (CV)-based methods have the advantages of being low cost, simple to operate, remote, and non-contact, and have been widely used in bridge inspection and monitoring in recent years. Therefore, this paper reviews three significant aspects of CV-based methods, including surface defect detection, vibration measurement, and vehicle parameter identification. Firstly, the general procedure for CV-based surface defect detection is introduced, and its application for the detection of cracks, concrete spalling, steel corrosion, and multi-defects is reviewed, followed by the robot platforms for surface defect detection. Secondly, the basic principle of CV-based vibration measurement is introduced, followed by the application of displacement measurement, modal identification, and damage identification. Finally, the CV-based vehicle parameter identification methods are introduced and their application for the identification of temporal and spatial parameters, weight parameters, and multi-parameters are summarized. This comprehensive literature review aims to provide guidance for selecting appropriate CV-based methods for bridge inspection and monitoring.

Title: A systematic literature review of defect detection in railways using machine vision-based inspection methods
Venue: International Journal of Transportation Science and Technology
Abstract: Train rolling stock and track inspections are necessary for the safe operation of the train. For this reason, a regular inspection of defects is required for the train rolling stock. The conventional defect detection methods yield low efficiency, consume more time, are unreliable, and are less cost-effective. These obstacles may be mitigated by integrating a machine vision-based inspection system (MVIS). This systematic literature review explores the landscape of railway defect detection methodologies, primarily focusing on leveraging image processing techniques. This comprehensive analysis encompasses many studies examining the evolution of image processing applications in the context of railway rolling stock and rail track defect detection. From traditional methods to the latest advancements, a nuanced understanding of the challenges and innovations in this domain is required. Key themes include utilizing computer vision algorithms, machine learning models, and deep learning techniques for enhanced accuracy in identifying defects. We delve into the intricacies of image acquisition, preprocessing, and feature extraction, shedding light on the pivotal role of these processes in refining defect detection systems. Also, the current gaps and opportunities for future research, emphasizing the need for standardized datasets, benchmarking methodologies, and the integration of emerging technologies, are highlighted. This review not only consolidates the existing knowledge but also serves as a roadmap for researchers invested in advancing the field of railway defect detection. By synthesizing insights from many studies, this review contributes to a deeper understanding of the state-of-the-art in railway defect detection using image processing, fostering dialogue and collaboration for improving railway safety and reliability.

Title: A systematic survey: role of deep learning-based image anomaly detection in industrial inspection contexts
Abstract: Industrial automation is rapidly evolving, encompassing tasks from initial assembly to final product quality inspection. Accurate anomaly detection is crucial for ensuring the reliability and robustness of automated systems. The intelligence of an industrial automation system is directly linked to its ability to detect and rectify abnormalities, thereby maintaining optimal performance. To advance intelligent manufacturing, sophisticated methods for high-quality process inspection are indispensable. This paper presents a systematic review of existing deep learning methodologies specifically designed for image anomaly detection in the context of industrial manufacturing. Through a comprehensive comparison, traditional techniques are evaluated against state-of-the-art advancements in deep learning-based anomaly detection methodologies, including supervised, unsupervised, and semi-supervised learning methods. Addressing inherent challenges such as real-time processing constraints and imbalanced datasets, this review offers a systematic analysis and mitigation strategies. Additionally, we explore popular anomaly detection datasets for surface defect detection and industrial anomaly detection, along with a critical examination of common evaluation metrics used in image anomaly detection. This review includes an analysis of the performance of current anomaly detection methods on various datasets, elucidating strengths and limitations across different scenarios. Moreover, we delve into the domain of drone-based, manipulator-based and AGV-based anomaly detections using deep learning techniques, highlighting the innovative applications of these methodologies. Lastly, the paper offers scholarly rigor and foresight by addressing emerging challenges and charting a course for future research opportunities, providing valuable insights to researchers in the field of deep learning-based surface defect detection and industrial image anomaly detection.

Title: Review on the Advancements in Wind Turbine Blade Inspection: Integrating Drone and Deep Learning Technologies for Enhanced Defect Detection
Abstract: The increasing demand for wind power requires more frequent inspections to identify defects in the Wind Turbine Blades (WTBs). These defects, if not detected, can compromise the structural integrity and safety of wind turbines. As WTBs are crucial and costly components, they may suffer material degradation and fatigue failure, which affects their performance and safety. Thus, the urgency for efficient and regular monitoring to maintain their structural integrity is greater than ever. This review paper explores innovative methods in fatigue testing, damage detection, and structural reliability in WTBs, focusing on the use of recent inspection methods, including those that take advantage of drones. Drones are used to identify defects such as cracks, erosion, and coating irregularities using high-resolution imagery with the onboard cameras. Various investigators have developed novel data-driven approaches, incorporating machine learning and deep learning, to accurately identify these defects. Although deep learning-based image processing has been successful in other public infrastructure contexts, its application to wind turbine inspection from aerial images presents unique challenges. This paper also highlights the critical role of failure inspection in enhancing the operational integrity of WTBs, showcasing state-of-the-art deep learning techniques that are pivotal for identifying and analyzing failures in WTBs from images captured by drones. The paper provides insights into the latest developments in using drone imagery for blade defect detection, contrasting this method with traditional non-destructive techniques. This approach could significantly transform the wind energy industry by offering a more efficient, automated, and precise way of ensuring the structural health of wind turbines. Unlike previous studies that predominantly focus on isolated aspects such as inspection or fatigue, this review paper not only integrates the three major aspects of WTBs integrity in terms of aerial inspection, image processing using machine learning, and structural integrity of the blade but also undertakes an extensive examination of the prevailing methodologies in the field, pinpointing crucial gaps and challenges. It provides a detailed review of existing research, covering various areas including automated inspection, image processing techniques, fatigue analysis, and the reliability of wind turbines. This approach enriches the discourse by offering a multifaceted perspective on WTB maintenance, thereby advancing the understanding of operational integrity within the field of wind energy.

Title: State of the Art in Defect Detection Based on Machine Vision
Venue: International Journal of Precision Engineering and Manufacturing-Green Technology
Abstract: Abstract Machine vision significantly improves the efficiency, quality, and reliability of defect detection. In visual inspection, excellent optical illumination platforms and suitable image acquisition hardware are the prerequisites for obtaining high-quality images. Image processing and analysis are key technologies in obtaining defect information, while deep learning is significantly impacting the field of image analysis. In this study, a brief history and the state of the art in optical illumination, image acquisition, image processing, and image analysis in the field of visual inspection are systematically discussed. The latest developments in industrial defect detection based on machine vision are introduced. In the further development of the field of visual inspection, the application of deep learning will play an increasingly important role. Thus, a detailed description of the application of deep learning in defect classification, localization and segmentation follows the discussion of traditional defect detection algorithms. Finally, future prospects for the development of visual inspection technology are explored.

Title: A Comprehensive Review of Surface Defect Detection in Manufacturing Using Convolutional Neural Networks
Venue: International journal of engineering science & humanities.
Abstract: Surface defect detection is a critical component of quality assurance in modern manufacturing, directly influencing product reliability and operational efficiency. With the rise of Industry 4.0, traditional inspection methods have been increasingly replaced by intelligent vision-based systems powered by Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). This paper presents a comprehensive review of CNN-based approaches for detecting surface defects across various manufacturing domains, including metal, textile, and electronics industries. It examines key architectures, detection strategies such as classification, object detection, and segmentation, and widely used industrial datasets. The review also highlights recent advancements, including transfer learning, attention mechanisms, and hybrid CNN-Transformer models, which enhance detection accuracy and robustness. Furthermore, it discusses major challenges such as data imbalance, small defect detection, and real-time deployment constraints, while outlining future research directions for scalable and explainable solutions.

Title: A Systematic Review of Computer Vision Techniques for Quality Control in End-of-Line Visual Inspection of Antenna Parts
Abstract: The rapid evolution of wireless communication technologies has underscored the critical role of antennas in ensuring seamless connectivity. Antenna defects, ranging from manufacturing imperfections to environmental wear, pose significant challenges to the reliability and performance of communication systems. This review paper navigates the landscape of antenna defect detection, emphasizing the need for a nuanced understanding of various defect types and the associated challenges in visual detection. This review paper serves as a valuable resource for researchers, engineers, and practitioners engaged in the design and maintenance of communication systems. The insights presented here pave the way for enhanced reliability in antenna systems through targeted defect detection measures. In this study, a comprehensive literature analysis on computer vision algorithms that are employed in end-of-line visual inspection of antenna parts is presented. The PRISMA principles will be followed throughout the review, and its goals are to provide a summary of recent research, identify relevant computer vision techniques, and evaluate how effective these techniques are in discovering defects during inspections. It contains articles from scholarly journals as well as papers presented at conferences up until June 2023. This research utilized search phrases that were relevant, and papers were chosen based on whether or not they met certain inclusion and exclusion criteria. In this study, several different computer vision approaches, such as feature extraction and defect classification, are broken down and analyzed. Additionally, their applicability and performance are discussed. The review highlights the significance of utilizing a wide variety of datasets and measurement criteria. The findings of this study add to the existing body of knowledge and point researchers in the direction of promising new areas of investigation, such as real-time inspection systems and multispectral imaging. This review, on its whole, offers a complete study of computer vision approaches for quality control in antenna parts. It does so by providing helpful insights and drawing attention to areas that require additional exploration.

Title: ANALYSIS OF COMPUTER VISION METHODS FOR RECOGNISING SOLAR PANEL DEFECTS (REVIEW)
Venue: Известия Южного федерального университета. Технические науки
Abstract: In today's world, where environmental problems are becoming more and more urgent, the searchfor alternative energy sources is becoming a priority. One of the most promising areas is solar energy.Solar energy is a renewable energy source, which makes it attractive for use in various areas, includingpower generation, heating and cooling of buildings, and transport. The development of solar energy cancontribute to solving a number of environmental problems such as pollution and climate change. However,solar panel equipment is subject to various types of defects and contamination. Defects can adverselyaffect the performance and efficiency of solar panels, so their detection is critical to improve the reliabilityand durability of photovoltaic power generation systems. Effective fault finding can minimise energy losses,improve system reliability and equipment life, and reduce maintenance costs. In addition, improvedperformance of electrical equipment contributes to the sustainable development of alternative energy, thusreducing dependence on conventional energy sources and reducing greenhouse gas emissions. The paperpresents an overview of existing methods for detecting various solar panel faults using computer vision and deep learning techniques. Infrared thermography (IR), electroluminescence (EL) imaging, or visiblespectrum imaging can be used to find the faults. This paper includes an analysis of the advantages anddisadvantages of existing methods for finding defects and contamination in solar panels, discusses thefactors affecting their performance, and presents conclusions for possible future research in this area.

Title: Computer Vision for Smart Energy Systems: A Review on Deep Learning Approaches for Solar Panel Fault Detection
Venue: International Conference on Wireless and Telematics (ICWT)
Abstract: Photovoltaic (PV) systems are susceptible to various environmental and operational stressors that can lead to visual faults such as hotspots, cracks, delamination, corrosion, and junction box failure ultimately affecting system performance and reliability. Visual inspection, supported by imaging techniques such as standard imaging, electroluminescence (EL), infrared thermography (IR), photoluminescence (PL), provides a more scalable and efficient alternative to traditional manual methods on-site electrical testing. In recent years, deep learning (DL) techniques, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), autoencoders, transfer learning, and hybrid models have shown promising results in automatically detecting and classifying PV faults across various image modalities. This article presents a focused survey of recent deep learning approaches for visual PV fault detection, emphasizing their integration within smart energy systems. Beyond summarizing state-of-the-art models and challenges such as data scarcity and generalization, this work highlights emerging trends like multimodal learning and self-supervised strategies as critical enablers for next-generation, scalable PV monitoring solutions.

Title: Review for "Unsupervised and Few-Shot Segmentation in Photovoltaic Electroluminescence Images for Defects Detection via a Novel Enhanced Iterative Autoencoder with Simple Implementation"
Review for "Unsupervised and Few-Shot Segmentation in Photovoltaic Electroluminescence Images for Defects Detection via a Novel Enhanced Iterative Autoencoder with Simple Implementation"
Review for "Unsupervised and Few-Shot Segmentation in Photovoltaic Electroluminescence Images for Defects Detection via a Novel Enhanced Iterative Autoencoder with Simple Implementation"
Recent advances in deep learning for aircraft surface defect detection: a comprehensive survey
Abstract: Abstract Aircraft surface inspection is a critical component of aviation safety, yet conventional inspection procedures remain labor-intensive, time-consuming, and susceptible to human error. Recent advances in unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) imaging and deep learning have created new opportunities for automated detection of cracks, corrosion, dents, paint defects, and other surface anomalies. This survey reviews recent developments in aircraft surface defect detection from 2019 to 2026, tracing the evolution of the field from early CNN-based approaches and geometric measurement techniques to modern one-stage detectors, segmentation frameworks, transformer-based and multi-modal architectures, lightweight hybrid models, and UAV-integrated inspection systems. A taxonomy is presented to organize the literature according to architectural characteristics, deployment objectives, and inspection workflows. Emerging paradigms, including vision foundation models, label-efficient learning, and data-centric approaches based on generative synthetic data, are also examined in relation to their potential for aircraft inspection.
